rationale: Mechanical rooms contain high-voltage electrical, high-pressure piping, and moving machinery, requiring limited access for safety and security.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: Heavy equipment like chillers, boilers, and large air handlers impose significant dead loads on the structure, often requiring reinforced slabs and larger structural members.

name: Sufficient maintenance clearance
rationale: Building codes and equipment manufacturer requirements mandate minimum clearances around mechanical equipment for service, repair, and replacement access.

name: Improved water pressure reliability
rationale: Water supply systems must maintain adequate and consistent pressure to meet demand across all fixtures and floors; this is a core hydraulic design requirement.

name: Reduced risk of contamination
rationale: Backflow prevention, pipe material selection, and system isolation are driven by the need to prevent contamination of potable water — a fundamental public health constraint.

name: Minimised water wastage
rationale: Codes and sustainability goals push for leak detection, pressure regulation, and efficient fixture sizing to reduce water loss.

name: Expanded capacity for peak demand
rationale: Storage tank sizing, pipe diameters, and pump selection must accommodate peak hourly demand and fire flow requirements, not just average usage.

name: adequate drainage capacity
rationale: Drainage and vent systems must provide sufficient hydraulic capacity to handle peak wastewater and stormwater flows, preventing backups and overflows.

name: reduced clogging risk
rationale: Blockages from debris, grease, or sediment reduce system functionality; design seeks to minimise obstructions through proper sizing, slope, and cleanout access.

name: improved venting performance
rationale: Adequate venting maintains trap seals and prevents siphoning or pressurisation issues; improved vent design ensures reliable air flow to balance pressure fluctuations.

name: minimised water infiltration into vent pipes
rationale: Vent pipes should remain dry to function properly; water ingress from rain or condensation impairs vent performance and can cause corrosion or freezing.

name: Improved water efficiency
rationale: Water conservation standards and green building certifications (e.g., LEED) drive demand for plumbing fixtures with higher efficiency, such as low-flow toilets, faucets, and showerheads.

name: Reduced water consumption
rationale: Regulatory codes and environmental goals pressure plumbing fixtures to minimise water usage per cycle or per use, affecting design choices like flow rates and flush volumes.

name: Enhanced durability and reliability
rationale: Building owners and facility managers demand fixtures that withstand frequent use, corrosion, and wear, driving material and construction choices toward more robust solutions.

name: Restricted installation footprint
rationale: Space constraints in building layouts, especially in multi-unit residential or commercial buildings, limit the physical size and mounting requirements of plumbing fixtures.

name: Increased hot water capacity
rationale: Building codes and user demand drive a need for sufficient hot water supply; larger or more efficient water heaters increase available capacity.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency regulations (e.g., ASHRAE, IECC) and operational cost goals push water heater designs toward lower energy use through better insulation, heat pump technology, or solar integration.

name: Reduced storage volume
rationale: Space constraints in mechanical rooms or residential utility closets push toward smaller or tankless water heater configurations.

name: reduced pressure drop across valves
rationale: Valves inherently create resistance to flow; minimising pressure drop is a standard design objective to maintain system efficiency.

name: improved sealing/leakage prevention
rationale: Valves must provide reliable shut-off and sealing to prevent leakage; enhanced sealing performance is a fundamental design pressure.

name: reduced cost of valves
rationale: Cost constraints typically push toward more economical valve selections without sacrificing critical performance.

name: adequate flow control precision
rationale: Valves are often required to provide accurate throttling or modulation of flow; sufficient control precision is a key design requirement.

name: higher flow rate
rationale: Pumps must deliver sufficient flow to meet system demand; inadequate flow rate is a common design pressure pushing toward larger or more capable pumps.

name: higher pressure head
rationale: Pumps must overcome system friction and elevation differences; required discharge pressure drives pump sizing and selection.

name: reduced energy consumption
rationale: Pump efficiency and operational cost pressures push toward minimising power draw, influencing motor sizing, variable speed drives, and pump selection.

name: reduced lifecycle cost
rationale: Capital and maintenance cost constraints influence pump material choice, redundancy configuration, and technology selection.

name: adequate reliability
rationale: Pumps in critical services require redundancy and robust design to ensure continuous operation; reliability is a key design driver.

name: Improved backflow protection
rationale: Backflow prevention devices must provide adequate sealing and check-valve reliability to prevent contamination of potable water supplies from reverse flow. This pressure pushes for higher-quality, better-sealing, and more reliable devices to meet code requirements and public health standards.

name: Reduced pressure loss across device
rationale: Backflow prevention assemblies (e.g., reduced pressure zone devices, double check valves) introduce hydraulic head loss. Design pressures exist to minimise this pressure drop to maintain adequate flow and pressure downstream in the water distribution system.

name: Reduced installation footprint
rationale: These devices are often installed in tight mechanical rooms, valve pits, or property line enclosures. There is a practical pressure to keep the assembly compact to fit within available space and allow for maintenance access.

name: higher gas supply pressure
rationale: Gas utility companies often supply natural gas at a specific pressure range; the piping system must be designed to handle the incoming supply pressure from the utility main, which is a fundamental engineering design parameter.

name: reduced pressure drop across piping
rationale: To ensure adequate gas flow to all connected appliances, the piping system design must minimise pressure losses due to friction and fittings, which is a standard engineering requirement for gas distribution systems.

name: restricted maximum allowable operating pressure
rationale: Building codes and safety regulations impose a maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP) for natural gas piping inside buildings (typically <5 psi in many jurisdictions), constraining the design pressure to prevent over-pressurisation hazards.

name: adequate pressure rating for components
rationale: All piping components (valves, fittings, regulators) must have a pressure rating sufficient to withstand the maximum operating pressure plus a safety margin, as required by engineering standards like ASME B31.8.

name: Increased system reliability and redundancy
rationale: Medical gas systems (oxygen, nitrous oxide, medical air, vacuum) are life-critical; codes and standards (NFPA 99, HTM 02-01) mandate redundant supply sources, alarms, and backup to ensure uninterrupted patient care.

name: Reduced risk of cross-contamination
rationale: Cross-connection between different gas types or with non-medical gases can cause patient harm or death; strict zoning, colour-coding, and dedicated piping prevent this.

name: Reduced system leakage
rationale: Leaks in medical gas piping waste expensive gases (e.g., heliox, nitric oxide) and compromise system pressure; brazed joints, pressure testing, and continuous monitoring minimise leakage.

name: higher water pressure
rationale: Fire standpipe systems require adequate water pressure at the most hydraulically remote outlet to meet fire flow demands per NFPA 14; insufficient pressure renders the system ineffective for firefighting.

name: reduced obstruction risk
rationale: Standpipe risers and hose connections must be kept clear of obstructions, debris, and blockages to ensure reliable water delivery; obstructions reduce flow and compromise firefighting operations.

name: minimised corrosion and scaling
rationale: Internal corrosion and mineral scaling over time can reduce pipe diameter and increase friction loss, lowering available pressure and flow at hose outlets; material selection and water treatment aim to minimise this.

name: Improved current carrying capacity
rationale: Conductor & cable systems are designed to carry electrical current; increasing ampacity (current-carrying capacity) is a fundamental design pressure driven by load requirements and thermal limits.

name: Reduced electrical resistance
rationale: Lower resistance reduces I²R losses and heat generation, improving efficiency and safety; this drives material selection (e.g., copper vs. aluminium) and cross-sectional design.

name: Minimised voltage drop
rationale: Voltage drop over cable length must be limited to ensure proper equipment operation, influencing conductor sizing and length constraints.

name: Adequate insulation withstand
rationale: Cables must have sufficient insulation to withstand operating voltage, fault conditions, and environmental stresses without breakdown, driving insulation material and thickness choices.

name: Increased protection from environmental exposure
rationale: Conduit & raceway systems must withstand moisture, corrosion, temperature extremes, and physical impact, creating pressure for increased protective ratings (e.g., NEMA/IP ratings) to ensure long-term reliability.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints drive pressure to minimise material costs (e.g., choosing lighter-gauge or non-metallic conduit) and simplify labour-intensive routing and supports.

name: Adequate cable fill capacity
rationale: NEC and other codes mandate maximum cable fill percentages to prevent overheating and permit proper pulling, exerting pressure for sufficient cross-sectional area or larger raceway sizes.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Conduit runs and junction boxes should be placed to allow future cable pulls, inspections, and modifications, creating pressure for accessible routing and adequate pull points.

name: Reduced electromagnetic interference
rationale: In sensitive installations, metallic conduit is used to shield cables from EMI, creating pressure to minimise interference by specifying bonded/grounded metal raceways.

name: greater cable capacity
rationale: Cable trays and ladder systems must accommodate increasing numbers of cables (e.g., power, data, control) as building systems expand. There is a persistent engineering demand for greater cable fill capacity to avoid overcrowding and ensure future-proofing.

name: reduced material weight
rationale: Structural and installation constraints often push toward lighter-weight tray/ladder materials (e.g., aluminum instead of steel) to ease mounting on overhead supports, catwalks, or wall brackets, and to reduce overall structural load.

name: improved cable segregation
rationale: Coding and safety requirements demand physical separation of power, data, and control cables to minimise electromagnetic interference and fire risk, driving the design of trays with dividers, deeper side rails, or multiple tiers.

name: Increased capacity
rationale: As electrical load grows in a building, the sub-distribution board must have sufficient breaker slots and busbar rating to accommodate additional circuits. This is a standard electrical engineering design pressure.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in electrical rooms, risers, or corridors often push designers to select more compact sub-distribution boards to fit within allocated wall space or enclosures.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget limitations drive selection of a sub-distribution board with the minimum acceptable component quality and number of ways, avoiding oversizing or premium features.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Regulatory codes (e.g., IEC 61439, BS 7671, NEC) mandate specific enclosure ratings, earth leakage protection, and accessible clearances for sub-distribution boards to ensure safe operation.

name: Adequate electrical capacity
rationale: Main Switchboard must have sufficient electrical capacity (ampacity, fault rating) to handle the connected loads and fault currents without overheating or failing.

name: Sufficient physical space and ventilation
rationale: The switchboard enclosure requires adequate clearance for safe operation, maintenance access, and heat dissipation from electrical components.

name: Reduced fire and arc-flash risk
rationale: Design pressures to minimise arc-flash incident energy and fire hazard through appropriate protection devices, segregation, and materials selection.

name: Restricted voltage drop
rationale: Voltage drop from the switchboard to downstream loads must be limited to within regulatory standards to ensure equipment performance.

name: Increased fault current interruption capacity
rationale: Circuit breakers and fuses must be rated to safely interrupt the maximum prospective fault current in the circuit. A higher interrupting capacity ensures the device can clear faults without arcing damage or explosion.

name: Reduced contact resistance
rationale: Lower contact resistance at breaker or fuse holder connections reduces I²R heating, preventing thermal degradation and ensuring reliable long-term operation.

name: Minimised arc flash energy
rationale: Design pressures exist to reduce arc flash incident energy through faster clearing times or current-limiting fuse designs, protecting personnel and equipment.

name: Adequate short-circuit withstand rating
rationale: The assembly must withstand the thermal and mechanical stresses of through-fault currents until the overcurrent device clears, requiring sufficient short-time withstand and peak withstand ratings.

name: improved monitoring coverage
rationale: Metering and monitoring equipment must provide adequate coverage of building systems (energy, water, HVAC performance) to enable data-driven decisions. There is a design pressure to increase the scope and granularity of monitored points.

name: higher data accuracy and resolution
rationale: Accurate, high-resolution data from meters and sensors is essential for performance verification, fault detection, and regulatory compliance, creating a pressure to specify more precise instruments.

name: redundant/backup sensing avoided
rationale: Cost pressures often push toward eliminating duplicate or backup sensors and meters unless required by criticality or code, limiting the overall instrumentation count.

name: limited deployment to critical points only
rationale: Budget and spatial constraints restrict metering and monitoring equipment to only the most critical systems or regulatory-required points, rather than comprehensive deployment.

name: Improved ground conductivity for fault current dissipation
rationale: Lower soil resistivity and lower resistance-to-ground improve fault current dissipation and system safety; this is a direct engineering requirement for grounding design.

name: Reduced step and touch potential hazards
rationale: Safety standards (e.g., IEEE 80) require limiting step and touch potentials to protect personnel; this drives design of conductor spacing, depth, and rod placement.

name: Adequate lightning discharge capacity
rationale: The grounding system must safely dissipate lightning strike currents without damaging equipment or causing dangerous voltage gradients; this influences conductor sizing and number of ground rods.

name: Minimised ground loop interference
rationale: Ground loops can introduce noise in sensitive equipment; proper single-point or star grounding topologies are used to minimise interference, especially in communication and control systems.

name: Improved lightning protection effectiveness
rationale: Safety regulations and standards (e.g., NFPA 780, IEC 62305) drive the need for effective lightning protection to prevent structural damage, fire, and electrical surges.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints push for minimising material and labour costs of rods, conductors, and grounding components, especially in large or complex buildings.

name: Reduced visual impact
rationale: Architectural concerns often demand that lightning rods, cables, and terminations be concealed or minimised to preserve the building's aesthetic appearance.

name: Improved detection sensitivity
rationale: Fire alarm systems benefit from more sensitive detection (e.g., smoke/heat sensors) to ensure early warning, which is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Minimizing nuisance alarms is a critical design pressure to maintain occupant trust and avoid unnecessary evacuations.

name: Increased reliability and redundancy
rationale: Fire alarm systems must have high reliability (backup power, fail-safe operation) to ensure functionality during emergencies.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure designers to keep system costs low while meeting code requirements.

name: Increased accessibility
rationale: Switches and socket outlets need to be placed at accessible heights and locations (e.g., avoiding obstructed areas) to comply with building accessibility codes and human ergonomics.

name: Reduced electrical hazard risk
rationale: Electrical safety codes (e.g., IP ratings, distance from water sources, earthing requirements) pressure designs to minimise shock and fire hazards associated with switch and outlet placement.

name: Sufficient quantity of outlets
rationale: Building regulations and modern occupancy demands require adequate numbers of socket outlets per room area to avoid over-reliance on extension cords and to meet functional needs.

name: Improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Switches and sockets are visible finish elements; interior design expectations pressure selection of styles, colours, and flush-mounting that blend with wall finishes and decor.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints pressure toward standardised, commonly available switches/sockets with simpler wiring configurations, rather than custom or premium alternatives.

name: Increased backup power capacity
rationale: UPS systems are designed to provide backup power; a design pressure for greater capacity (kVA/kW) or longer runtime ensures critical loads remain supported during outages.

name: Reduced footprint and space requirement
rationale: UPS equipment occupies valuable floor space in data centers or electrical rooms; there is a design pressure to minimise the physical footprint to allow more space for other systems or future expansion.

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: Modern UPS designs face pressure for higher efficiency (e.g., >96% in online mode) to reduce operational costs, cooling loads, and energy waste over the system's lifecycle.

name: Reduced total cost of ownership
rationale: Design decisions are pressured to minimise lifecycle costs including capital expenditure, installation, maintenance, and replacement battery costs.

name: Increased reliability requirement
rationale: Standby generators are designed to provide backup power during mains failure. The primary design pressure is the need for high reliability — the generator must start and run when called upon. This drives decisions on fuel type, automatic transfer switch specification, regular testing regimes, and redundant components.

name: Reduced emissions / noise limit
rationale: Standby generators are subject to environmental regulations limiting exhaust emissions (NOx, CO, particulates) and noise emissions, especially in urban or sensitive sites. This pressure acts to constrain engine choice, exhaust after-treatment, acoustic enclosure design, and siting decisions.

name: Reduced fuel consumption requirement
rationale: Although standby generators run infrequently, operational cost and fuel storage logistics create pressure to minimise fuel consumption during both standby/idle and runtime. This influences engine sizing, load management, and fuel system design choices.

name: Improved power reliability for HVAC Power Connection
rationale: HVAC systems require stable and reliable power to operate critical components like compressors, fans, and controls. There is an engineering pressure to improve the reliability of the power connection to prevent system downtime.

name: Reduced electrical load from HVAC Power Connection
rationale: Energy efficiency codes and sustainability goals create a pressure to minimise the electrical load drawn through the HVAC power connection, driving more efficient equipment and demand-side management.

name: Restricted electrical safety risk for HVAC Power Connection
rationale: Electrical codes and safety standards impose constraints on voltage, current, and grounding of HVAC power connections to prevent fire, shock, and arc-flash hazards.

name: Adequate current-carrying capacity
rationale: Busway and bus duct must have sufficient ampacity to handle the electrical load without overheating, which is a fundamental electrical engineering requirement.

name: Minimized voltage drop
rationale: Long busway runs or undersized conductors can cause excessive voltage drop, so design pressures push toward lower impedance routing and appropriate sizing.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Bus duct systems are capital-intensive; there is a constant design pressure to minimise material, labour, and footprint costs while meeting performance requirements.

name: Improved short-circuit withstand rating
rationale: Busway must withstand fault currents without damage; a higher short-circuit rating drives decisions on bracing, insulation class, and enclosure design.

name: Limited physical space for routing
rationale: Bus ducts run through ceiling plenums, shafts, and utility corridors where space is constrained by structure, HVAC, and other services, pressuring compact layouts.

name: Reduced heat generation from Transformers (Step-down)
rationale: Step-down transformers inherently dissipate heat due to copper and iron losses. There is a design pressure to minimise heat generation to reduce cooling loads and improve efficiency, typically addressed through higher-efficiency core materials or lower-loss winding designs.

name: Increased electrical load capacity of Transformers (Step-down)
rationale: Design pressure to provide adequate power capacity (kVA rating) to meet downstream demand. Transformers must be sized for peak loads with appropriate margin to avoid overloading.

name: Improved electrical safety clearances around Transformers (Step-down)
rationale: Step-down transformers operate at medium-to-low voltages but require safe working clearances, ventilation spacing, and arc-flash mitigation per electrical codes (NEC, IEC). Design pressure to increase clearance distances and physical protection.

name: Reduced footprint of Transformers (Step-down)
rationale: Space within electrical rooms is often constrained. There is a pressure to minimise transformer dimensions, particularly in retrofit or compact building designs, which can push toward dry-type or cast-coil transformers with smaller footprints.

name: Adequate space for electrical equipment
rationale: Electrical rooms must accommodate switchgear, panelboards, transformers, and other equipment with sufficient clearance for operation, maintenance, and code compliance (e.g., NEC 110.26 working clearances).

name: Reduced fire risk from electrical faults
rationale: Electrical rooms contain equipment that can arc-fault or overheat; design must minimize fire risk through proper ventilation, fire-rated construction, and arc-flash mitigation.

name: Maximized ventilation and heat dissipation
rationale: Electrical equipment generates heat; adequate ventilation or mechanical cooling is required to prevent overheating and equipment failure.

name: Limited access to authorized personnel only
rationale: Electrical rooms should be secured and access-restricted to prevent tampering, injury, or unauthorized use of the space.

name: Minimized moisture and water exposure
rationale: Moisture can cause short circuits, corrosion, and equipment damage; designs should locate electrical rooms away from water sources and include proper waterproofing.

name: Improved reliability for fire detection and activation
rationale: The control panel must reliably detect fire signals and activate suppression systems; higher reliability directly reduces failure risk in emergencies.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: False alarms cause disruption and desensitization; engineering design pressure exists to minimise nuisance alarms through better sensing and logic.

name: Enhanced integration with building fire alarm and sprinkler systems
rationale: The control panel must communicate effectively with other fire safety systems (alarm panels, sprinkler flow switches, notification appliances) for coordinated response.

name: Restricted physical access for tamper prevention
rationale: Unauthorized access to control panels can disable suppression systems; design limits access via locked cabinets, secure locations, and key controls.

name: Reduced pipe corrosion risk
rationale: Corrosion in fire suppression piping can lead to blockages, leaks, and system failure. Design decisions aim to minimise corrosion risk through material selection (e.g., galvanised steel, CPVC), protective coatings, and proper water treatment.

name: Optimised hydraulic performance
rationale: Fire suppression piping must deliver adequate flow and pressure to sprinkler heads or nozzles. Design decisions optimise pipe sizing, routing, and friction loss calculations to meet hydraulic demands under NFPA standards.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Cost pressures push toward minimising material quantities, simplifying routing, and selecting economical joining methods (e.g., grooved vs. welded connections) without compromising safety performance.

name: Restricted spatial footprint
rationale: Piping must fit within confined ceiling plenums, shafts, and chases alongside other building services (HVAC, electrical, plumbing), constraining pipe diameters and routing options.

name: Enhanced seismic resilience
rationale: In seismic zones, fire suppression piping requires flexible couplings, seismic bracing, and sway restraints to maintain integrity during earthquakes, as mandated by NFPA 13 and ASCE 7.

name: adequate water flow pressure
rationale: Sprinkler heads require sufficient water pressure and flow rate to properly distribute water during fire suppression. Inadequate pressure leads to poor coverage.

name: reduced obstruction clearance
rationale: Objects near sprinkler heads (e.g., storage, lighting, or ceiling features) can obstruct spray patterns. Building codes typically mandate minimum clearance distances to ensure unobstructed water distribution.

name: Sufficient agent storage capacity
rationale: The tank must hold enough suppression agent (e.g., water, foam, clean agent) to meet code-required discharge duration and flow rates for the protected hazard area.

name: Reduced tank footprint
rationale: Space constraints in mechanical rooms or equipment areas create pressure to minimise the physical size and footprint of the storage tank.

name: Higher pressure rating
rationale: For compressed gas or pressurised agent systems (e.g., nitrogen-pressurised clean agent), the tank must withstand regulated storage pressures to ensure proper agent delivery.

name: Reduced material corrosion risk
rationale: Tank material selection and protective coatings must minimise corrosion from stored agents (especially water-based solutions) to maintain structural integrity over the service life.

name: Improved water supply pressure
rationale: Dry pipe valves require sufficient water supply pressure to operate correctly — they rely on differential pressure to hold the clapper closed; inadequate supply pressure can cause false tripping or failure to open when needed.

name: Reduced air pressure in system piping
rationale: The dry pipe valve is designed to trip when air pressure in the system piping drops (due to sprinkler activation); lower supervised air pressure reduces the force holding the clapper closed, enabling the valve to open and admit water.

name: Reduced contamination/debris in water supply
rationale: Sediment, debris, or scale in the water supply can interfere with the sealing surfaces or moving parts of a dry pipe valve, causing leakage or failure to trip.

name: Improved priming water level quality
rationale: Many dry pipe valves use a small amount of priming water above the clapper to maintain a seal; correct and clean priming water helps prevent air loss and corrosion at the seat.

name: Increased water pressure reliability
rationale: The zone valve must reliably handle and distribute water at adequate pressure to serve downstream sprinkler heads; insufficient pressure compromises fire suppression effectiveness.

name: Reduced risk of unintended closure
rationale: The valve must not inadvertently close or restrict flow during a fire event; design must prevent accidental or premature shutoff that would disable suppression in the zone.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Valve internals and body exposed to water over long periods require enhanced corrosion resistance to maintain long-term operational reliability and prevent blockage or leakage.

name: Lower pressure drop across valve
rationale: Excessive pressure loss through the zone valve reduces available pressure at sprinkler heads; the valve design should minimise flow resistance to maintain system hydraulic performance.

name: reduced agent discharge time
rationale: Clean agent suppression systems must discharge within a specified time window (typically 10 seconds) to achieve correct concentration before fire damage occurs, driving design toward reduced discharge time.

name: higher agent concentration for extinguishment
rationale: The system must deliver and maintain a sufficient concentration of clean agent (e.g., FM-200, Novec 1230, or inert gas) to extinguish the fire, driving design toward higher concentration levels.

name: minimised enclosure leakage
rationale: To maintain extinguishing concentration for the required hold time, leakage from the protected enclosure must be kept to a minimum, affecting both the suppression system design and enclosure sealing.

name: Improved fire suppression coverage
rationale: Water mist systems need to achieve adequate coverage area and droplet distribution to effectively suppress fire; this drives design decisions around nozzle placement, pressure rating, and system layout.

name: Reduced water damage risk
rationale: A key advantage of water mist over traditional sprinklers is using less water, minimising collateral water damage; this pressure influences nozzle design, droplet size requirements, and activation thresholds.

name: Higher system pressure requirements
rationale: Effective water mist generation requires high operating pressures (typically 50-120 bar for single-fluid systems); this drives pump selection, pipe material/rating, and energy supply decisions.

name: Restricted space for system components
rationale: Water mist system components (high-pressure pumps, storage tanks, control panels) compete for building space; this constrains equipment sizing, layout integration, and may push toward more compact configurations.

name: improved fire suppression effectiveness
rationale: Foam suppression systems are designed to extinguish flammable liquid fires by smothering and cooling. The primary design pressure is to maximize the system's ability to rapidly suppress fires, which drives decisions on foam concentrate type, proportioning rate, discharge density, and system layout.

name: reduced system cost
rationale: Like all building systems, there is pressure to minimise capital and maintenance costs. This affects decisions on tank sizing, pump selection, piping material, and choice between balanced-pressure proportioning versus simpler but less precise methods.

name: limited environmental impact of foam discharge
rationale: Modern regulations and sustainability goals create pressure to use fluorine-free (PFAS-free) foam concentrates and to minimise the volume of foam discharged during testing or accidental activation. This affects concentrate selection, containment design, and testing protocols.

name: sufficient foam concentrate storage capacity
rationale: Codes and standards (e.g., NFPA 11) require a minimum foam concentrate supply duration for the largest single fire scenario. This pressure drives decisions on tank volume, reserve supply provisions, and space allocation for storage.

name: adequate water pressure
rationale: Standpipe systems require adequate water pressure to deliver firefighting water to upper floors of a building. Building codes and fire engineering standards mandate minimum pressure at the most hydraulically remote outlet.

name: minimised pressure loss
rationale: Pressure losses due to friction, elevation changes, and fittings must be minimised to ensure the standpipe system can deliver required flow at sufficient residual pressure at the highest or most remote hose connection.

name: sufficient code compliance
rationale: Standpipe systems must comply with relevant building and fire codes (e.g., NFPA 14, IBC) which dictate pipe sizing, valve placement, hose connection locations, and testing requirements.

name: improved fire suppression effectiveness
rationale: The primary function of a kitchen hood suppression system is to extinguish grease fires rapidly. There is a consistent engineering pressure to improve the effectiveness (coverage, agent discharge rate, detection sensitivity) of these systems to meet fire codes and reduce property damage risk.

name: reduced false discharge incidents
rationale: False discharges of suppression agent (e.g., wet chemical) cause costly kitchen shutdowns, cleanup, and food spoilage. There is a design pressure to minimise nuisance trips by improving detection logic and sensor placement.

name: adequate suppression agent capacity
rationale: Codes (e.g., NFPA 96, UL 300) mandate specific agent quantities to cover all protected appliances and ductwork. There is a pressure to ensure sufficient agent is stored and properly distributed for the full design hazard.

name: restricted manual tampering risk
rationale: Kitchen staff may accidentally or intentionally disable or obstruct the suppression system (e.g., blocking nozzles, turning off gas line). There is a design pressure to incorporate tamper-resistant features and clear signage to prevent such actions.

name: Sufficient water flow pressure
rationale: Fire hydrant connections must maintain adequate water pressure to support firefighting operations; low pressure can render the hydrant ineffective in emergencies.

name: Restricted risk of physical damage
rationale: Fire hydrant connections are vulnerable to impact from vehicles or debris; damage must be minimised to ensure operational readiness.

name: Reduced obstruction around connection point
rationale: Clearance around the hydrant connection must be maintained for fire hose attachment; obstructions like landscaping or parking should be avoided.

name: Improved freeze protection
rationale: In cold climates, hydrant connections must be protected against freezing to remain functional during winter fire events.

name: higher water pressure
rationale: Fire pumps must produce adequate pressure to overcome friction losses and elevation differences in the fire sprinkler system, ensuring water reaches the highest or most remote sprinkler heads at required flow rates.

name: reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints typically push toward selecting the smallest or simplest fire pump that meets code requirements, avoiding oversizing or unnecessary features.

name: adequate fire flow capacity
rationale: The fire pump must be sized to deliver the required flow (gpm/Lpm) based on the building's occupancy hazard classification and fire protection system demand as per NFPA 20.

name: reduced space footprint
rationale: Fire pump rooms compete for valuable building floor area; architects and owners often prefer compact pump configurations to minimize loss of usable space.

name: increased load capacity
rationale: Elevator cars must support greater passenger or freight loads, driving structural reinforcement and larger suspension systems.

name: reduced car weight
rationale: Lighter car materials (e.g., aluminium, composites) reduce energy consumption and stress on ropes and motors, a common engineering goal.

name: improved safety compliance
rationale: Building codes and safety standards demand features like emergency brakes, door interlocks, and overload sensors, which directly shape elevator car design.

name: reduced interior noise and vibration
rationale: Passenger comfort requirements drive design decisions for sound dampening, rail alignment, and vibration isolation within the car.

name: maximised usable interior space
rationale: Architectural and user requirements push for efficient floor-plan layouts within the car to accommodate more passengers or cargo.

name: Increased vertical load capacity
rationale: Hoistway shafts must structurally support the weight of elevator cars, counterweights, guide rails, and equipment, requiring adequate vertical load-bearing capacity in the supporting structure.

name: Improved fire-rating containment
rationale: Building codes require hoistway shafts to have fire-resistance-rated enclosures to prevent vertical fire and smoke spread between floors, demanding enhanced fire-rated construction.

name: Reduced structural vibration transfer
rationale: Vibrations from elevator operation through the hoistway must be minimised to prevent noise and structural disturbance to adjacent occupied spaces.

name: Sufficient clear internal dimensions
rationale: Hoistway requires adequate cross-sectional clear dimensions to accommodate the elevator car, counterweight, guide rails, and required clearances per elevator code standards.

name: increased structural integrity
rationale: Guide rails must withstand impact loads from vehicles or moving equipment, requiring sufficient structural strength to prevent failure.

name: reduced lateral deflection
rationale: Guide rails need to limit lateral movement under load to maintain their guiding function and prevent derailment or misalignment.

name: adequate corrosion resistance
rationale: Guide rails exposed to environmental conditions require sufficient corrosion protection to maintain long-term performance and safety.

name: minimised wear rate
rationale: Guide rails experience friction from contact with moving components; lower wear rates extend service life and maintain precision.

name: Reduced space requirement for machine room
rationale: Roomless controllers are designed to eliminate the need for a separate machine room, directly reducing space demands on the building.

name: Increased electrical capacity demand
rationale: Roomless elevator controllers house all drive and control electronics within the hoistway or adjacent to the shaft, requiring adequate electrical supply and heat dissipation provisions.

name: Improved accessibility and maintenance access
rationale: Despite being roomless, the controller still needs accessible location for servicing, which pressures design to provide safe maintenance provisions (clearance, lighting, lockable disconnects).

name: Increased load capacity
rationale: Traction/hydraulic systems in building contexts (e.g., elevators, lifts, hydraulic platforms) are designed to bear specific loads. There is a persistent engineering pressure to increase load capacity to accommodate heavier equipment, more passengers, or greater material handling requirements.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Hydraulic systems and traction drives consume significant energy. Building codes and sustainability goals create a design pressure to reduce energy consumption through more efficient pumps, motors, or regenerative systems.

name: Higher reliability
rationale: As a critical building component for vertical transportation or mechanical actuation, there is a strong design pressure for higher reliability to avoid downtime, safety hazards, and maintenance disruptions.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Hydraulic systems in particular require regular fluid checks, filter changes, and leak management. There is a design pressure to reduce these maintenance demands through sealed systems, improved filtration, or dry-running components.

name: improved sealing pressure
rationale: Car door seals must resist water, dust, and noise intrusion. There is a persistent engineering pressure to improve sealing performance of car doors to enhance cabin comfort and durability.

name: reduced weight pressure
rationale: Car doors are significant contributors to overall vehicle weight. There is a continual design pressure to reduce door weight for fuel efficiency, emissions reduction, and handling improvements.

name: enhanced crash safety pressure
rationale: Car doors are critical for occupant protection in side-impact collisions. There is a strong regulatory and safety-driven pressure to enhance impact resistance, side intrusion beams, and energy absorption in door designs.

name: reduced manufacturing cost pressure
rationale: As high-volume components with complex assembly (inner panel, outer panel, latch, window regulator, wiring, trim), car doors face constant pressure to minimise production and assembly costs.

name: increased braking reliability
rationale: A safety brake/governor in an elevator or hoist system must reliably engage to prevent free-fall or overspeed; engineering standards drive a pressure toward higher fail-safe reliability and stronger braking force.

name: reduced response time
rationale: The governor must trigger the safety brake with minimal delay to arrest motion quickly; codes and performance requirements push for lower (faster) activation time.

name: eliminated unintended engagement
rationale: False or nuisance braking can cause sudden stoppages, passenger injury, or equipment damage; design pressures aim to prevent unwanted activation under normal operating conditions.

name: adequate buffers
rationale: Buffers (e.g., setbacks, buffer zones, interstitial spaces) are designed to provide separation, noise attenuation, or thermal transition. Engineering design pressures push for adequate or sufficient buffer dimensions to meet code requirements, acoustic performance, or energy performance targets.

name: reduced slack cable vibrations
rationale: Traveling cables in elevator systems experience sway and vibrations during car movement; minimizing slack and vibration is a standard engineering requirement to prevent entanglement and ensure reliable power/signal transmission.

name: increased cable flexibility
rationale: Traveling cables must flex repeatedly as the elevator car moves; greater flexibility (optimized bending radius) reduces stress on conductors and extends service life.

name: adequate cable length for full travel range
rationale: The traveling cable must be long enough to accommodate the full range of elevator car movement from the lowest to the highest landing, a fundamental kinematic requirement.

name: Enhanced visibility
rationale: Hall call fixtures (buttons/panels at elevator lobbies) need to be easily seen by users, so there is a design pressure to make them visually prominent through contrast, illumination, or size.

name: Reduced physical effort to operate
rationale: Hall call buttons must require minimal force to press, be reachable at accessible heights, and be operable by users with limited dexterity to comply with accessibility standards.

name: Improved tactile feedback
rationale: Hall call fixtures should provide clear tactile (and audible) feedback upon activation so that visually impaired users can confirm their call has been registered.

name: Reduced vandalism risk
rationale: Hall call fixtures in public areas are subject to potential abuse or vandalism; design pressures push toward flush, rugged, tamper-resistant construction.

name: improved positional accuracy
rationale: Position indicators (e.g., dials, digital readouts, needle gauges) in building systems benefit from greater accuracy to reduce reading errors and improve system monitoring.

name: reduced visual clutter
rationale: In architectural contexts, position indicators should be visually clear and not overly crowded with markings or unnecessary detail, to support quick and unambiguous reading.

name: Enhanced accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes (e.g., ADA, EN 81-40) require wheelchair lifts to provide barrier-free access. This drives design toward higher capacity, more reliable operation, and integration with accessible pathways.

name: Reduced space footprint
rationale: Platform lifts often serve existing buildings with limited space. A smaller footprint (shaft, platform size, pit depth) is pressured to fit within tight retrofits without sacrificing adjacent usable area.

name: Lower installation and maintenance cost
rationale: As a specialized accessibility device, cost pressures push toward simpler drive mechanisms (e.g., screw vs. hydraulic), standardized components, and reduced maintenance complexity.

name: Greater load capacity
rationale: The lift must accommodate standard wheelchair-plus-occupant loads (typically 250-500 kg). Codes and practical use drive toward adequate rated capacity, influencing structural design and motor sizing.

name: Sufficient grip surface on handrail
rationale: A moving handrail (e.g., on escalators or moving walkways) requires sufficient surface area and texture to allow users to maintain a secure grip, preventing slips and falls during motion.

name: Reduced handrail motion speed
rationale: To ensure user safety, the moving handrail's speed must be limited relative to the step/walkway speed to prevent users from losing balance or being pulled forward/backward.

name: Improved handrail-to-step synchronization
rationale: The moving handrail must maintain precise synchronization with the moving steps or walkway to prevent a dangerous lag or lead, which could cause tripping or loss of support.

name: Increased mechanical efficiency
rationale: The drive mechanism must efficiently transfer power to move the handrail, so design pressure exists to increase mechanical efficiency (reducing friction, improving gear/sprocket engagement) for reliable escalator/moving walk operation.

name: Reduced maintenance complexity
rationale: Handrail drive mechanisms are subject to wear and require periodic servicing; there is a design pressure to reduce maintenance complexity (fewer parts, easier access, simpler adjustment) to minimise downtime and lifecycle cost.

name: Improved durability and wear resistance
rationale: Components such as drive wheels, belts/chains, and bearings experience continuous friction and loading, creating pressure to improve durability and wear resistance for longer service intervals.

name: Reduced noise and vibration
rationale: Handrail drives can generate operational noise and vibration that affects user comfort; there is a design pressure to reduce noise and vibration through smoother profiles, damping, or precision alignment.

name: Enhanced synchronisation with step chain
rationale: The handrail speed must closely match the step or pallet speed to prevent drag or slack; this creates a design pressure for enhanced synchronisation accuracy between the handrail drive and the main drive system.

name: higher torque capacity
rationale: Drive motors and gearboxes must generate sufficient torque to overcome load demands, accelerate masses, and maintain motion under varying operational conditions. Higher torque capacity ensures the system can handle peak loads without stalling or overloading.

name: reduced mechanical losses
rationale: Friction, heat generation, and inefficiencies in gear meshing and motor windings reduce overall drivetrain efficiency. Minimising these losses improves energy efficiency, reduces thermal stress, and prolongs component life.

name: adequate thermal dissipation
rationale: Motors and gearboxes generate significant heat during operation. Sufficient cooling pathways, ventilation, or thermal management are necessary to prevent overheating, lubricant degradation, and insulation failure.

name: minimised vibration and noise
rationale: Unbalanced rotating masses, gear tooth meshing errors, and bearing anomalies produce vibration and acoustic noise. Reducing these improves operational smoothness, structural fatigue life, and acoustic comfort.

name: limited physical envelope
rationale: Space constraints within the building or machine layout often restrict the allowable size of the motor and gearbox assembly, driving demand for compact designs with high power density.

name: reduced backlash and play
rationale: In gear and chain drive systems, minimising backlash between sprockets and shafts improves precision, reduces wear, and avoids impact loading.

name: increased torque capacity
rationale: Drive shafts and sprockets must withstand torsional loads; higher torque capacity ensures reliable power transmission without failure.

name: adequate shaft hardness and wear resistance
rationale: Sprockets and shafts experience sliding/rolling contact; sufficient surface hardness extends service life and maintains alignment under load.

name: Improved load-bearing capacity
rationale: The landing platform must support the static and dynamic loads from aircraft landings, personnel movement, and equipment. Increased structural capacity ensures safety and prevents collapse under operational loads.

name: Reduced surface degradation
rationale: The platform surface is exposed to weather, repeated impact, and potential chemical exposure (fuel, hydraulic fluids). Minimising wear, corrosion, and surface cracking extends service life and maintains safe landing conditions.

name: Enhanced drainage performance
rationale: Effective water drainage is critical to prevent ponding, ice formation, and hydroplaning risks on landing surfaces. Improved slope design and drainage systems reduce standing water and improve operational safety.

name: Restricted vertical deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection during landing impacts can damage the platform structure or cause instability. Limiting deflection through stiffness design ensures structural integrity and safe landings.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: As a side beam in a truss stringer system, this component must bear significant tensile/compressive loads. Engineering principles dictate the side beam requires sufficient strength and stiffness to transfer loads between truss nodes without buckling or excessive deflection.

name: Reduced lateral deflection
rationale: Side beams in truss systems must limit out-of-plane buckling and lateral-torsional buckling under load. Restricting lateral deflection is critical for structural stability and load path integrity.

name: Optimised material usage
rationale: The side beam cross-section and material grade should be optimised to achieve required strength-to-weight ratio, avoiding over-design while ensuring structural adequacy for its span and connection detailing.

name: Improved reliability of safety sensor readings
rationale: Safety sensors must produce reliable, accurate readings to ensure safe system operation; higher reliability reduces false positives/negatives.

name: Reduced response time of safety switches
rationale: Safety switches need to actuate quickly in fault conditions to prevent injury or damage; faster response time is a core safety requirement.

name: Increased coverage of monitored safety zones
rationale: Comprehensive monitoring of all relevant areas/personnel zones is needed to eliminate blind spots where hazards could go undetected.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Excessive false alarms from safety sensors lead to operator desensitisation and unnecessary system downtime, undermining trust in the safety system.

name: increased accessibility
rationale: Emergency stop switches must be easily reachable and visible in emergency situations; accessibility is a key design pressure (e.g., OSHA, ISO 13850 standards).

name: reduced accidental actuation
rationale: Emergency stops must be designed to prevent unintended activation (e.g., shrouded buttons, twist-to-release mechanisms, or two-step actuation per IEC 60947-5-5 and ISO 13850).

name: higher reliability
rationale: The switch must maintain guaranteed operation under fault conditions including mechanical failure, power loss, and environmental stress, requiring fail-safe design principles.

name: limited physical footprint
rationale: The switch must fit within available panel space or equipment layout without obstructing other controls, while still being prominent enough to locate quickly.

name: Optimized equipment density
rationale: Machine rooms benefit from higher equipment density to consolidate mechanical/electrical systems into a smaller footprint, improving space efficiency and reducing circulation waste.

name: Reduced heat gain
rationale: Machine rooms house equipment that generates heat; minimizing heat gain from external sources (solar, adjacent spaces) is critical to maintaining equipment performance and preventing overheating.

name: Improved accessibility for maintenance
rationale: Building codes and operational requirements demand adequate clearance around equipment for servicing, repair, and replacement, driving the need for accessible layouts within integrated machine rooms.

name: Increased visibility
rationale: Step demarcation lighting must be bright enough to clearly reveal the leading edge of each step, preventing trips and falls. This is a core safety and accessibility requirement.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Glare from step lighting can disorient users, especially those with visual impairments. The fixture design and light distribution must minimise direct glare into eyes.

name: Improved uniformity
rationale: Patchy or uneven illumination along the step edge can create misleading visual cues. Uniform light distribution along the tread edge is needed for consistent step detection.

name: increased pit depth
rationale: An escalator pit must be deep enough to accommodate the escalator machinery, truss endpoint, and safety clearances. Greater depth ensures proper installation and compliance with building codes.

name: reduced pit footprint
rationale: Space constraints in building floor plates often demand a compact escalator pit to maximise usable floor area and minimise structural disruption.

name: adequate sump drainage
rationale: Escalator pits typically require a sump pump or drainage system to prevent water accumulation, which can damage machinery and create safety hazards.

name: Greater structural strength for railing
rationale: As a fixed railing adjacent to an escalator, it must withstand lateral loads from users leaning or pushing against it, as well as potential impact loads from people or objects. Building codes typically require handrails/guardrails on escalator sides to have adequate structural capacity.

name: Higher height requirement for fall prevention
rationale: Escalator-adjacent railings serve as fall protection barriers. Building codes and safety standards specify minimum railing heights (typically 42 inches in commercial settings) to prevent people from falling over the side of the escalator.

name: Reduced baluster spacing for child safety
rationale: To prevent children from slipping through or getting stuck, building codes limit the spacing between railing balusters (typically 4 inches maximum) for railings near escalators and other elevated areas.

name: Eliminated sharp edges on railing surface
rationale: Railings adjacent to escalators must have smooth, rounded surfaces without sharp protrusions to prevent injury to passengers' hands and clothing as they move past the railing on the escalator.

name: increased passenger throughput capacity
rationale: Travelators are designed to move people horizontally or on slight inclines. A key design pressure is to increase throughput capacity (people per hour) to manage peak traffic flows in transport hubs, airports, and shopping centres efficiently.

name: improved safety compliance
rationale: Moving walks must meet stringent safety standards (e.g., handrail speed synchronization, emergency stop mechanisms, anti-slip surfaces). There is a persistent pressure to improve safety features to prevent accidents and comply with regulations such as EN 115.

name: reduced energy consumption
rationale: Sustainability goals and operational cost pressures drive the need to reduce energy consumption of travelators, through features like standby slow modes, regenerative drives, and lightweight materials.

name: minimised physical footprint
rationale: Travelators must fit within constrained architectural spaces (e.g., between airport gates, retail corridors). There is a design pressure to minimise the structural footprint and pit depth to allow integration without major structural alterations.

name: reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: To minimise downtime and operational disruption in high-traffic environments, there is pressure to design travelators with durable components and systems that require less frequent maintenance.

name: improved vertical circulation efficiency
rationale: A spiral escalator must provide adequate vertical transport in a compact footprint; there is a design pressure to increase throughput and reduce waiting times.

name: reduced mechanical complexity
rationale: Spiral escalators involve complex curved tracks and chain mechanisms; there is a strong pressure to minimise mechanical complexity for reliability and cost.

name: enhanced passenger safety
rationale: Curved escalator geometry creates unique pinch points and balance challenges; codes and liability drive a pressure for greater safety features.

name: restricted spatial footprint
rationale: Spiral escalators are often chosen when a straight run is impossible due to limited floor area; the design pressure is to keep the footprint as small as possible.

name: higher structural load capacity
rationale: The self-supporting spiral frame must bear both vertical and torsional loads from passengers and machinery, demanding greater structural strength.

name: Increased durability and structural capacity
rationale: As a heavy-duty/metro escalator, the system must withstand high traffic volumes, heavy loads, and continuous operation in transit environments, requiring greater structural strength, more robust mechanical components, and enhanced wear resistance compared to standard escalators.

name: Reduced downtime for maintenance
rationale: Metro escalators operate in critical 24/7 transit environments where breakdowns cause major disruption, creating pressure to minimise maintenance frequency and duration through robust design, modular components, and integrated diagnostics.

name: Higher safety compliance requirements
rationale: Public transit escalators must meet stringent safety codes for public use, including emergency stops, step demarcation, handrail speed synchronisation, and fire resistance, driving pressure for enhanced safety features.

name: Limited space envelope for installation
rationale: Existing metro stations often have constrained structural geometry, limiting the available space for escalator installation and requiring compact drive systems and optimised truss designs within fixed architectural boundaries.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy-efficient operation is increasingly required for metro systems to meet sustainability targets and reduce operational costs, creating pressure for regenerative drives, standby modes, and efficient motor systems.

name: Increased passenger throughput capacity
rationale: A funicular-style escalator must handle bidirectional passenger flow on a steep incline; design must ensure sufficient capacity to avoid bottlenecks, especially at peak times in transit-oriented buildings.

name: Reduced mechanical complexity and maintenance needs
rationale: The unique inclined mechanism (combining elevator and escalator principles) tends to have higher maintenance demands; design pressure pushes toward simpler, more reliable drive systems and fewer moving parts.

name: Enhanced passenger safety and emergency braking
rationale: Steep incline operation introduces additional fall and rollback risks; redundant braking, emergency stops, and fail-safe mechanisms are critical design requirements beyond those of standard elevators or escalators.

name: Reduced energy consumption per passenger trip
rationale: Continuous operation on an incline demands significant energy; counterbalancing (funicular principle) and regenerative drive systems are design pressures to lower operational energy use.

name: Adequate structural integration with building architecture
rationale: The inclined path often cuts through multiple floor levels and requires custom structural supports, shafts, and alignments that must be seamlessly integrated into the building's overall structural and spatial design.

name: optimised energy efficiency
rationale: Lighting fixtures are designed to maximise energy efficiency (lumens per watt), influencing selection of LED vs. incandescent technology, driver design, and fixture optics.

name: reduced heat output
rationale: Lighting fixtures generate waste heat; minimising heat output is a design pressure to prevent overheating, reduce cooling loads, and prolong LED lifespan.

name: adequate illuminance level
rationale: Lighting fixtures must provide sufficient light levels (lux) for the intended task or space, per lighting standards (e.g., IES, building codes), driving fixture count, placement, and lumen output.

name: minimised glare
rationale: Glare from lighting fixtures causes visual discomfort; design pressures include shielding, diffusers, and cutoff angles to limit direct glare and reflected glare.

name: reduced embodied carbon
rationale: Increasing emphasis on sustainable design pressures fixture manufacturers to lower embodied carbon through material choices (e.g., recycled aluminium, bio-based plastics) and manufacturing processes.

name: Improved light quality
rationale: Building design decisions often push for higher colour rendering index (CRI), better colour temperature tunability, and reduced flicker from light sources to improve visual comfort and task performance.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes (e.g., ASHRAE, IECC) and sustainability goals drive selection of more efficient light sources (LED over incandescent, higher lumens-per-watt) and lower wattage fixtures to minimise operational energy use.

name: Reduced heat output
rationale: Lamps generate heat that adds to cooling loads; selecting sources with lower heat emission (e.g., LEDs vs. halogen/incandescent) is a common design pressure to reduce HVAC demand.

name: Increased lifespan
rationale: Longer-rated-life lamps (e.g., LED vs. fluorescent vs. incandescent) reduce maintenance costs and replacement frequency, a standard specification criterion in building design.

name: Improved controllability
rationale: Demand for dimming, colour tuning, and integration with occupancy/daylight sensors creates a design pressure toward lamps compatible with advanced control systems.

name: Reduced size / form factor
rationale: Architectural integration often pressures toward compact, low-profile or miniaturised light sources to fit into tight ceiling plenums, coves, or decorative fixtures.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Lighting control systems are primarily designed to minimise unnecessary energy use through occupancy sensing, daylight harvesting, scheduling, and dimming, reducing overall electricity consumption.

name: Improved occupant comfort
rationale: Lighting control systems are configured to provide appropriate light levels for tasks, reduce glare, and maintain visual comfort, which is a core design pressure on control strategies.

name: Enhanced system responsiveness
rationale: There is a design pressure for faster and more accurate response to sensor inputs (occupancy, daylight) to avoid delays that annoy occupants or waste energy.

name: Reduced installation and maintenance complexity
rationale: Designers typically seek to minimise the number of components, wiring complexity, and commissioning effort for lighting control systems to lower first cost and ongoing maintenance.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Design pressures push for lighting switches to be placed at accessible heights and locations (e.g., ADA compliance, near entryways) to ensure ease of use for all occupants.

name: Reduced electrical hazard risk
rationale: Electrical safety codes and best practices drive the design of switches to minimize shock or fire risk through proper insulation, grounding, and placement away from moisture sources.

name: Improved energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Occupancy sensors are used to automate lighting and HVAC based on presence detection, directly improving building energy efficiency by reducing wasted energy in unoccupied spaces.

name: Reduced false triggering pressure
rationale: False triggers (e.g., from pets, moving curtains, or HVAC drafts) reduce reliability and user acceptance, so design pushes toward minimizing such erroneous detections.

name: Higher detection accuracy pressure
rationale: Accurate detection of human presence (distinguishing people from other heat sources or motion) is a core functional requirement for occupancy sensors.

name: Minimised installation cost pressure
rationale: Cost constraints in building systems push toward lower-cost sensor solutions, especially in large-scale deployments where many units are installed.

name: Improved daylight harvesting accuracy
rationale: Photocell sensors perform better with accurate calibration and proper placement, directly influencing the reliability of daylight-responsive lighting controls.

name: Reduced glare and visual discomfort
rationale: Photocell sensors help modulate electric lighting based on available daylight, but glare conditions can mislead the sensor. Reducing glare improves sensor reliability and occupant comfort.

name: Minimized false triggering from adjacent light sources
rationale: Photocells can be triggered by artificial light sources or reflections not representing true daylight, leading to incorrect dimming. Minimizing this improves system performance.

name: Optimized sensor placement relative to window/glare zones
rationale: Placement of the photocell relative to windows and daylight apertures is critical for accurate readings — poorly placed sensors do not represent the actual daylight level in the space.

name: Expanded integration with automated shading systems
rationale: Coordinating photocell readings with motorized blinds or shades enables holistic daylight management, which is a growing trend in advanced building controls.

name: Increased centralization of controls
rationale: In modern building design, lighting control functions are increasingly consolidated into centralized or smart panels, driving demand for more capable, centralized lighting control panels with digital interfaces and network connectivity.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in electrical rooms and the trend toward miniaturized electronic components create pressure to reduce the physical size of lighting control panels while maintaining functionality.

name: Greater integration with building automation systems
rationale: Lighting control panels are increasingly required to integrate with BMS/BAS protocols (e.g., BACnet, DALI, KNX), driving pressure for enhanced communication capabilities and interoperability features in the panel design.

name: Improved visibility during power failure
rationale: Emergency lighting must provide adequate illumination for safe egress during mains power loss; building codes (e.g., NFPA 101, IBC) mandate minimum illuminance levels and duration.

name: Reduced energy consumption during standby
rationale: Emergency lighting systems typically draw power for battery charging or inverter standby; minimizing standby power waste is a standard energy-efficiency goal and often required by codes like ASHRAE 90.1 or local green building regulations.

name: Minimised maintenance burden
rationale: Emergency lighting requires periodic testing, battery replacement, and bulb/LED replacement; design pressures push toward self-testing fixtures, longer-life batteries/LEDs, and centralized monitoring to reduce labour and cost.

name: increased visibility
rationale: Building codes and safety standards require exit signs to be highly visible during emergencies, including in smoke or power failure conditions. This drives decisions toward brighter illumination, larger typography, and strategic placement.

name: reduced energy consumption
rationale: Exit signs operate continuously (24/7), so there is a consistent design pressure to reduce their energy draw through LED technology, photoluminescent materials, or occupancy-based dimming when the space is unoccupied.

name: restricted placement locations
rationale: Building codes strictly limit where exit signs can be placed (e.g., above exit doors, along egress paths, at stairwell landings), constraining design freedom in favour of standardised, predictable locations.

name: improved battery backup reliability
rationale: Exit signs must remain illuminated during power outages, creating a pressure to enhance battery backup systems, test their longevity, and ensure they meet code-required minimum duration (typically 90 minutes).

name: Increased light diffusion uniformity
rationale: Lighting diffusers are designed to scatter and soften light from bulbs/LEDs, creating even illumination. Greater uniformity reduces glare and hot spots.

name: Reduced glare intensity
rationale: A primary function of diffusers is to prevent direct view of bright light sources, reducing discomfort glare. Lower glare improves visual comfort and safety.

name: Reduced light transmission loss
rationale: While diffusing light, the material should not excessively absorb or block light output. Minimising transmission loss maintains energy efficiency of the lighting system.

name: Adequate fire/safety rating
rationale: Diffuser materials (often plastics or acrylics) must meet fire code requirements for flame spread and smoke development in ceiling applications.

name: optimised light distribution
rationale: The shape, angle, and surface treatment of reflectors/baffles/louvers are designed to direct, diffuse, or block light in specific patterns. Optimising this directional control is a primary design pressure for this component.

name: reduced glare
rationale: Baffles and louvers are specifically employed to shield direct view of light sources, thereby reducing uncomfortable glare. This is a fundamental functional requirement for these components.

name: higher reflectance efficiency
rationale: Reflectors are designed to maximise the amount of light reflected onto the target area, requiring high-reflectance materials and optimised geometry to minimise absorption loss.

name: minimised visual obstruction
rationale: While directing or blocking light, these components should minimise unnecessary obstruction of views or daylight apertures, balancing light control with visual transparency.

name: Increased electrical load capacity
rationale: Lighting circuits/feeders must be designed to handle the electrical load from connected lighting fixtures. Increasing demand (more/larger lights) exerts a pressure to increase circuit capacity (wire gauge, breaker rating).

name: Reduced voltage drop
rationale: Long runs of lighting feeders must be designed to minimise voltage drop to ensure proper operation of lighting. This exerts a pressure to reduce resistance (larger conductors, shorter runs).

name: Adequate fault current protection
rationale: Circuit breakers and overcurrent protection devices must be adequately sized to protect the lighting feeder from faults while avoiding nuisance tripping.

name: Restricted routing constraints
rationale: Architectural and structural constraints (ceiling plenum depth, fire-rated barriers, column locations) restrict where lighting conduit/cable can be routed, exerting a pressure to limit feeder path flexibility.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: A primary design pressure is to allow more natural light into interior spaces, which reduces reliance on artificial lighting and improves occupant wellbeing. This drives decisions about window size, orientation, and glazing selection within the daylighting integration system.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: While admitting daylight, excessive solar heat gain must be avoided to prevent thermal discomfort and increased cooling loads. This creates a well-known tension with increased daylight penetration, influencing choices like low-solar-gain glazing, shading devices, or light shelves.

name: Reduced glare risk
rationale: Direct sunlight or high contrast ratios can cause visual discomfort and disability glare. Daylighting integration must balance light admission with glare control through strategies such as diffusing glazing, blinds, or optimized window placement.

name: Optimised daylight uniformity
rationale: Beyond total light quantity, the even distribution of daylight across a space is a key design pressure. Poor uniformity leads to dark zones or overly bright spots, reducing visual comfort and requiring supplementary lighting.

name: Improved view quality
rationale: Daylighting integration decisions are also pressured by the desire to provide occupants with quality views to the outside. Window placement and size must balance view provision with thermal and glare performance.

name: Increased accent lighting intensity for visual impact
rationale: Accent/display lighting is often designed to highlight merchandise, artwork, or architectural features. Designers frequently apply higher intensity (intentional over-lighting relative to ambient) to draw visual attention and create focal points.

name: Reduced glare and harsh shadows
rationale: Effective accent lighting must minimise glare and harsh shadowing on the displayed object. Beam angle control and fixture shielding are common design pressures to ensure comfortable viewing of the lit subject.

name: Improved color rendering for display accuracy
rationale: Display and accent lighting requires high color rendering index (CRI) to accurately reveal the colors of exhibited items. This is a well-established design pressure based on the physics of light spectrum and human color perception.

name: Reduced energy consumption from accent fixtures
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals create pressure to limit the power density of accent lighting, often via LED sources, zoning, or dimming controls — while still achieving the visual goals.

name: Reduced ceiling depth requirement
rationale: Recessed downlights require clearance above the ceiling for the housing/body. Designers often seek slimmer, low-profile units to fit into shallow plenum spaces, especially in retrofits or tight floor-to-floor heights.

name: Improved thermal management
rationale: Recessed lights trap heat in the ceiling cavity, which can reduce lamp life and pose fire risk. Designers prefer fixtures with better heat dissipation (e.g., larger heatsinks, airflow design) to improve safety and longevity.

name: Reduced air leakage
rationale: Recessed can lights are a major source of air leakage in building envelopes unless specified as airtight/IC-rated. Energy codes drive the selection of fixtures that minimise air bypass through the ceiling.

name: Adequate IC (Insulation Contact) rating
rationale: In insulated ceiling assemblies, downlights must be IC-rated to allow direct contact with insulation without overheating or fire risk. This is a code and safety requirement.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Downlights positioned in occupied spaces can cause discomfort glare. Designers prefer fixtures with baffles, lenses, or deep recessed cones to minimise direct glare.

name: Reduced glare and visual comfort
rationale: Surface-mount luminaires are often used in spaces where ceiling plenum access is limited. There is a design pressure to reduce glare and improve visual comfort through appropriate lensing, shielding, and light distribution patterns.

name: Optimised luminous efficacy
rationale: Energy codes and performance standards drive a design pressure toward higher lumens per watt in surface-mount fixtures, pushing selection of efficient LED sources and optical designs.

name: Reduced profile and protrusion
rationale: In spaces with low ceiling height or aesthetic requirements for a flush appearance, there is pressure to minimise the depth and visual prominence of surface-mount luminaires.

name: Adequate thermal management
rationale: Surface-mount luminaires lack the heat-sinking benefits of recessed housings, creating a design pressure for sufficient heat dissipation to maintain LED life and performance.

name: reduced energy consumption
rationale: Wall sconces in lighting design often face a design pressure to use energy-efficient bulbs (e.g., LED) and minimize power draw, especially in commercial or residential contexts where energy codes or sustainability goals apply.

name: adequate light output
rationale: A wall sconce must provide sufficient illumination for its intended purpose (ambient, accent, or task lighting), creating a design pressure toward adequate lumen output and proper light distribution.

name: improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Wall sconces are often decorative fixtures that must harmonize with interior architecture, finish materials, and style themes, creating a pressure toward improved visual appeal and coherence with the surroundin space.

name: reduced heat generation
rationale: Heat emitted by the sconce's light source can affect adjacent wall surfaces, occupant comfort, and fixture longevity, creating a design pressure to minimize heat output, especially in confined spaces or near heat-sensitive materials.

name: Increased luminous efficacy
rationale: Strip lights/linear fixtures benefit from higher lumens per watt to improve energy efficiency and light output, a core engineering pressure in lighting design.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Linear fixtures with bare strips can cause direct glare; architectural and visual comfort considerations push for lower glare through shielding, diffusers, or lower surface luminance.

name: Optimised colour rendering (CRI)
rationale: Higher CRI is desired for accurate colour perception in spaces using linear strip lighting, particularly in retail, healthcare, and hospitality applications.
