name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes (e.g., ASHRAE, Title 24) and sustainability goals drive the need for lower wattage consumption per linear foot in strip/linear fixtures.

name: Adequate thermal management
rationale: Linear LED strips generate heat that must be dissipated to prevent lumen depreciation and premature failure; sufficient heat sinking is an engineering requirement.

name: Higher light output pressure
rationale: High-bay luminaires are used in tall spaces (warehouses, factories) and require higher lumen output to provide adequate illumination at floor level. Low-bay applications also need sufficient light for safety and task visibility.

name: Improved energy efficiency pressure
rationale: Regulatory standards (e.g., Title 24, ASHRAE) and operational cost goals drive the need for maximized lumens-per-watt efficiency, pushing toward LED technology and optimized optical designs.

name: Reduced glare pressure
rationale: In both high-bay and low-bay settings, uncontrolled glare can impair visibility and cause discomfort. Optics and shielding are designed to minimize direct glare while maintaining useful light distribution.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency pressure
rationale: Luminaires mounted at high ceiling heights are difficult and costly to access for cleaning, relamping, or repair, so designs that extend component life and reduce service intervals are strongly preferred.

name: Constrained physical size pressure
rationale: Compact form factors are often desired to fit within ceiling grids, truss spaces, or low-clearance areas, while still accommodating the necessary optical and thermal management components.

name: Increased visibility and safety
rationale: Exterior lighting is primarily designed to ensure safe navigation, security, and visibility of pathways, entrances, and surrounding landscape features at night. Codes and best practices push for adequate illumination levels.

name: Reduced light pollution and glare
rationale: Dark-sky regulations, LEED credits, and neighbourhood considerations require shielding and limiting of uplight and spill light to minimise skyglow and neighbour disturbance.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes (e.g., ASHRAE 90.1, Title 24) and sustainability goals limit exterior lighting power density, favouring LED fixtures and controls (occupancy sensors, timers, dimming).

name: Enhanced aesthetic and landscape integration
rationale: Design intent often requires lighting to highlight specimen trees, architectural features, and garden elements, creating visual interest and nighttime ambiance.

name: Improved accessibility for FACU
rationale: Fire codes (e.g., NFPA 72, IBC) require the Fire Alarm Control Unit to be accessible to fire personnel, typically in a well-lit, unobstructed location near a main entrance. This pressure demands that the FACU be placed where it can be easily reached and operated during an emergency.

name: Reduced environmental exposure for FACU
rationale: The FACU contains sensitive electronic components that must be protected from moisture, dust, extreme temperatures, and physical damage. This pressure pushes for locating the panel in a clean, conditioned, and protected indoor environment, away from wet areas or potential impact.

name: Restricted interference with FACU operations
rationale: The FACU should not be obstructed by stored materials, equipment, or building finishes that could hinder its operation, ventilation, or visual/audible indicators. This creates a pressure to keep the area around the panel clear and free from clutter or encroachment.

name: increased sensitivity
rationale: Smoke detectors must have adequate sensitivity to detect smoke particles reliably in the early stages of a fire, ensuring prompt alarm activation.

name: reduced false alarms
rationale: False alarms (e.g., from cooking, steam, or dust) degrade occupant trust and lead to unnecessary building evacuations; designs aim to minimise nuisance alarms through appropriate sensor selection and placement.

name: improved placement
rationale: Proper placement (on ceilings, away from dead air spaces, near bedrooms) is critical for effective early warning; codes specify coverage and spacing requirements.

name: limited maintenance burden
rationale: Designs seek to minimise the frequency and cost of battery replacement, cleaning, and testing to ensure long-term reliability without excessive operational effort.

name: improved reliability
rationale: Heat detectors must reliably sense temperature thresholds to trigger fire alarms; reliability is a core design pressure.

name: reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Heat detectors should avoid nuisance alarms from non-fire heat sources (e.g., kitchen equipment, HVAC), so minimizing false triggers is a key design goal.

name: minimised response time
rationale: Detection speed is critical for life safety; the detector must respond quickly to temperature rise to enable early fire suppression and evacuation.

name: improved environmental tolerance
rationale: Heat detectors are exposed to ambient temperature variations, humidity, dust, and potential physical impacts, requiring robust design to maintain functionality.

name: Improved visibility for manual pull stations
rationale: Manual pull stations must be highly visible and easily located in emergencies. Design standards (e.g., NFPA 72, ADA) require conspicuous placement with contrasting colours and clear signage, acting as a design pressure to increase visibility features.

name: Reduced false alarm accessibility
rationale: To minimize nuisance alarms, pull stations are often designed with protective covers (e.g., plastic break-away covers) or placed in supervised locations, creating a pressure to reduce unintentional or casual access while still allowing deliberate emergency use.

name: Optimised placement height and reach range
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (ADA/EN 81-70) mandate specific mounting heights (typically 42-48 inches above floor) and clear floor space to ensure reachability by all occupants including wheelchair users, exerting a pressure to optimise positioning.

name: higher audibility
rationale: Fire alarm sounders must be loud enough to be heard throughout the building above ambient noise to ensure occupant safety, per fire safety engineering standards.

name: reduced visual obstruction
rationale: Sounder placement should minimise obstruction of sightlines, architectural finishes, or circulation paths, though this is a secondary concern.

name: lower power consumption
rationale: Standby power draw for fire alarm components may be a consideration in battery-backed or energy-efficient building designs.

name: higher visibility
rationale: Visual alarms/strobe lights must be bright enough to be seen by occupants, especially in emergency conditions, so there is a design pressure to increase light output for adequate visibility.

name: reduced energy consumption
rationale: Building energy codes and sustainability goals pressure designers to minimize power draw of all electrical devices, including notification appliances like strobes.

name: minimised false triggering
rationale: False or nuisance alarms degrade system trust and occupant response, so design pressure exists to limit unintended activation of strobes.

name: improved audibility and clarity
rationale: Voice evacuation systems must provide clear, intelligible voice instructions during emergencies. Engineering standards (e.g., NFPA 72, AS 1670.4) mandate audibility and speech intelligibility requirements so occupants can understand evacuation messages.

name: increased reliability and redundancy
rationale: As a life-safety system, the voice evacuation system must be highly reliable, often requiring backup power, redundant amplifiers, and fault-tolerant wiring to ensure operation during a fire or other emergency.

name: reduced background noise interference
rationale: Background noise (from HVAC, equipment, or crowd noise) can mask emergency messages. Design pressures seek to minimise such interference through speaker placement, power levels, and acoustic treatment to maintain intelligibility.

name: Sufficient electrical capacity for loop devices
rationale: The loop interface module must provide adequate power and signaling capacity for all addressable devices on the loop; insufficient capacity leads to device failure or communication errors.

name: Minimised signal degradation on communication loop
rationale: Signal loss, noise, or impedance mismatch on the loop must be minimised to maintain reliable addressable device communication; the loop interface is directly responsible for signal integrity.

name: Optimised addressing and configuration flexibility
rationale: The module must support flexible device addressing and configuration to accommodate varying system layouts and device counts; limited addressing capability restricts system design.

name: reduced footprint
rationale: The enclosure must fit within limited wall space, often in mechanical rooms or corridors, and not obstruct egress paths.

name: adequate environmental protection
rationale: The enclosure must protect sensitive electronics from dust, moisture, and temperature extremes, typically requiring an NEMA-rated enclosure suitable for the installed location.

name: restricted accessibility constraints
rationale: Access to the enclosure must be limited to authorized personnel only (e.g., via locked doors or tamper-resistant hardware) to prevent tampering, while still allowing service access.

name: Increased backup capacity
rationale: Designers face pressure to increase battery capacity (kWh rating) to ensure adequate backup duration during grid outages, which is a core functional requirement of backup power supplies.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in buildings (e.g., mechanical rooms, basements) create pressure to minimise the battery unit's physical size and volume, especially in urban or retrofit projects.

name: Reduced cost
rationale: Budget constraints exert pressure to minimise the capital cost of the battery system, which can be a significant line item in electrical and life-safety systems.

name: Improved safety compliance
rationale: Regulatory and safety codes (e.g., thermal runaway prevention, ventilation, fire rating) pressure designers to enhance safety features of battery enclosures and battery management systems.

name: Reduced maintenance burden
rationale: Pressure to minimise ongoing maintenance needs (e.g., battery testing, cell replacement, fluid levels) to reduce lifecycle cost and facility staff workload.

name: increased rigidity
rationale: Detector Base must provide a stable, vibration-free platform for sensitive detection equipment. Greater rigidity minimises deflection and ensures alignment accuracy.

name: reduced thermal expansion mismatch
rationale: The base material must have a coefficient of thermal expansion compatible with the detector assembly to prevent misalignment or stress under temperature changes.

name: limited weight
rationale: Excessive weight in the detector base may impose impractical mounting or support requirements, so a lower mass is often desired where structural constraints exist.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: Duct smoke detectors are prone to nuisance alarms from dust and airflow turbulence; designs aim to minimise false triggers through improved sensing technology or placement strategies.

name: Improved sensitivity to actual smoke
rationale: The primary function of a duct smoke detector is to reliably detect smoke in HVAC airstreams; design pressure exists to enhance detection sensitivity for real fire events while discriminating from non-fire particulates.

name: Sufficient airflow sampling
rationale: Duct smoke detectors rely on a sampling tube that extends into the duct; adequate airflow through the sensing chamber is critical for proper operation, influencing placement, tube length, and duct geometry decisions.

name: Reduced maintenance burden
rationale: Duct smoke detectors in HVAC systems require periodic cleaning and testing; design decisions aim to minimise access difficulty and servicing frequency.

name: Increased ceiling height sensitivity requirement
rationale: Projected beam smoke detectors require adequate clearance from ceiling obstructions and sufficient vertical space for the projected beam to operate effectively without false alarms.

name: Reduced beam path obstruction
rationale: Beam detectors need an unobstructed line-of-sight between transmitter and receiver; obstructions compromise detection reliability.

name: Increased environmental condition tolerance
rationale: Building environments with dust, steam, or temperature stratification can cause false alarms or misalignment, necessitating robust tolerance in detector design.

name: Reduced alignment sensitivity
rationale: Beam detectors are sensitive to building settlement, vibration, and structural movement; reducing alignment sensitivity improves long-term reliability.

name: Increased air sampling sensitivity
rationale: ASDs work by actively drawing air through pipes to a detector, so higher sensitivity is a fundamental design pressure — detecting smoke at very early (incipient) stages requires maximised sampling capability and sensitivity to microscopic particles.

name: Reduced airflow resistance in sampling network
rationale: The aspirator/fan must overcome pipe friction and orifice resistance. Minimising airflow resistance in the pipe network is critical to maintain adequate transport time and detection performance, especially in long-distance sampling runs.

name: Limited false alarm susceptibility
rationale: Because of their extreme sensitivity, ASDs are prone to false alarms from dust, condensation, or transient environmental conditions. A design pressure is to constrain or eliminate nuisance triggers through filtration, algorithm tuning, and alarm threshold management.

name: reduced false alarm rate
rationale: False alarms from non-flame sources (sunlight, welding, heaters) cause nuisance shutdowns and erode trust; minimising false triggers is a key design pressure.

name: adequate spectral sensitivity range
rationale: The detector must be sensitive to the appropriate wavelengths (UV, IR, or combined) to reliably discriminate flames from background radiation.

name: limited environmental interference
rationale: Design must constrain interference from dust, moisture, vibration, and temperature extremes to maintain reliable flame detection.

name: Improved detection sensitivity
rationale: Higher sensitivity ensures early detection of low concentrations of CO or combustible gases, which is critical for life safety and preventing explosions.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Minimising nuisance alarms is important to maintain occupant trust and avoid unnecessary evacuations or system desensitisation.

name: Enhanced environmental durability
rationale: The detector must withstand temperature extremes, humidity, dust, and potential corrosive atmospheres found in building service areas or garages where these detectors are typically installed.

name: Restricted placement interference
rationale: Placement must avoid obstructions (beams, partitions, HVAC diffusers) that could prevent gas from reaching the sensor, ensuring effective coverage per code requirements.

name: Increased switching reliability
rationale: Interface relays and control modules must reliably switch signals/loads; higher reliability reduces failure risk in critical control paths.

name: Improved signal isolation
rationale: These modules often need galvanic isolation between control and load circuits to prevent interference and protect sensitive electronics.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: As part of building control systems, minimising power draw is important for energy efficiency and thermal management of panels.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Compact form factor allows dense packaging in control cabinets and reduces overall panel size requirements.

name: Sufficient contact rating
rationale: The relay contacts must have adequate current and voltage ratings to handle the loads they switch without premature failure.

name: Improved fire safety compliance
rationale: Magnetic door releases must reliably hold doors open under normal conditions but release immediately upon fire alarm activation to enable fire compartmentation. Building codes and fire safety regulations strongly pressure designs toward improved compliance with these fail-safe requirements.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Magnetic door holders consume continuous electricity to hold doors open. Energy efficiency standards and operational cost considerations create a pressure to reduce standby power draw through more efficient magnets or duty-cycling designs.

name: Increased holding force reliability
rationale: The magnetic hold must be strong enough to keep doors securely open against drafts, manual bumps, and building movement, while still releasing reliably. This creates a pressure for adequate holding force with safety margin.

name: Eliminated accidental release failures
rationale: Malfunctions where the magnet fails to release (door stays open during a fire) or fails to hold (door closes unexpectedly) must be prevented. Reliability engineering and life safety concerns drive pressure to eliminate these failure modes.

name: Improved ground fault detection sensitivity
rationale: Ground fault protectors need higher sensitivity to detect small leakage currents that could indicate insulation breakdown or moisture ingress in fire alarm wiring, preventing false alarms and ensuring system integrity.

name: Reduced false tripping from transient surges
rationale: Surge protectors must discriminate between dangerous surges and harmless transients to avoid unnecessary disconnection of fire alarm circuits, which could compromise life safety functions.

name: Enhanced surge current handling capacity
rationale: Fire alarm systems require robust surge protection to withstand lightning-induced and switching surges without failing, maintaining operation during critical emergency conditions.

name: Lower ground fault trip threshold
rationale: A lower trip threshold helps detect developing ground faults early, reducing risk of undetected faults that could render the fire alarm system inoperable during a fire event.

name: Improved access control security
rationale: Security is the primary purpose of an access control system; design decisions consistently aim to increase authentication reliability, authorization precision, and resistance to bypass.

name: Reduced intrusion risk
rationale: Access control systems are designed to minimise unauthorised entry; this is a fundamental design pressure that shapes choice of credential types, lock mechanisms, and integration with alarms.

name: Improved user convenience
rationale: Building occupants require smooth, low-friction entry/exit; this pressure pushes toward faster credential reading, hands-free operation, and reduced false rejections.

name: Reduced operational complexity
rationale: Facility managers prefer systems that are simple to administer, with minimal credential management overhead and straightforward user provisioning workflows.

name: More comprehensive perimeter detection coverage
rationale: Security engineering principles call for complete coverage of all perimeter points (doors, windows, roof hatches, etc.) to eliminate blind spots. This pressure drives designs toward additional sensors and more detection zones.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: False alarms degrade system credibility and cause costly/unnecessary responses. Engineering best practice and security standards (e.g., UL, EN) push for technologies and configurations (e.g., dual-technology sensors, signal processing) that minimise nuisance alarms.

name: Decreased vulnerability to tampering and bypass
rationale: Physical security engineering requires that sensors, wiring, and control panels be designed to resist tampering (e.g., tamper switches, supervised loops, encrypted communications) so that an intruder cannot easily disable the system before or during an intrusion event.

name: Optimised response time to intrusion events
rationale: From a security performance standpoint, faster detection and alarm transmission (e.g., immediate local alarm, rapid notification to monitoring station) is pressured by the need to intercept intruders before asset loss or harm occurs.

name: improved coverage and image quality
rationale: CCTV systems benefit from higher resolution cameras and broader coverage to enhance security monitoring effectiveness.

name: reduced bandwidth and storage requirements
rationale: Video data transmission and long-term archiving impose infrastructure costs, creating pressure to minimise data volume through compression, motion-triggered recording, or lower frame rates.

name: adequate lighting for camera performance
rationale: Cameras require sufficient ambient or IR illumination to capture usable footage, especially at night or in dim spaces.

name: minimised system downtime and data loss
rationale: Security systems must be highly reliable; outages or lost footage compromise the surveillance function, creating pressure for redundancy and failover.

name: Improved detection reliability
rationale: Door Contact Sensors need reliable detection of door open/close states to trigger alarms or access events; higher reliability directly improves security system performance.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: False alarms from door contact sensors (due to misalignment, vibration, or environmental factors) cause nuisance and desensitization; minimising them is a core design pressure for the sensor and the broader security system.

name: Minimized installation intrusiveness
rationale: Door contact sensors physically attach to doors/frames; architectural concerns push for smaller, less visible, and less obtrusive mounting to preserve aesthetics and door operation.

name: Greater environmental robustness
rationale: Sensors at door interfaces are exposed to temperature variations, moisture, dust, and mechanical wear, so design must emphasise robustness to ensure long-term functionality.

name: Improved detection sensitivity
rationale: PIR sensors need adequate sensitivity to reliably detect infrared heat signatures from occupants, ensuring proper automation triggering.

name: Reduced false triggering
rationale: False triggers from pets, HVAC drafts, or environmental temperature changes degrade system reliability and user trust; design aims to minimise these.

name: Minimised detection blind zone
rationale: Blind spots between sensor zones or near the base of the sensor can allow undetected movement; minimising these improves coverage.

name: Limited power consumption
rationale: PIR sensors are often battery-powered or part of energy-efficient systems; design pressures push for lower standby and active power draw.

name: Increased detection sensitivity
rationale: A glass break detector must have sufficient sensitivity to reliably detect the frequency and pattern of breaking glass, avoiding false negatives while balancing against false positives from ambient noise.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: The detector must minimise false alarms triggered by non-breaking-glass sounds (e.g., thunder, jingling keys, slamming doors) to maintain trustworthiness and avoid unnecessary security responses.

name: Adequate frequency bandwidth
rationale: The detector needs an adequate frequency range to capture both the impact thud and the subsequent shatter frequencies characteristic of glass breakage, typically spanning from low to mid-high frequencies.

name: increased security
rationale: Card readers and keypad readers are access control devices; a key design pressure is to increase security (e.g., encryption, tamper resistance, credential verification strength) to prevent unauthorised entry.

name: reduced vandalism risk
rationale: These devices are often mounted in public or semi-public areas, making them targets for physical tampering or vandalism. A design pressure is to reduce vulnerability to damage through ruggedised housings, weatherproofing, or recessed mounting.

name: improved user convenience
rationale: Users expect fast, intuitive interaction with access control devices. Design pressure exists to improve ease of use (e.g., reader placement at accessible height, clear feedback, responsive touch) to avoid bottlenecks or user frustration.

name: Improved security accuracy
rationale: Biometric scanners must provide accurate identity verification; pressure to increase accuracy drives algorithmic and hardware improvements.

name: Reduced false rejection rate
rationale: False rejections (denying legitimate users) degrade user experience and security workflow; there is a design pressure to minimise them.

name: Reduced false acceptance rate
rationale: False acceptances (admitting impostors) are a critical security failure; the system must minimise this risk via threshold tuning and sensor quality.

name: Limited environmental interference
rationale: Lighting, temperature, moisture, and dust can impair sensor readings; design pressure to restrict these physical interferences.

name: Improved scan speed
rationale: User throughput and convenience create pressure for faster capture and processing of biometric data.

name: Higher durability
rationale: Scanners are often deployed in public or high-traffic areas, requiring robust hardware to withstand repeated use and vandalism.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: Energy efficiency is a common design constraint for electronic hardware, especially in battery-backed or sustainability-focused deployments.

name: Improved accessibility and clear signage
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) require emergency exits to be clearly marked and readily accessible to ensure safe egress during emergencies; this drives designs that increase visibility, directness of path, and unobstructed access to the device.

name: Reduced false activation / accidental triggering
rationale: Request-to-exit devices are subject to accidental or nuisance activations (e.g., by persons leaning on or bumping the bar); engineering design pressures push toward lower false-trigger rates through mechanisms like delayed action or sensor integration without compromising emergency release functionality.

name: Greater robustness and durability
rationale: Emergency exit devices must withstand repeated use, vandalism, and environmental conditions; this drives designs with stronger materials, better corrosion resistance, and higher mechanical reliability to ensure long-term function.

name: Lower maintenance requirements
rationale: Facility operators prefer exit devices that require minimal periodic adjustment, cleaning, or part replacement to reduce operational costs and ensure consistent readiness; this pressure acts to simplify mechanisms and use durable components.

name: Improved integration with fire alarm and access control systems
rationale: Modern emergency exits are often electronically monitored and must interface with fire alarm panels, magnetic locks, and access control systems; this pressure drives designs with better electrical connectivity, signaling, and compatibility with standard security/fire protocols.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: DVRs/NVRs rely on hard drives (HDDs) to store recorded footage. Higher-resolution cameras, more cameras, and longer retention periods all exert pressure to increase storage capacity (e.g., larger HDDs or RAID arrays).

name: Higher video processing throughput
rationale: As camera resolutions (e.g., 4K, 8K) and frame rates increase, the DVR/NVR must process more video data per second. This drives pressure for more powerful CPUs, GPUs, and encoding/decoding capabilities.

name: Reduced physical footprint
rationale: DVRs/NVRs are often installed in server racks, equipment closets, or wall-mounted enclosures, where space is at a premium. There is a design pressure to minimise the unit's physical size (chassis depth, height, width) to fit constrained spaces.

name: Improved network bandwidth efficiency
rationale: For NVRs receiving IP camera streams over a network, limited network capacity creates pressure for better compression standards (e.g., H.265, H.265+), bandwidth management, and optimised streaming to avoid network congestion.

name: Reduced power consumption
rationale: DVRs/NVRs operating 24/7 in equipment rooms with heat dissipation and energy cost concerns create pressure to minimise power draw through efficient components, low-power processors, and power management features.

name: Increased illumination for surveillance coverage
rationale: Security lighting must provide adequate brightness to enable CCTV cameras and human observers to detect and identify intruders or suspicious activity, a fundamental engineering requirement for security systems.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals push for lower power draw from lighting systems, which acts as a counter-pressure against simply maximising brightness or run-time.

name: Reduced light trespass and glare
rationale: Security lighting must be directed and shielded to prevent light pollution onto neighbouring properties and to avoid blinding glare for pedestrians or drivers, an architectural and neighbourhood-compatibility concern.

name: Improved reliability and redundancy
rationale: Security lighting is a life-safety system; backup power, robust fixtures, and fail-safe operation are critical to ensure it functions during power outages or component failures.

name: improved detection sensitivity
rationale: Sensor-based perimeter fences require adequate sensitivity to reliably detect intrusion attempts (e.g., climbing, cutting) without generating excessive false alarms. This pressure pushes for higher detection capability to ensure security.

name: reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Excessive false alarms degrade trust in the sensor system and can lead to alarm fatigue for security personnel. The system must minimise nuisance triggers from environmental factors (wind, animals, debris).

name: limited physical bypass vulnerability
rationale: Fence and gate structures must restrict opportunities for undetected physical intrusion (e.g., digging under, climbing over, cutting through) to maintain the effectiveness of the integrated sensor system.

name: enhanced environmental durability
rationale: As an outdoor exposed component, the fence/gate and its sensors must withstand weather (rain, wind, UV, temperature extremes) and corrosion over the intended service life without degradation of sensing or structural function.

name: Improved accessibility and visibility
rationale: A duress alarm button must be easily reachable and identifiable in an emergency. Ergonomic standards and security engineering codes of practice require the button to be placed at an accessible height, clearly marked, and unobstructed to ensure rapid activation during a crisis.

name: Reduced false alarm triggers
rationale: To prevent nuisance alarms and desensitisation of responders, the button design must incorporate features such as recessed placement, two-stage activation, or protective covers that minimise accidental presses while still allowing intentional activation.

name: Enhanced tamper resistance
rationale: Security standards require duress alarm buttons to be resistant to vandalism and unauthorised disabling. This drives design decisions toward robust enclosures, anti-tamper switches, and secure mounting that prevents easy removal or damage.

name: Increased wiring and power reliability
rationale: Life-safety systems demand highly reliable power and connectivity. Decisions about wired vs. wireless connections, battery backup, and supervision (line monitoring) are driven by the need to ensure the button remains operational at all times, including during power outages.

name: Increased physical protection for cabling
rationale: Security system cabling carries sensitive signals and power; physical protection (conduit, trunking, armoured cable) is needed to prevent tampering, accidental damage, or environmental degradation.

name: Reduced signal interference on cabling runs
rationale: Security system cabling (especially for CCTV and alarm sensors) must be routed away from high-voltage power cables and EMI sources to prevent false alarms or signal degradation.

name: Minimised cable exposure (concealment)
rationale: Exposed security cabling is vulnerable to vandalism and detracts from aesthetics; concealed routing via ceiling voids, walls, or dedicated trays is preferred.

name: increased automation and control capability
rationale: Field Controllers and PLCs are at the core of automated building control; operational demands for more sophisticated and reliable automation drive a need for greater processing power, I/O capacity, and networking capability.

name: reduced physical footprint per control point
rationale: Space constraints in electrical rooms, MCCs, and field enclosures push toward compact controllers with higher density of I/O points per unit volume, minimising physical space requirements.

name: higher reliability and redundancy requirements
rationale: Critical building systems (life safety, HVAC for sensitive areas) demand fault-tolerant PLC architectures with redundant power supplies, CPUs, and networks, driving up reliability specifications.

name: Increased data processing capacity
rationale: The BMS Controller / Head-End Server must handle growing volumes of building sensor data, control signals, and analytics workloads. Insufficient processing power would cause latency or failures in building management operations.

name: Reduced network latency
rationale: Real-time building control and monitoring require low-latency communication between the head-end server and field devices. High latency can degrade system responsiveness and compromise timely fault detection or energy optimization.

name: Improved cybersecurity robustness
rationale: As the central aggregation point for building data and control commands, the head-end server is a high-value target for cyberattacks. Strong security measures (encryption, authentication, access control) are critical to prevent unauthorized manipulation of building systems.

name: Sufficient data storage capacity
rationale: The head-end server stores historical trend logs, alarm records, configuration backups, and energy reports. Inadequate storage can force data purges, losing information needed for analytics, compliance, and troubleshooting.

name: Improved interoperability across building systems
rationale: As a protocol gateway, its core purpose is to enable communication between BACnet, LonWorks, and Modbus networks. Higher interoperability means more seamless data exchange between HVAC, lighting, and metering systems.

name: Reduced protocol translation latency
rationale: Real-time building automation requires fast translation between protocol formats. Lower latency in the gateway improves responsiveness of control loops that cross different networks.

name: Expanded device support across protocols
rationale: The gateway's value increases with the number of device types and manufacturers it can bridge. Broader compatibility reduces the need for multiple vendor-specific gateways.

name: Limited security vulnerabilities from multi-protocol exposure
rationale: A gateway bridging multiple protocols creates additional attack surfaces. Reducing security vulnerabilities is critical to prevent unauthorized access across interconnected building systems.

name: Improved user interface clarity
rationale: The operator workstation's UI must be clear and intuitive for effective building management, reducing operator error and improving response times.

name: Higher data refresh rate
rationale: Real-time monitoring of building systems requires sufficiently fast data update rates on the BMS workstation to enable timely operator decisions.

name: Reduced system latency
rationale: Low latency between sensor data acquisition and display on the workstation is critical for operators to respond promptly to building system events.

name: Enhanced alarm management
rationale: Effective alarm prioritisation and clear presentation help operators identify critical issues quickly without being overwhelmed by nuisance alarms.

name: Improved energy data granularity
rationale: Building energy metering hardware must provide sufficient granularity (e.g., sub-metering per floor, zone, or end-use) to enable effective energy management, benchmarking, and identification of savings opportunities. This drives the selection of meters with appropriate resolution and data logging capabilities.

name: Higher measurement accuracy
rationale: Regulatory requirements (e.g., IPMVP, utility-grade metering standards) and the need for reliable billing-grade data push for higher accuracy meters (e.g., ±0.5% or better), influencing the choice of meter class, calibration frequency, and signal conditioning hardware.

name: Reduced installation cost
rationale: Budget constraints place downward pressure on the cost of metering hardware, favoring simpler, non-intrusive solutions (e.g., clamp-on current transformers over in-line meters) and limiting the number of metering points installed.

name: Improved communication interoperability
rationale: The need to integrate metering hardware with building management systems (BMS) and energy management software favors meters supporting open protocols (BACnet, Modbus, MQTT) over proprietary systems, influencing hardware selection and gateway requirements.

name: Minimised physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in electrical rooms and distribution panels push for compact metering hardware designs (e.g., panel-mounted meters rather than large enclosure-based systems), affecting form factor selection.

name: Improved visibility and audibility
rationale: An alarm annunciation panel must be clearly visible and audible to alert operators of building system faults (e.g., fire, security, HVAC failures). This drives design decisions around display brightness, size, sound output levels, and placement at eye level in control rooms.

name: Reduced false alarms
rationale: Excessive nuisance alarms desensitize operators and undermine trust in the system. Design pressures push for better signal filtering, alarm validation logic, and discrimination between critical and non-critical events to minimize false annunciations.

name: Adequate labelling and intuitiveness
rationale: Operators must quickly interpret which zone or system is alarming. This drives design decisions toward clear, logically grouped labels, consistent colour coding (e.g., red for fire, amber for faults), and intuitive panel layout matching building floor plans.

name: Minimised panel footprint
rationale: In control rooms or security desks, wall and console space is limited. There is pressure to consolidate annunciation into a compact form factor without sacrificing readability or the number of displayed alarm points.

name: optimized energy efficiency
rationale: An integrated lighting control interface is typically designed to optimize energy efficiency by automating dimming, scheduling, and occupancy-based control. The design pressure pushes toward greater energy performance.

name: reduced user complexity
rationale: Control interfaces must be intuitive; there is pressure to minimize the learning curve and operational complexity for occupants and facility managers.

name: increased system responsiveness
rationale: Users and building automation systems require near-instantaneous response from lighting controls to changes in sensor input or manual commands.

name: Improved detection and response speed
rationale: Fire alarm and life safety interfaces must detect fires and initiate response actions quickly; this is a core functional requirement driving design decisions toward faster detection algorithms, better sensor placement, and reduced signal latency.

name: Reduced false alarm rate
rationale: False alarms desensitize occupants and lead to costly evacuations or shutdowns; therefore design decisions must minimize nuisance alarms through appropriate sensor selection, discrimination algorithms, and environmental compensation.

name: Higher reliability and fault tolerance
rationale: Life safety systems must operate correctly on demand, even during partial failures. Designs are pressured toward redundancy, self-diagnostics, backup power, and fail-safe architectures to ensure reliability.

name: Increased integration with building management systems
rationale: Modern fire alarm interfaces increasingly need to communicate with HVAC, access control, elevator, and other building systems for coordinated response (e.g., smoke control, floor recall, occupant egress), driving design toward open protocols and more communication points.

name: sufficient structural capacity
rationale: The primary structural frame must have adequate strength and stiffness to safely resist gravity loads (dead/live), lateral loads (wind/seismic), and environmental loads. This is a fundamental engineering requirement for structural safety and serviceability.

name: reduced structural weight
rationale: Minimising the self-weight of the primary structural frame reduces foundation demands, material costs, and seismic mass. This is typically achieved through material selection (e.g., steel vs. concrete) and efficient structural geometry.

name: optimised material efficiency
rationale: Design pressures push toward economical use of structural materials (steel, concrete, timber) to minimise construction cost while meeting strength and deflection limits, often through framing layouts, member sizing, and connection detailing.

name: optimised structural efficiency
rationale: Secondary structural framing (e.g., purlins, girts, joists) must be designed for efficient load distribution between primary frames and building envelope, so optimizing member sizes and spacing is a key engineering pressure.

name: reduced material weight
rationale: To minimise dead load on primary structure and reduce costs, secondary members are typically designed with minimal feasible cross-sections while still meeting strength and deflection criteria.

name: adequate deflection control
rationale: Secondary framing supports roof and wall cladding; excessive deflection can damage finishes and compromise weathertightness, so sufficient stiffness is required.

name: increased lateral stability
rationale: Bracing systems are primarily designed to resist lateral forces (wind, seismic). A key design pressure is the need to provide increased lateral stability to the overall structure.

name: improved load path continuity
rationale: Bracing must efficiently transfer lateral loads to the foundation; ensuring a continuous and improved load path is a fundamental design pressure.

name: minimised structural interference
rationale: Architectural and programmatic requirements often pressure bracing systems to minimise interference with spatial planning, openings, and sightlines.

name: sufficient stiffness-to-weight ratio
rationale: The bracing system must be stiff enough to control building drift under lateral loads while not being excessively heavy; achieving a sufficient stiffness-to-weight ratio is a key design pressure.

name: increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Floor framing systems must be designed to support vertical gravity loads (dead and live loads) and transfer them to columns or walls. Increased load-bearing capacity is a fundamental engineering requirement to ensure structural safety and serviceability.

name: reduced deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection in floor framing can cause cracking of finishes, discomfort to occupants, and serviceability failures. Engineering design codes impose deflection limits that create pressure to minimise vertical displacement under load.

name: reduced structural depth
rationale: Shallower floor framing reduces overall building height for a given floor-to-floor height, lowering façade costs, reducing vertical circulation volume, and allowing more floors within height restrictions. This creates pressure to minimise the structural zone depth.

name: sufficient fire resistance rating
rationale: Building codes require floor assemblies to have a minimum fire-resistance rating to prevent vertical fire spread. This creates a design pressure for the framing system to achieve adequate fire protection, typically through material selection, concrete cover, or fireproofing.

name: Increased gravity load resistance
rationale: The roof framing system must resist gravity loads (dead load, live load, snow load). This is a fundamental physical requirement that drives the structural design of the roof framing.

name: Reduced structural weight
rationale: Lighter roof framing reduces the load on supporting columns, walls, and foundations, and can reduce material costs. This is a common engineering optimization consideration.

name: Increased lateral load resistance
rationale: The roof framing must resist wind and seismic lateral loads and transfer them to the lateral load-resisting system below. This is a physical requirement for structural stability.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost optimization is a key engineering and economic driver affecting the selection of roof framing materials, spans, and member sizes.

name: Enhanced load-bearing capacity
rationale: Foundation connections must transfer loads from the superstructure to the foundations; greater load-bearing capacity ensures structural integrity and prevents failure at the interface.

name: Improved seismic resilience
rationale: Foundation connections are critical in seismic design; stronger connections improve ductility and energy dissipation during earthquakes, preventing detachment of the superstructure.

name: Reduced corrosion risk
rationale: Foundation connections (often steel anchor bolts, embedded plates) are vulnerable to moisture and soil-borne corrosion; limiting corrosion extends service life and maintains connection strength.

name: Adequate anchorage depth
rationale: Sufficient embedment of anchor bolts or rebar into the foundation is essential for developing full tensile and shear capacity of the connection.

name: improved fatigue resistance
rationale: Steel connections under repetitive loading are susceptible to fatigue cracking; improved fatigue resistance is a key design pressure that governs connection detailing, weld quality, and bolt pre-tensioning.

name: reduced stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at weld toes, bolt holes, and geometry transitions drive connection failure; minimising these through smooth load paths and reinforcing details is a fundamental design pressure.

name: adequate strength capacity
rationale: Connections must safely transfer axial, shear, and moment forces between members; ensuring adequate strength relative to factored loads is the primary structural design requirement.

name: limited ductility demand
rationale: Brittle fracture in connections is a critical failure mode; design pressures push toward limiting ductility demand on connections, especially in seismic or high-strain scenarios, by promoting capacity-protected design.

name: minimised weld defects
rationale: Porosity, lack of fusion, undercut, and other weld defects reduce connection reliability; design and inspection standards impose pressure to minimise such defects through proper detailing and quality control.

name: Improved durability against moisture
rationale: Composite decking is often chosen over timber for its enhanced resistance to moisture, rot, and insect damage, which drives a design pressure to improve its long-term durability performance.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: As a structural deck surface, composite decking must support live loads (people, furniture) and dead loads (self-weight), creating a design pressure to achieve adequate or greater load-bearing capacity.

name: Reduced thermal expansion and contraction
rationale: Composite materials can expand and contract with temperature changes more than wood; there is a design pressure to minimise this movement to prevent buckling, gap formation, and fastener issues.

name: Reduced surface temperature
rationale: Dark-coloured composite decking can absorb significant solar heat; there is a design pressure to limit surface temperature for occupant comfort (barefoot use) and to prevent material degradation.

name: improved energy efficiency
rationale: Corridor lighting is often left on for long durations, making energy-efficient fixtures (e.g., LED) a key design pressure to reduce operational costs and meet building codes.

name: reduced light pollution / glare
rationale: Corridors near occupied spaces require controlled light distribution to avoid glare spill into adjacent rooms and to meet visual comfort standards.

name: adequate illumination levels
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards mandate minimum illuminance levels in egress corridors for safety and wayfinding.

name: minimized maintenance access disruption
rationale: Corridor lighting fixtures should be positioned and specified to reduce the frequency and difficulty of maintenance, as corridors are high-traffic circulation spaces.

name: optimised load-bearing efficiency
rationale: Trusses and space frames are designed to efficiently distribute loads through triangulated networks. There is a consistent design pressure to increase/optimise their load-bearing efficiency relative to material used, as this is the primary engineering rationale for choosing this structural typology.

name: reduced self-weight
rationale: A defining characteristic of trusses and space frames is their high strength-to-weight ratio. Design decisions are constantly driven by the need to minimise self-weight (through member sizing, hollow sections, and material selection) to maximise spans and reduce foundation loads.

name: greater spanning capacity
rationale: Trusses and space frames are typically selected specifically for long-span applications (roofs, bridges, stadiums). The design pressure to achieve longer spans with the same or less material is a core driver of topology, member sizing, and joint detailing decisions.

name: reduced material usage
rationale: Efficiency in truss and space frame design directly targets minimising material volume while maintaining structural integrity. This pressure influences member cross-section selection, optimization of grid geometry, and choice of steel versus aluminium.

name: higher joint stiffness
rationale: Joint behaviour critically affects the performance of space frames and trusses. There is a design pressure to increase joint stiffness (e.g., welded vs bolted, node connectors in space frames) to ensure the structure behaves as assumed in the analytical model and to prevent buckling in compression members.

name: Improved visibility
rationale: Building codes and life safety regulations (e.g., NFPA 101, IBC) mandate that exit signs be clearly visible, legible, and illuminated under normal and emergency conditions. This pressure drives decisions on placement height, luminance, font size, contrast, and backup power.

name: Reduced obstructions
rationale: Exit signs must be unobstructed by architectural elements, furniture, decorations, or other building components to ensure egress path visibility. This pressure acts on decisions regarding sign placement relative to doors, corridors, and potential blockages.

name: Adequate illumination
rationale: Emergency exit signs require reliable illumination — either internally lit (electroluminescent, LED) or externally lit — with backup battery or generator power to remain functional during power loss. This influences design choices for power supply, lighting technology, and testing access.

name: improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire doors in corridor locations must resist fire spread per building codes (e.g., IBC). A higher fire-resistance rating (e.g., 20-minute vs. 45-minute) increases safety and code compliance.

name: reduced air leakage
rationale: Fire doors in corridors often serve smoke-control functions; minimizing air and smoke leakage around the door assembly helps maintain tenable conditions in means of egress.

name: adequate door width for egress
rationale: Corridor fire doors are part of the means of egress; sufficient clear opening width is required by accessibility and life safety codes (e.g., minimum 32 inches clear).

name: improved latching and self-closing reliability
rationale: Fire doors must latch and self-close properly to maintain fire and smoke compartmentation; unreliable hardware compromises the door's intended performance.

name: reduced hardware projection into corridor
rationale: Projecting hardware (e.g., lever handles, push bars) on corridor fire doors can obstruct egress or cause injury; minimizing projection improves safety and code compliance.

name: Optimised structural support
rationale: Handrails must be designed to bear anticipated loads (e.g., people leaning/pulling) without failure, requiring adequate structural capacity.

name: Reduced slip/grip failure risk
rationale: The handrail surface must minimise slipping to ensure user safety; friction and ergonomic design are key constraints.

name: Adequate accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes mandate handrail height, clearance, and continuity for accessibility; this pressure drives design toward meeting those standards.

name: Reduced obstruction in corridor
rationale: The handrail must not project excessively into the corridor width, ensuring safe passage and egress clearance.

name: adequate structural support
rationale: The corridor wall base must provide adequate support to the wall above, resisting vertical loads and transferring them to the floor structure.

name: reduced moisture intrusion
rationale: The wall base in corridors is vulnerable to moisture from floor cleaning and foot traffic; design should minimise water ingress at the base junction.

name: improved impact resistance
rationale: Corridor wall bases are subject to impacts from carts, equipment, and heavy foot traffic, requiring enhanced durability at the base zone.

name: adequate drainage capacity
rationale: The corridor floor drain must have sufficient hydraulic capacity to handle expected rainwater, washdown water, or spillage in the corridor without overflow or ponding. This is a standard plumbing engineering requirement.

name: reduced clogging risk
rationale: Corridor floor drains are prone to debris accumulation from foot traffic and cleaning. Design should minimise blockage potential through appropriate grate design, trap access, and solids-handling capability.

name: adequate impact resistance
rationale: Corridor walls are subject to impacts from carts, trolleys, gurneys, and foot traffic in high-traffic hospital/care settings. Protection elements must provide adequate impact resistance to prevent damage and reduce maintenance.

name: reduced abrasion and wear
rationale: Corridor wall protection is typically made of durable materials like vinyl, rubber, or metal that resist scuffing, scratching, and abrasion from frequent contact. The design pressure is to minimise surface wear over time.

name: improved cleanability
rationale: In healthcare and commercial corridors, wall protection surfaces must be smooth, non-porous, and easily cleanable to maintain hygiene standards. This drives decisions on material selection and joint detailing.

name: improved visibility and legibility
rationale: Signage must be clearly visible and legible at typical walking speeds and distances within corridors to effectively communicate wayfinding information. This is a fundamental design requirement for corridor signage systems.

name: reduced visual clutter and information overload
rationale: Too many signs or excessive information in a corridor can overwhelm users and reduce wayfinding efficiency. Design pressures push toward minimal, well-organised information presentation.

name: greater compliance with accessibility standards
rationale: Corridor signage must comply with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA, building codes) regarding letter height, contrast, braille, mounting height, and tactile features to serve all users, including those with visual impairments.

name: limited number of mounting locations
rationale: Physical constraints in corridors (doorways, fire equipment, wall width, structural elements) restrict where signage can be placed, pressuring toward fewer but more strategically positioned signs.

name: increased smoke containment effectiveness
rationale: Corridor smoke barriers must effectively contain smoke within or out of a corridor during a fire event to maintain tenable egress paths. This drives design toward better sealing, tighter construction, and automatic activation.

name: reduced opening size in barrier
rationale: Openings such as doors, dampers, and penetrations compromise smoke barrier performance. Building codes and pressurization design push toward minimising the数量和 size of openings to limit smoke leakage.

name: higher pressure differential resistance
rationale: Smoke barriers in corridors must withstand pressure differentials created by HVAC pressurization or fire-induced stack effect without excessive deflection or leakage, driving stronger structural design and tighter seals.

name: lower leakage through barrier joints
rationale: Leakage at joints, edges, and penetrations directly undermines smoke barrier performance. Design seeks to minimise leakage rates to comply with smoke-tightness standards such as UL 1784 or ASTM E90.

name: Improved accessibility
rationale: Fire extinguisher cabinets must be easily accessible in an emergency — codes (e.g., NFPA 10, IBC) mandate unobstructed access, clear signage, and no locked doors obstructing retrieval.

name: Reduced obstruction risk
rationale: The cabinet should not protrude into egress paths or be blocked by furniture/equipment; building/fire codes restrict placement that could impede occupant evacuation or become a tripping hazard.

name: Adequate mounting height
rationale: NFPA 10 and ADA standards specify a maximum mounting height (typically ≤ 48 inches to the handle) to ensure reachability by all occupants, including those with disabilities.

name: Improved visibility and signage
rationale: Fire extinguisher locations must be readily visible or have clear identification signs per NFPA 10 and IBC; cabinets often have a red exterior or contrasting sign to aid quick location.

name: Reduced tampering or misuse risk
rationale: Cabinets may have break-glass or latch mechanisms to deter unauthorized access or vandalism while still allowing rapid use in an emergency.

name: increased seating capacity
rationale: Corridor benches are designed to provide seating in circulation spaces; a key design pressure is to increase the number of seats or seating length to accommodate more users, especially in high-traffic corridors.

name: reduced corridor obstruction
rationale: Benches placed in corridors must not impede circulation or egress; design pressures push for minimising the bench's footprint, protrusion, or placement that blocks the path of travel.

name: improved durability and maintenance
rationale: As a public-use item in a high-traffic corridor, the bench must withstand wear, cleaning, and occasional abuse, driving pressures for robust materials and easy-to-clean surfaces.

name: limited visual clutter
rationale: Corridor benches should be visually restrained to avoid cluttering the corridor environment; this pressure drives simpler forms, neutral colours, and integration with the surrounding architecture.

name: reduced damage from impacts
rationale: Kickplates protect corridor walls from scuffs, impacts, and abrasions from foot traffic, carts, and cleaning equipment. A durable kickplate reduces physical damage and maintenance needs.

name: improved durability
rationale: Higher material durability (e.g., thicker gauge metal, impact-resistant composites) ensures the kickplate withstands repeated contact without denting or cracking over its lifespan.

name: optimised ease of cleaning
rationale: Kickplates with smooth, non-porous surfaces and minimal crevices are easier to clean, which is important in high-traffic corridors subject to dirt and scuff marks.

name: Improved thermal performance of corridor glazing
rationale: Corridor glazing should have improved thermal insulation properties (e.g., double or triple glazing, low-E coatings) to reduce heat loss/gain and improve energy efficiency in conditioned corridors.

name: Reduced solar heat gain through corridor glazing
rationale: To prevent overheating in corridors and reduce cooling loads, the glazing should minimise solar heat gain, potentially through tinted glass, reflective coatings, or external shading devices.

name: Adequate natural light transmission through corridor glazing
rationale: Corridor glazing should allow sufficient daylight transmission to reduce reliance on artificial lighting, improve wayfinding, and enhance occupant comfort, while balancing thermal performance.

name: optimised water discharge coverage
rationale: The sprinkler head must provide adequate coverage area and water distribution to effectively suppress fires in the corridor, driving design toward optimised spray patterns and flow rates.

name: obstruction interference minimised
rationale: Corridors often contain light fixtures, signage, ducts, or ceiling-mounted equipment that can block sprinkler spray; design pressures push to reduce or eliminate such obstructions to maintain effective coverage.

name: aesthetic visibility reduced
rationale: In finished corridors, architects often prefer sprinkler heads that are less visually intrusive (e.g., concealed or recessed models), creating a pressure to minimise their visual prominence.

name: improved detection sensitivity
rationale: Smoke detectors in corridors must reliably detect smoke from fires to trigger alarms and enable safe egress. Higher sensitivity improves early warning capability, which is critical in egress paths.

name: reduced false alarm rate
rationale: Corridors are occupied and trafficked spaces where nuisance alarms (e.g., from dust, humidity, or cooking odors) can cause unnecessary evacuations and disrupt building operations. Minimising false alarms is a key design pressure.

name: restricted placement interference
rationale: Architectural features, ceiling obstructions, HVAC supply/return grilles, and lighting fixtures can interfere with smoke flow and detector performance. Placement must avoid such obstructions while respecting code-required spacing.

name: adequate coverage spacing
rationale: Building codes (e.g., NFPA 72) mandate maximum spacing between detectors in corridors to ensure no point is beyond detection range. Ensuring sufficient coverage is a regulatory and life-safety requirement.

name: adequate lighting power to corridor outlet
rationale: Electrical outlets in corridors must provide sufficient power capacity for cleaning equipment, maintenance tools, and temporary lighting, driving a need for adequately rated outlets.

name: limited outlet count to reduce clutter and cost
rationale: Architectural and aesthetic considerations often restrict the number of visible electrical outlets in a corridor to maintain clean wall surfaces and minimize construction costs.

name: Reduced energy consumption pressure
rationale: Corridor lights are often left on unnecessarily; a corridor light switch enables selective activation only when illumination is needed (e.g., via manual or sensor-triggered switching), directly reducing standby and unnecessary energy use.

name: Adequate illumination pressure
rationale: Building codes and occupant safety require sufficient light levels in corridors for safe circulation; the corridor light switch must allow turning lights on to meet minimum illuminance standards when the corridor is occupied.

name: Reduced maintenance burden pressure
rationale: A corridor light switch can reduce bulb replacement frequency and maintenance costs by ensuring lights are off when not needed, thus extending lamp life and lowering maintenance demands.

name: Optimized temperature control for comfort
rationale: A corridor thermostat is designed to maintain comfortable temperatures in hallway spaces, so there is a design pressure to optimize its temperature control settings for occupant comfort.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Building energy codes and sustainability goals create a pressure to minimize HVAC energy use, which applies to corridor thermostats by avoiding unnecessary heating or cooling in transient spaces.

name: Limited setpoint adjustment by occupants
rationale: Corridor thermostats are typically in semi-public zones where unauthorized occupant adjustments should be prevented or restricted to maintain consistent building operation.

name: Improved corner protection
rationale: Corner guards are specifically designed to protect corridor corners from impact damage (e.g., from carts, equipment, furniture). There is a design pressure to improve/provide adequate impact resistance, durability, and coverage to prevent damage to the wall surface behind.

name: Reduced visual obstruction
rationale: Corner guards should be as low-profile and visually unobtrusive as possible to avoid interfering with circulation, sight lines, and the aesthetic finish of the corridor. This drives design toward slimmer profiles, low reflectance, and color integration.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: There is a design pressure to minimise the effort, cost, and skill required to install corner guards, favouring simple adhesive-mount or snap-on mechanisms over complex mechanical fastening systems.

name: reduced width
rationale: Building codes (e.g., ADA, IBC) and corridor egress requirements often constrain door frame width to minimum clear opening widths (typically 32-36 inches), creating a design pressure to limit/reduce the frame's overall dimensions relative to the opening.

name: enhanced fire rating
rationale: Corridor door frames often require fire-rated assemblies (e.g., 20-minute or 1-hour ratings) per building and fire codes, imposing a design pressure for improved fire resistance through materials, seals, and construction.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: If the corridor separates conditioned from unconditioned spaces or exterior walls, the door frame may need to minimize heat transfer, creating a pressure to reduce thermal bridging through the frame material.

name: Improved fire and smoke containment
rationale: Corridor door closers are critical components in fire-rated corridor doors; building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) require doors to self-close and latch to contain smoke and fire. This is a primary design pressure.

name: Reduced opening force for accessibility
rationale: ADA and accessibility standards limit the force required to open doors (typically max 5 lbf for interior doors). This creates a competing pressure against stronger closing force.

name: Increased closing force for reliable latching
rationale: The door closer must provide enough force to overcome hinges, air pressure differentials, and door weight to ensure the door fully latches, preventing unwanted opening.

name: Minimised slamming and noise
rationale: In occupancies like hotels, hospitals, and offices, door closers must be adjusted to avoid loud slamming that disturbs occupants, often addressed by backcheck and latching speed adjustments.

name: Reduced maintenance and wear failure risk
rationale: Door closers are subject to heavy cycling in corridors; the design must minimise hydraulic fluid leaks, spring fatigue, and seal failure over the product lifespan.

name: increased accessibility
rationale: Corridor thresholds must provide accessible passage for wheelchairs, walkers, and people with mobility aids, requiring a flush or low-profile transition between spaces.

name: reduced tripping hazard
rationale: Thresholds with excessive height change or abrupt edges create trip risks for pedestrians, especially in high-traffic corridors.

name: improved weather sealing
rationale: If the corridor threshold is at an exterior or semi-exterior location, it needs to resist air infiltration, water ingress, and thermal bridging.

name: reduced material wear
rationale: High foot traffic across a corridor threshold causes surface wear; specifying durable materials can decrease the need for frequent replacement.

name: Increased sprinkler coverage
rationale: Building codes (e.g., NFPA 13, IBC) require corridor sprinkler piping to provide adequate coverage for egress paths, driving a need for sufficient pipe sizing and head spacing to ensure fire suppression effectiveness.

name: Reduced pipe run complexity
rationale: Corridor sprinkler piping is often constrained by corridor width, ceiling plenum depth, and the need to avoid clashes with other MEP services, creating a pressure to minimise routing complexity and bends.

name: enhanced structural strength
rationale: Balustrades must meet building code requirements for structural load resistance (e.g., lateral loads, live loads from people leaning or pushing), driving a need for greater strength and stiffness in the balustrade system.

name: increased height
rationale: Building codes and safety regulations mandate minimum balustrade heights (typically 900-1100 mm depending on jurisdiction and fall height), creating a design pressure to increase or maintain adequate height.

name: reduced baluster spacing
rationale: Child-safety codes restrict gaps between balusters (typically max 100-120 mm) to prevent children passing through, creating a design pressure to limit or reduce spacing.

name: improved corrosion resistance
rationale: If the balustrade is exposed to outdoor or coastal environments, material selection is driven by the need for better resistance to rust and weathering to ensure longevity and safety.

name: improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Stairwell walls serve as critical fire barriers in egress paths. Building codes (e.g., IBC) require fire-resistance-rated construction for stairwell enclosures to protect occupants during evacuation.

name: enhanced structural stability
rationale: Stairwell walls often contribute to lateral load resistance and must maintain integrity under gravity and seismic/wind loads to keep egress paths operational.

name: reduced smoke infiltration
rationale: Stairwells are designated smoke-protected areas; minimizing smoke penetration through gaps, joints, or penetrations in stairwell walls is essential for safe egress.

name: restricted wall penetrations
rationale: Penetrations (e.g., ducts, pipes, cables) through stairwell walls compromise fire and smoke integrity; building codes limit their number, size, and require firestopping.

name: adequate ventilation capacity
rationale: Smoke vents must provide sufficient flow area and capacity to exhaust smoke during a fire, as required by building codes and smoke control engineering principles.

name: restricted unintended airflow
rationale: Smoke vents must minimise air leakage when closed to avoid compromising compartmentation and to ensure they activate only when intended.

name: higher fire resistance rating
rationale: Smoke vent assemblies and their surrounding structure require adequate fire resistance to maintain integrity during a fire event.

name: enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Stairwell doors serve as critical fire barriers in egress paths. Building codes require fire-rated doors to contain smoke and flames, so there is a design pressure to increase fire resistance.

name: reduced opening force
rationale: Accessibility codes (e.g., ADA) mandate that stairwell doors require minimal force to open, typically not exceeding 5 lbf (22 N) for interior doors, to ensure egress for all occupants including those with disabilities.

name: improved door closing reliability
rationale: Stairwell doors must reliably self-close and latch to maintain fire and smoke compartmentation, creating a design pressure for robust automatic closers and positive latching mechanisms.

name: adequate emergency stairwell lighting
rationale: Building codes and life safety regulations (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) mandate minimum illumination levels in stairwells for safe egress during power failure.

name: reduced energy consumption of stairwell lighting
rationale: Energy codes and sustainability goals drive use of occupancy sensors, LED fixtures, and daylight harvesting to limit unnecessary lighting operation and power use.

name: minimised maintenance requirements for stairwell lighting
rationale: Stairwell fixtures are difficult to access, so design prefers long-life LEDs and durable components to reduce relamping and servicing frequency.

name: improved visibility and legibility
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC) require stairwell signage to be highly visible and legible to support emergency egress and firefighter access. There is an upward pressure to increase text size, contrast, illumination, and reflectivity to meet code compliance and safety standards.

name: reduced obstruction or concealment
rationale: Signage must not be blocked by doors in the open position, storage, or wall finishes that could hide it from view. Design pressures act to minimise/eliminate physical obstructions to ensure the sign remains visible at all times.

name: Increased heat transfer rate
rationale: Heat exchangers are fundamentally designed to transfer thermal energy between fluids; a higher heat transfer coefficient or larger surface area is a primary design pressure to improve thermal performance.

name: Reduced pressure drop
rationale: Minimising pressure loss across the heat exchanger is critical to reduce pumping power and operating costs, directly influencing flow path design and tube/plate geometry.

name: Reduced fouling
rationale: Fouling (deposit buildup) degrades thermal performance over time; design pressures favour geometries and materials that minimise fouling to maintain efficiency and reduce maintenance.

name: Increased compactness
rationale: Space and weight constraints often drive heat exchanger designs toward higher area-to-volume ratios (compact heat exchangers), especially in aerospace, automotive, and marine applications.

name: adequate water flow pressure
rationale: A circulation pump must provide adequate water flow to overcome system resistance and meet heating/cooling demand; insufficient flow is a common engineering design pressure.

name: minimised energy consumption pressure
rationale: Circulation pumps consume significant electrical energy; reducing pump energy use is a standard engineering design objective, driving selection of efficient pumps and variable-speed drives.

name: minimised noise and vibration pressure
rationale: Pumps generate mechanical noise and vibration that can propagate through piping; limiting these is a common design constraint, especially in occupied spaces.

name: sufficient expansion capacity
rationale: An expansion vessel must have adequate volume to accommodate thermal expansion of the system fluid, preventing overpressure events.

name: higher maximum working pressure
rationale: The expansion vessel must be rated to withstand the maximum operating pressure of the system it serves, ensuring structural integrity.

name: reduced pre-charge pressure loss
rationale: Minimising loss of the nitrogen pre-charge pressure over time is critical for maintaining the vessel's ability to absorb expansion and keep system pressure stable.

name: Optimised heat retention
rationale: Hot water cylinders benefit from optimised insulation to retain heat, reducing standby losses and improving energy efficiency.

name: Reduced heat loss
rationale: Minimising heat loss from the cylinder surface and pipework connections is a key design pressure to maintain water temperature efficiently.

name: Adequate storage capacity
rationale: The cylinder must provide sufficient hot water storage volume to meet peak demand without excessive reheat time.

name: Lower standing losses
rationale: Design standards and regulations push for reduced standing heat losses through better insulation and cylinder design.

name: adequate water storage capacity
rationale: Cold water storage tanks must provide sufficient volume to meet building demand (potable, fire, flushing) and maintain reserve for peak usage or emergencies. This is a primary functional requirement.

name: reduced thermal gain
rationale: To maintain water quality and prevent bacterial growth (e.g., Legionella), heat ingress into the tank must be minimised through insulation, location, and material selection.

name: reduced physical footprint
rationale: Space constraints in plant rooms or roof areas often push toward more compact tank designs, affecting shape, material, and location choices.

name: enhanced sealing integrity
rationale: Valve assemblies must maintain leak-tight sealing under operating pressures and thermal cycles; this is a fundamental engineering requirement for valve components.

name: reduced pressure drop across valve
rationale: Minimising flow resistance through the valve assembly is a standard design pressure to avoid excessive energy losses and ensure system efficiency.

name: minimised actuation force requirement
rationale: Lower force needed to open/close the valve reduces actuator size and energy consumption, a typical mechanical design consideration for valve assemblies.

name: higher structural load capacity
rationale: A piping manifold must withstand internal pressure from fluid media, thermal expansion stresses, and external loads (e.g., from connected equipment or supports). Increased load capacity ensures structural integrity and leak-free operation.

name: restricted pressure drop
rationale: Piping manifolds distribute fluid to multiple branches; excessive pressure drop reduces system efficiency. Minimising pressure drop is a key design objective for manifold sizing and layout.

name: minimised leakage risk
rationale: Manifolds have multiple joints and connections; leaks can cause safety hazards, fluid loss, and environmental damage. Design decisions (joint type, gasket selection, welding quality) aim to eliminate leakage pathways.

name: optimised flow distribution
rationale: For manifolds with multiple outlets, achieving balanced flow distribution across branches is critical to process performance. Design pressure drives selection of manifold geometry (header size, branch spacing, tapering).

name: Improved energy efficiency
rationale: VSDs inherently improve motor energy efficiency by matching motor speed to load demand, reducing energy consumption compared to fixed-speed operation.

name: Reduced mechanical stress
rationale: VSDs enable soft-start/stop and gradual speed changes, which reduce mechanical shock, wear, and stress on motors and driven equipment.

name: Reduced harmonic distortion
rationale: Design decisions for VSDs often target minimising harmonic distortion through input filters or multi-pulse configurations to protect power quality.

name: Adequate electrical capacity and fault current rating
