rationale: Fan vaults are masonry structures that require sufficient load-bearing capacity to support their own weight and any superimposed loads; this is a fundamental structural engineering requirement for their design.

name: reduced lateral thrust
rationale: Fan vaults generate lateral thrust at their bases, which must be minimised or contained through buttressing or tie mechanisms to prevent structural failure.

name: optimised geometric precision
rationale: Fan vaults depend on highly precise radial and conical geometry to interlock stone ribs correctly; this is central to their architectural design and structural integrity.

name: Reduced material stress
rationale: The dome/sail vault geometry distributes loads efficiently through compression, reducing tensile stress concentrations compared to flat spans.

name: Enhanced structural stability
rationale: Curved form of dome/sail vault provides inherent stability through arching action, resisting buckling and lateral forces better than simple planar systems.

name: Adequate vertical load capacity
rationale: Dome/sail vault efficiently transfers gravity loads (self-weight, live loads) to supports along its perimeter through membrane action.

name: Greater compressive load capacity
rationale: Tile vaults (Guastavino vaults) rely on compression rather than tension; increasing compressive load capacity directly improves structural performance and safety.

name: Reduced tensile stress
rationale: Guastavino tile vaults are masonry systems weak in tension; minimizing tensile stress is critical to prevent cracking and failure.

name: Improved bond between tiles and mortar
rationale: The structural integrity of layered tile vaults depends on strong adhesion between successive tile layers and mortar; better bonding enhances stiffness and durability.

name: Optimised arch geometry
rationale: The thin-shell efficiency of Guastavino vaults is highly dependent on precise curvature; optimised geometry ensures pure compression paths and material savings.

name: Improved sound absorption performance
rationale: The primary design purpose of vault acoustic treatment is to absorb sound and control reverberation. There is a consistent engineering pressure to increase/improve its sound absorption coefficient (NRC rating) to meet acoustic design targets in spaces like auditoriums, recording studios, or lecture halls.

name: Reduced visual intrusion
rationale: Acoustic treatments (panels, baffles, diffusers) installed on or within a vaulted ceiling can conflict with the architectural aesthetic. There is a design pressure to minimise their visual prominence — e.g., through colour matching, concealment, or slim profiles — so the vault's form remains visually clean.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Vault acoustic treatment components (panels, insulation, mounting hardware) add dead load to the vault structure. There is a structural/engineering pressure to keep this added weight minimal to avoid overloading the vault or requiring additional structural reinforcement.

name: Increased installation cost
rationale: Higher-performance acoustic treatments (custom shapes, high-NRC materials, fire-rated finishes) tend to increase material and labour costs. Budget constraints create a pressure that pushes back against selecting the most acoustically effective option.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Acoustic materials installed on ceilings/vaults must comply with fire safety codes (e.g., Class A or Class 1 fire rating per building regulations). There is a persistent design pressure to ensure the acoustic treatment meets or exceeds required flame-spread and smoke-development indices.

name: Improved drainage capacity
rationale: A vault drainage/weep system must adequately handle water ingress to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup and moisture damage. Increasing drainage capacity directly improves performance.

name: Reduced blockage risk
rationale: Weep systems and drainage paths are prone to clogging from debris, sediment, or biological growth. Designing to minimise blockage is critical for long-term functionality.

name: Sufficient weep hole sizing
rationale: Weep holes must be adequately sized to allow water egress while preventing ingress of pests or debris, per standard retaining wall and vault drainage practice.

name: Lower risk of frost damage
rationale: In cold climates, trapped water in drainage systems can freeze and cause spalling or pipe fracture. Reducing this risk is a key design pressure.

name: Increased structural depth
rationale: Vault web panels derive their stiffness and load-bearing capacity from their depth; increasing structural depth improves their ability to resist shear and bending moments without buckling.

name: Reduced panel thickness
rationale: Thinner web panels reduce material usage and self-weight, which is a common optimisation goal, but must be balanced against buckling resistance and shear capacity.

name: Increased buckling resistance
rationale: Vault web panels are slender by nature and susceptible to buckling under compressive or shear forces; designing for higher buckling resistance (via stiffeners, corrugation, or increased thickness) is a primary engineering pressure.

name: increased lateral thrust resistance at springing points
rationale: Vault springing points are the critical transition zones where vault thrust transfers to supports; increased resistance to lateral thrust (via heavier piers, buttresses, or tie rods) is a primary structural concern.

name: minimised differential settlement at springing supports
rationale: Uneven settlement at the springing points causes cracking and vault instability; minimising differential movement is essential for vault integrity.

name: adequate load-bearing capacity at springing level
rationale: The springing points must safely carry the accumulated dead and live loads from the vault above; ensuring sufficient vertical load capacity is a fundamental design requirement.

name: increased lateral thrust resistance
rationale: Vault lateral buttressing must provide sufficient resistance to the lateral thrust generated by a vault or arch. The design pressure is to increase the structural capacity of the buttressing to counteract horizontal forces and prevent outward displacement or collapse.

name: reduced horizontal displacement
rationale: A key design objective for lateral buttressing is to limit or minimise horizontal movement/deformation at the springing points of vaults. This ensures the stability and integrity of the overall vaulted structure under both dead and live loads.

name: optimized geometric proportioning
rationale: The mass, depth, and taper of buttressing elements are designed (often optimised) to efficiently transfer lateral loads to the foundation while respecting architectural form and spatial constraints.

name: reduced number of penetrations
rationale: Structural continuity of thin-shell vaults is critical; penetrations create stress concentrations and weaken the structure. Engineering logic pressures designers to minimise openings to preserve structural integrity.

name: adequate structural reinforcement around openings
rationale: Where penetrations are unavoidable, ring beams, thickened edges, or local reinforcement are typically required to redistribute forces around the opening, preserving vault stability.

name: limited opening size relative to vault span
rationale: Large openings relative to vault span compromise the membrane action of a shell. Engineering guidelines restrict opening dimensions to a fraction of the span to avoid failure modes.

name: Increased structural continuity at connections
rationale: Vault-to-wall connections require sufficient structural continuity to transfer thrust and lateral forces from the vault safely into the supporting wall, preventing separation or collapse.

name: Reduced differential movement between vault and wall
rationale: Differential settlement, thermal expansion, or seismic movement between vault and wall creates stress concentrations at the connection; minimising such movement improves connection durability.

name: Improved resistance to horizontal thrust
rationale: Vaults generate significant horizontal thrust at their springing points where they meet walls; connections must be designed to resist this thrust without excessive deformation or failure.

name: Adequate detailing for cracking prevention
rationale: The interface between vault edge and wall is prone to cracking from differential stiffness; proper detailing (e.g., reinforcement, expansion joints, bonding agents) is needed to prevent serviceability issues.

name: Improved water evacuation capacity
rationale: Vault drainage elements (e.g., drains, pipes, weep holes, sumps) must handle water ingress from rain, groundwater, or leakage. An 'improved' (increased) capacity ensures water is evacuated faster, preventing hydrostatic pressure buildup and water damage to the vault structure and contents.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Drainage systems in vaults are prone to debris, sediment, or biological growth that blocks flow. A 'reduced' (decreased) clogging risk — via filters, larger pipe diameters, or self-cleaning designs — is a key design pressure to maintain long-term drainage performance without frequent maintenance.

name: Minimised vulnerability to freezing
rationale: In cold climates, water in vault drainage components can freeze, causing blockages or pipe bursts. Design pressure to 'minimise' (decrease) freezing risk — via insulation, deep placement below frost line, or heat tracing — is a specific concern for vault drainage systems.

name: increased natural ventilation
rationale: Operable windows allow controllable natural ventilation; increasing airflow through the opening is a primary design pressure.

name: reduced air infiltration when closed
rationale: Operable windows must seal effectively when closed to minimise uncontrolled air leakage, balancing operability with airtightness.

name: improved thermal insulation
rationale: The window assembly (frame and glazing) is subject to pressure for better thermal performance to reduce heat loss/gain.

name: restricted opening size for safety
rationale: Building codes and fall safety requirements limit the clear opening dimensions (e.g., max 100mm gap) for windows above ground floor.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Thermal bridging through curtain wall framing reduces energy efficiency; design efforts aim to minimise heat transfer through mullions and transoms.

name: increased structural wind resistance
rationale: Curtain walls must resist wind loads; stronger framing, thicker glass, and robust anchorage are needed to withstand design wind pressures.

name: optimised daylight transmittance
rationale: Glass selection and frit patterns are tuned to balance daylight admission with solar heat gain and glare control.

name: reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Low-e coatings, spectrally selective glazing, and shading are employed to minimise solar heat gain through the curtain wall.

name: adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: Laminated glass, insulated glazing units, and proper sealing are designed to achieve sufficient sound transmission class ratings.

name: improved thermal insulation
rationale: French doors have large glass panes that are weak points for heat transfer. Improved thermal insulation (e.g., double/triple glazing, low-E coatings) is a key design pressure to reduce energy loss through the door assembly.

name: reduced air infiltration
rationale: The hinged double-leaf configuration of French doors creates multiple seal points where air leakage can occur. Design pressures push for reduced air infiltration through better weatherstripping and tighter clearances.

name: enhanced structural rigidity
rationale: French doors have a wider unspan than standard doors due to the paired-leaf configuration, and the large glass area reduces inherent stiffness. Enhanced structural rigidity is needed to resist wind loads and prevent sagging over time.

name: greater security resistance
rationale: French doors are historically considered vulnerable entry points because of the large glass panes and the interlocking mechanism between the two leaves. Design pressures push for greater security resistance through tempered/ laminated glass, multi-point locks, and reinforced frames.

name: improved swing clearance
rationale: Pivot doors require adequate clearance on both sides (push/pull) due to their full-swing arc, unlike hinged doors. Insufficient space limits operation and accessibility.

name: reduced pivot friction
rationale: Lower friction at the top and bottom pivot points ensures smooth operation and reduces wear on the door mechanism over time.

name: higher structural rigidity
rationale: Pivot doors carry their weight at top and bottom pivots rather than along a side jamb, requiring greater stiffness to prevent sagging and misalignment.

name: improved weather sealing
rationale: The continuous gap around a pivot door's perimeter makes it more challenging to seal against air and water infiltration compared to a standard hinged door.

name: improved thermal insulation
rationale: Bi-fold doors often consist of large glazed panels, making thermal insulation a key design pressure to reduce heat loss/gain through the large surface area.

name: reduced operational friction
rationale: Bi-fold doors rely on tracks, hinges, and rollers; minimising friction is critical for smooth folding and sliding operation, preventing jamming and wear.

name: enhanced structural rigidity
rationale: As a multi-panel folding assembly, the door needs adequate stiffness to resist wind loads and maintain alignment without sagging or buckling.

name: minimised clearance gaps
rationale: Tight tolerances between panels and frames are needed to prevent air/water infiltration and to ensure proper sealing when closed, but must be balanced against movement clearance.

name: improved weather sealing
rationale: Externally located bi-fold doors are subjected to rain and wind; effective gaskets and drainage are essential to prevent water ingress through the folding joints.

name: improved acoustic insulation
rationale: The primary purpose of an acoustic door is to block sound transmission. Design pressure exists to increase the acoustic insulation performance (STC rating) of the door assembly to meet project noise isolation requirements.

name: reduced air leakage
rationale: Sound flanking paths are the main failure mode for acoustic doors; air gaps around the door perimeter severely degrade acoustic performance. Therefore a design pressure exists to minimise air leakage through perimeter gaskets and seals.

name: increased mass
rationale: Sound transmission loss increases with mass (mass law). There is a design pressure to increase the mass per unit area of the door leaf (denser core materials, thicker construction) to improve acoustic attenuation.

name: reduced vibration transmission
rationale: Structural vibration can bypass the door's acoustic isolation. Design pressures exist to minimise vibration transfer through hinges, frames, and hardware, typically via resilient mounting or acoustic break hardware.

name: improved perimeter sealing
rationale: Compression seals, drop seals, and acoustic gaskets at all edges of the door are essential to maintain the acoustic barrier. There is a direct design pressure to improve the effectiveness and durability of perimeter sealing systems.

name: improved structural rigidity
rationale: The door frame must resist forces from door operation (closing, slamming) and lateral loads (wind, accidental impact) without excessive deflection or warping. Increased rigidity ensures dimensional stability over time.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: As part of the building envelope, the door frame should minimise conductive heat loss through its material (typically aluminium, steel, or timber) to maintain thermal performance and avoid condensation issues at the frame-to-wall interface.

name: adequate weather sealing
rationale: The frame must accommodate gaskets, seals, and drainage provisions to prevent water ingress, air leakage, and draughts. This directly influences the frame profile design and material selection.

name: minimised dimensional tolerances
rationale: Tight tolerances in frame fabrication and installation are required for proper door operation, consistent reveal gaps, and compatibility with ironmongery and door leaf.

name: increased structural strength
rationale: Window frame and sash must resist wind loads, impact loads, and support glazing weight. Engineering design standards (e.g., ASCE 7, Eurocode) prescribe strength requirements for frames and sashes.

name: improved thermal resistance
rationale: Frames and sashes are a critical part of the building envelope thermal performance. Requirements for U-value, thermal bridging mitigation, and energy codes drive the need for better thermal insulation in frame and sash assemblies.

name: reduced air infiltration
rationale: Air leakage through frame/sash joints is a key performance metric. Building codes and energy standards (e.g., AAMA/WDMA/CSA 101/I.S.2/A440, passive house standards) require low air leakage rates for window assemblies.

name: improved water penetration resistance
rationale: Frames and sashes must resist water ingress under wind-driven rain conditions. AAMA and NAFS standards specify water penetration resistance test pressures based on design pressure ratings.

name: reduced manufacturing complexity
rationale: Manufacturing constraints such as profile extrusion limits, joinery complexity, and cost pressures push toward simpler frame and sash geometries.

name: restricted visual obstruction
rationale: Architectural design preferences for daylighting and views drive demand for slim frame profiles and narrower sash sightlines to maximise the glazed area.

name: Increased security requirement
rationale: Building security codes and user safety demands necessitate robust, tamper-resistant door hardware. Handles and locks must resist forced entry, which drives a need for stronger materials and more sophisticated locking mechanisms.

name: Enhanced accessibility pressure
rationale: Accessibility standards (e.g., ADA, building codes) require lever-type handles (not knobs), appropriate heights, and easy-operation hardware to accommodate persons with disabilities, increasing the complexity and specificity of hardware choices.

name: Greater durability requirement
rationale: Door hardware experiences frequent cyclic loading (opening/closing) and wear. Hinges, handles, and locks must withstand repeated use over the building lifespan without failure, demanding robust materials and finishes.

name: Lower cost pressure
rationale: Budget constraints across a construction project push toward more economical hardware selections, potentially limiting material quality, finish grade, or brand choices.

name: improved water runoff management
rationale: The window sill must be designed to effectively shed water away from the wall and window assembly, preventing moisture ingress. A proper slope and drip edge on the sill are essential architectural details.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: The window sill and surround are potential locations for thermal bridging where the window frame meets the wall. Engineering design should minimise heat loss through these junctions.

name: adequate structural support for weight
rationale: The window sill must structurally support the weight of the window above and any live loads. This is a fundamental structural engineering requirement for window sill design.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: A lintel must bear the vertical load from the wall or structure above the opening. Increased load-bearing capacity directly improves the lintel's ability to span the opening without deflection or failure.

name: Reduced span length
rationale: The span of the opening directly affects bending moment and shear forces on the lintel. A reduced span lowers structural demands on the lintel, allowing for lighter sections.

name: Sufficient depth-to-span ratio
rationale: Adequate depth relative to span is critical to prevent excessive deflection. Engineers specify minimum depth-to-span ratios for lintel design to ensure stiffness and serviceability.

name: Increased lateral restraint
rationale: Lateral torsional buckling can occur in slender steel or timber lintels. Greater lateral restraint from surrounding masonry or connections improves stability.

name: Reduced point load concentration
rationale: Concentrated loads (e.g., from beams or columns bearing on the lintel) can cause localised failures. Minimising point loads or distributing them improves lintel performance.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Window shading/sunscreen primarily functions to decrease the amount of solar radiation entering a building, reducing heat gain and cooling loads.

name: Enhanced daylight control
rationale: Effective window shading must balance glare reduction with adequate daylight penetration, driving the need for optimised shading design.

name: Improved occupant comfort
rationale: Window shading directly impacts thermal and visual comfort for occupants, pushing toward design solutions that control glare and overheating.

name: Reduced cooling energy demand
rationale: By blocking unwanted solar heat, effective sunscreen reduces the need for mechanical cooling, a key design pressure on shading selection.

name: Increased water resistance
rationale: Low sill flashing must provide adequate water resistance to prevent moisture ingress at window or door sills.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: The flashing material and installation must withstand weathering, thermal cycling, and long-term exposure without degradation.

name: Improved drainage
rationale: Proper slope and weep provisions are needed to direct water away from the sill assembly.

name: Improved water drainage
rationale: Low sill weep holes serve to drain water from window assemblies; improving their drainage performance directly supports the function of the weep holes and protects the surrounding building envelope from moisture damage.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Weep holes are prone to clogging by debris, dirt, or insects; reducing the risk of clogging is a key design consideration to maintain drainage functionality without blockage.

name: Prevented insect ingress
rationale: Weep holes create openings in the building envelope; preventing insects and pests from entering through these openings is a standard design requirement addressed by weep hole covers or mesh.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at low sill
rationale: The low sill interface is a critical junction where heat loss through thermal bridging commonly occurs. Design pressures push to minimise thermal bridging at this transition between window frame and wall assembly.

name: Enhanced water penetration resistance at sill
rationale: The sill is the most water-exposed part of a window interface, requiring robust flashing, slope, and drainage detailing to resist water ingress. This is a fundamental design pressure at this specific interface.

name: Reduced air leakage at sill junction
rationale: The junction between window sill and wall assembly is a common air leakage path. Design seeks to minimise uncontrolled airflow at this interface to maintain envelope airtightness.

name: Adequate structural support at sill
rationale: The low sill must bear the weight of the window assembly and transfer loads to the structure below. Adequate support is needed to prevent sagging, deflection, or failure at this interface.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at window reveals
rationale: A thermal break in a window reveal is specifically designed to reduce thermal bridging, which improves the overall envelope thermal performance and minimises heat loss at the interface between window frame and wall opening.

name: Improved overall wall U-value
rationale: By interrupting the conductive path through the wall assembly at the window reveal, the thermal break contributes to a better (lower) effective U-value for the wall assembly.

name: Adequate structural connection and airtightness
rationale: The reveal thermal break must provide sufficient structural rigidity and maintain airtightness at the window-to-wall interface; inadequate detailing here can compromise both thermal and structural performance.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at reveal corners
rationale: Reveal angle beads are used at window/door openings to create crisp corners; a key design pressure is to minimise thermal bridging at these junctions by choosing materials with lower conductivity.

name: Greater durability against impact and corrosion
rationale: Angle beads at exposed reveal corners are vulnerable to knocks and moisture; the design is pressured toward using stronger, corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., stainless steel or PVC) to maintain long-term performance.

name: Adequate plaster adhesion and edge definition
rationale: The primary function of a reveal angle bead is to form a straight, sharp edge for plastering; design is pressured toward profiles with expanded wings or mesh that ensure sufficient keying of plaster and a clean finish.

name: sufficient load-bearing capacity
rationale: The header/lintel above a low doorway must bear the weight of the wall above and any superimposed loads. Insufficient capacity could lead to structural failure.

name: minimised deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection of the lintel could crack the surrounding masonry or finishes and compromise the doorway's function.

name: adequate headroom clearance
rationale: A low doorway inherently has restricted height; the lintel's depth directly reduces available headroom, so minimising structural depth helps maintain usable clearance.

name: adequate clearance height
rationale: Clearance height markers are used to indicate the maximum height of a vehicle or object that can safely pass under a structure. There is a design pressure to ensure the marker is set at an adequate (accurate) height to prevent vehicle collisions with overhead obstructions, balancing safety with practical access.

name: restricted marker placement height
rationale: The physical placement of the clearance height marker is constrained by the actual structural clearance available. The marker cannot indicate a height greater than the actual physical clearance, imposing a restriction on what height value the marker can display.

name: Reduced structural loading on arch
rationale: A low doorway arch bears less vertical load from the structure above compared to taller arches, reducing compressive stress on the arch ring and abutments.

name: Limited headroom clearance
rationale: The arch's low height restricts passage of tall objects/people, acting as a design constraint on usable space.

name: Greater lateral thrust at springing points
rationale: A low, wide arch geometry produces higher horizontal thrust at the springing points compared to a taller arch of the same span, requiring stronger abutments or tie-backs.

name: improved head impact protection
rationale: The core purpose of a head protection pad is to cushion impacts against a low doorway header. This force drives the selection of thicker, higher-density, or more energy-absorbing padding materials to better mitigate injury risk.

name: reduced thickness profile
rationale: Excessive pad thickness can itself reduce headroom in an already low doorway, creating a worse clearance problem or a tripping/stooping hazard. There is a design tension between padding effectiveness and maintaining as much usable headroom as possible.

name: improved durability and adhesion
rationale: The pad must remain securely attached and intact over repeated incidental impacts. This drives the selection of robust adhesives, tough outer cover materials, and secure mounting methods to prevent delamination or detachment.

name: restricted headroom
rationale: The doorway is described as 'low', meaning its height is intentionally restricted or constrained, which limits passage and vertical clearance.

name: reduced accessibility
rationale: A low doorway inherently decreases accessibility for taller individuals or those moving equipment, creating a design constraint on flow and usability.

name: Reduced doorway height
rationale: The low doorway is defined by its limited vertical clearance, which constrains access and movement through it.

name: Greater accessibility requirements
rationale: Modern accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) pressure increasing the doorway height for wheelchair and universal access, conflicting with the existing low condition.

name: optimized edge geometry for reduced wind load
rationale: Edge tapering is a structural/aerodynamic detailing strategy to reduce wind-induced pressure at building edges; optimized tapering improves aerodynamic performance.

name: minimised structural load at building perimeter
rationale: Tapering edges reduces localised wind loads and stress concentrations at the building perimeter, directly influencing the design of the edge detail.

name: Improved dimensional accuracy
rationale: Precise edge formwork is critical for achieving accurate concrete dimensions, alignment, and finish quality at slab edges and joints.

name: Sufficient structural rigidity
rationale: Edge formwork must resist hydrostatic concrete pressure and construction loads without deformation to maintain shape and alignment during pouring.

name: Reduced formwork deflection
rationale: Minimising deflection under wet concrete load is essential to prevent bulging, misalignment, or wavy edges in the finished concrete element.

name: Eliminated concrete leakage
rationale: Tight joints and proper sealing at edges prevent grout loss (leakage), which causes surface defects, honeycombing, and material waste.

name: Improved ease of stripping
rationale: Formwork should be designed for clean removal without damaging the concrete edge or requiring excessive force, impacting reuse and edge finish.

name: Sufficient load-bearing capacity
rationale: The load-bearing edge profile must have adequate structural capacity to transfer loads from roof/deck to supporting structure, preventing failure under expected dead, live, and environmental loads.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Minimizing the weight of the edge profile itself reduces the structural load on the overall system and can simplify installation, though this must be balanced against strength requirements.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: As an edge component exposed to environmental conditions, enhanced corrosion resistance ensures long-term structural integrity and service life of the load-bearing edge profile.

name: increased edge reinforcement
rationale: Structural integrity of slab edges often demands sufficient reinforcement to resist shear, torsion, and moment forces — especially at perimeter or opening edges.

name: reduced reinforcement congestion
rationale: Overcrowding of reinforcement bars at edges can impede concrete placement and consolidation, so a design pressure exists to limit bar count or optimize spacing while meeting strength requirements.

name: adequate concrete cover maintained
rationale: Edge reinforcement must maintain sufficient concrete cover to protect against corrosion and fire, which is a standard design requirement in reinforced concrete detailing.

name: higher tensile strength
rationale: Post-tensioning edge anchors must withstand high tensile forces from the tendons. Higher tensile strength in the anchor assembly ensures structural integrity and prevents anchorage failure.

name: reduced bearing stress concentration
rationale: Edge anchors create localized bearing stresses in the concrete. Reduced stress concentration at the anchor-concrete interface prevents crushing, spalling, or bursting failures in the anchorage zone.

name: adequate corrosion protection
rationale: Edge anchors are exposed to environmental conditions at slab edges. Sufficient corrosion protection (galvanizing, epoxy coating, or greased caps) ensures long-term durability of the post-tensioning system.

name: minimised anchor seating losses
rationale: Anchor seating losses (wedge draw-in) reduce effective prestress. Minimised seating losses at the edge anchor ensure the intended prestressing force is transferred to the concrete member.

name: improved thermal resistance
rationale: A thermal break assembly is specifically designed to interrupt heat flow; design decisions naturally push toward higher thermal resistance (R-value) to reduce heat transfer across the assembly, improving energy efficiency.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: The primary purpose of a thermal break is to minimise thermal bridging between interior and exterior building elements. Design decisions aim to reduce conductive heat flow through structural connections.

name: adequate structural strength
rationale: Thermal break materials (often polymers or lower-strength inserts) must still bear structural loads. There is a design pressure to maintain sufficient structural capacity despite the thermal interruption, balancing thermal performance with mechanical integrity.

name: Increased structural load resistance
rationale: Column enclosure/cladding must resist wind loads, seismic loads, and impact loads. Engineering standards require cladding systems to transfer these loads to the structural frame.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Column enclosures should minimise heat transfer through the building envelope to improve energy performance and prevent condensation issues.

name: Improved weather resistance
rationale: Cladding must provide adequate resistance to water infiltration, air leakage, and moisture penetration to protect the building interior.

name: Reduced cladding weight
rationale: Lighter cladding systems reduce dead load on columns, frame, and foundation, potentially lowering structural requirements and costs.

name: improved edge sealing performance
rationale: The edge closure must provide adequate sealing to prevent moisture ingress and air leakage at the composite deck perimeter, which directly affects thermal performance and durability of the deck assembly.

name: reduced thermal bridging at edge
rationale: The edge closure detail is a common location for thermal bridging, so design pressure exists to minimise heat loss through the edge condition by optimising the closure's thermal performance.

name: adequate structural load resistance
rationale: The edge closure must withstand wind uplift, live loads, and other forces transferred at the deck perimeter, requiring sufficient strength and attachment detailing.

name: increased vertical load capacity
rationale: Column base must be designed to carry greater vertical loads from the column above, requiring stronger base plates, anchor bolts, and foundation connections.

name: reduced eccentricity
rationale: Eccentric loading at the column base introduces bending moments; minimising eccentricity improves structural performance and prevents base plate rotation or anchor bolt failure.

name: increased uplift resistance
rationale: Column bases in tension (uplift) scenarios — from wind or overturning — require adequate anchorage and base plate strength to resist pull-out forces.

name: improved lateral load transfer
rationale: Column base must transfer shear and moment from lateral loads (wind, seismic) into the foundation; better connection stiffness and strength are needed.

name: reduced base plate thickness
rationale: Cost and material optimisation may drive a desire for thinner base plates, but this must be balanced against bearing stress and weld requirements.

name: improved moment capacity
rationale: Column-to-beam connections must resist bending moments from gravity and lateral loads; higher moment capacity ensures structural integrity and prevents brittle failure at the joint.

name: increased shear strength
rationale: Shear forces are significant at beam-column joints; adequate shear strength is essential to prevent diagonal cracking or joint shear failure.

name: limited rotation
rationale: Excessive rotation at the connection can lead to serviceability issues (excessive drift) and compromise the overall frame stability; rotation must be constrained within acceptable limits.

name: minimised stress concentration
rationale: Stress concentrations at connection details (e.g., welds, bolts, stiffeners) can initiate fatigue cracks or brittle fracture; geometric and detailing choices aim to reduce localised stress peaks.

name: adequate ductility
rationale: Ductility in the connection allows energy dissipation during seismic events, preventing sudden collapse and enabling moment redistribution.

name: Improved load transfer capacity
rationale: The embedded column base plate must transfer axial and moment loads from the steel column into the surrounding concrete foundation. Increasing its load transfer capacity (via greater bearing area, thicker plate, or more/better anchor studs) is a key design pressure.

name: Sufficient embedment depth
rationale: Adequate embedment depth is essential to develop the full strength of the base plate and to prevent concrete breakout failure. Design codes prescribe minimum embedment depths relative to plate dimensions and applied loads.

name: Reduced plate bending stress
rationale: The base plate experiences bending under the applied column loads, bearing against the concrete. Minimising bending stresses — via adequate thickness or stiffeners — prevents yielding and excessive deformation of the plate.

name: reduced shaft size
rationale: Architectural and service coordination often push to minimise the footprint of vertical shafts (voids) to maximise usable floor area, leading to a pressure to reduce the shaft's horizontal dimensions.

name: adequate shaft size
rationale: Building services (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, elevators) require sufficient cross-sectional area within the shaft. MEP engineering standards drive a pressure to maintain or enlarge shaft dimensions to accommodate required risers, ductwork, and clearance for maintenance.

name: increased structural continuity
rationale: Where a column void or shaft passes through floor slabs, structural engineers prefer larger openings or specific layouts to maintain slab continuity and transfer loads efficiently, creating a pressure to expand or properly position the void.

name: higher compressive strength
rationale: Pedestal columns are short, load-bearing components that transfer vertical loads from superstructure to foundation; they require adequate compressive strength to resist crushing and buckling under axial loads.

name: reduced slenderness ratio
rationale: Pedestal columns typically have a low height-to-width ratio; design seeks to limit slenderness to prevent buckling failure.

name: adequate lateral reinforcement
rationale: Pedestal columns benefit from sufficient transverse reinforcement (ties or spirals) to confine concrete and improve ductility under axial and lateral loads.

name: higher clamping force on bolts
rationale: Higher bolt clamping force (pretension) increases friction in the connection, improving shear resistance and stiffness. This is a fundamental mechanical requirement for bolted connections.

name: reduced bolt hole clearance
rationale: Tighter bolt hole tolerances reduce slip in the connection and improve load transfer. Excessive clearance can lead to deformation and reduced stiffness.

name: adequate bolt diameter and grade
rationale: Sufficient bolt diameter and material grade ensure the connection can resist design tension and shear forces without failure.

name: limited eccentricity in load transfer
rationale: Minimising eccentric loading reduces secondary bending moments in bolts and connected plates, which otherwise could cause premature failure.

name: higher strength demand
rationale: Welded column connections must resist significant axial and moment forces, requiring increased strength to ensure structural integrity under design loads.

name: reduced stress concentration
rationale: Welding details at column connections create stress risers; minimising stress concentration is critical to avoid brittle fracture and fatigue failure.

name: adequate weld toughness
rationale: Weld metal and heat-affected zone must have sufficient toughness to resist crack propagation under cyclic and impact loads, especially in seismic regions.

name: restricted deformation capacity
rationale: Excessive deformation in the connection can compromise column stability and load transfer; limiting rotation and displacement is essential for performance.

name: improved fatigue resistance
rationale: Welded connections under cyclic loading are susceptible to fatigue crack initiation at weld toes; improving fatigue detail and quality extends service life.

name: increased axial load capacity
rationale: Column base plates must transfer axial compression from the column to the foundation. Greater axial load capacity is a fundamental design pressure, requiring adequate plate thickness, sufficient bearing area, and proper anchorage.

name: increased moment resistance
rationale: In moment-resisting frames, base plate connections must resist overturning moments. Higher moment capacity demands stronger welds, thicker plates, and more robust anchor bolt arrangements.

name: reduced uplift displacement
rationale: Tension uplift from wind or seismic loading must be constrained. Limiting uplift displacement governs anchor bolt sizing, embedment depth, and base plate stiffness to prevent excessive movement or pull-out.

name: sufficient shear transfer capacity
rationale: Horizontal shear forces at the column base (from lateral loads) must be transferred through the base plate to the foundation via friction, shear lugs, or anchor bolts in bearing. Adequate shear capacity is a critical design pressure.

name: reduced base plate thickness
rationale: While structural demands push thickness higher, there is a practical/economic pressure to minimise plate thickness to reduce material cost, fabrication effort, and weight — this tension governs optimisation.

name: higher rotational stiffness and strength
rationale: Moment connections must resist bending moments and rotation; higher stiffness and strength are required to maintain structural integrity under gravity and lateral loads.

name: improved ductility and energy dissipation
rationale: Seismic design demands ductile moment connections that can undergo large inelastic deformations without brittle failure to dissipate earthquake energy.

name: reduced stress concentration at welds
rationale: Stress concentrations at weld toes and beam flanges can lead to brittle fracture; weld detailing, access holes, and reinforcement aim to minimise these concentrations.

name: limited bolt slip and deformation
rationale: In bolted moment connections, slip in bolt groups reduces stiffness and can cause serviceability issues; pre-tensioning and slip-critical design are used to restrict slip.

name: adequate flange and web compactness
rationale: Local buckling of beam flanges or web in the connection region must be avoided; sufficient width-to-thickness ratios (compact sections) are needed to develop full moment capacity.

name: Increased shear capacity
rationale: The connection must resist vertical shear forces from beam end reactions; design standards (e.g., AISC, Eurocode 3) require sufficient shear capacity to prevent failure.

name: Reduced bolt slip
rationale: In bolted shear connections, slip at the bolt interface under service loads can affect structural performance; slip-critical design limits relative movement.

name: Adequate weld strength
rationale: Welded shear tab or directly welded connections require sufficient weld throat thickness and length to transfer shear forces without fracture.

name: Minimised stress concentration
rationale: Geometric discontinuities at the connection region (e.g., cope holes, weld starts/stops) can create stress risers; detailing aims to reduce these to avoid fatigue or ductile fracture.

name: Increased axial load capacity
rationale: Column cap/head connections are designed to transfer loads from beams or slabs to columns. Increasing axial load capacity ensures the connection can safely transmit higher vertical forces from the supported structure.

name: Improved shear transfer
rationale: The column cap/head connection must resist shear forces at the column-beam or column-slab interface. Improving shear transfer prevents punching shear failure and ensures structural integrity.

name: Reduced stress concentration
rationale: Geometric transitions at the column head create stress concentrations. Minimising these reduces the risk of local cracking or failure at the connection zone.

name: Increased moment resistance
rationale: In moment-resisting frames, the column cap/head connection must transfer bending moments between beams and columns. Higher moment capacity improves frame stability under lateral loads.

name: increased stiffness
rationale: Stiffener plates are added to column connections specifically to increase local stiffness and prevent buckling or excessive deformation under load.

name: reduced stress concentration
rationale: Stiffener plates distribute concentrated forces at beam-to-column connections, reducing peak stresses and preventing premature failure.

name: sufficient thickness
rationale: The plate must be adequately thick to resist buckling and bearing stresses without being overly heavy or uneconomical.

name: restricted out-of-plane deformation
rationale: Stiffener plates are designed to limit out-of-plane deflection or buckling of the column web or flange at the connection region.

name: higher shear capacity
rationale: Gusset plates at column connections must resist shear forces from bracing members; higher shear capacity is a fundamental design requirement.

name: reduced buckling risk
rationale: Gusset plates are slender steel plates prone to buckling under compression; design aims to minimise buckling through adequate thickness and stiffeners.

name: adequate thickness for bolt bearing
rationale: Gusset plate thickness must be sufficient to prevent bearing failure at bolted connections to columns and braces.

name: limited stress concentration at weld zones
rationale: Weld details at gusset-to-column and gusset-to-brace interfaces create stress concentrations; design aims to minimise these through smooth load paths and proper weld sizing.

name: greater stiffness for lateral load transfer
rationale: Gusset plates are key components in lateral force-resisting systems (e.g., braced frames) and must have sufficient stiffness to transfer lateral loads between braces and columns without excessive deformation.

name: increased moment capacity
rationale: A column haunch connection is used at beam-to-column junctions to increase moment capacity and rotational stiffness at the connection, often to meet seismic or gravity load requirements.

name: reduced stress concentration
rationale: The haunch profile is designed to reduce stress concentrations at the weld or bolted interface between beam and column by distributing forces over a larger effective area.

name: adequate stiffener placement
rationale: Stiffeners or continuity plates are often required at the column haunch connection region to prevent local flange/web buckling and ensure load transfer.

name: adequate bolt shear and tension capacity
rationale: The end plate connection relies on bolts to transfer shear and tensile forces from the beam to the column. Adequate bolt capacity is essential to prevent connection failure under design loads.

name: sufficient end plate thickness for bending
rationale: The end plate must be thick enough to resist bending deformations induced by bolt prying forces and tension from the connected member, ensuring stiffness and preventing premature yielding.

name: reduced weld stress concentration at plate-to-column interface
rationale: Welds connecting the end plate to the column flange experience stress concentrations due to geometry transitions and load eccentricity. Minimising these concentrations improves fatigue performance and ductility.

name: Increased shear capacity
rationale: Shear tabs (also called shear lugs or shear connection plates) must resist vertical shear forces transferred from the beam to the column. The design pressure to increase shear capacity drives decisions about plate thickness, bolt size, bolt pattern, and weld strength.

name: Reduced eccentricity moment
rationale: The shear tab connection is eccentrically loaded (the load is applied at a distance from the bolt group centroid), creating a rotational moment. Design seeks to minimise this eccentricity or account for it, often through positioning the bolts close to the beam web or using a stiffened tab to reduce out-of-plane bending.

name: Adequate bolt bearing strength
rationale: The bolt holes in the shear tab must have sufficient bearing capacity to prevent ovalisation and tear-out under shear loads, driving decisions on plate thickness, edge distances, and bolt spacing.

name: Sufficient weld capacity
rationale: The weld between the shear tab and the column (typically a fillet weld) must be designed with adequate strength to transfer the full shear force and any induced moment, driving decisions on weld size, length, and electrode type.

name: higher axial load capacity
rationale: Dowel connections transfer axial loads between columns; higher axial capacity demands stronger dowel embedment, greater bar diameter, and adequate development length to prevent pullout failure.

name: reduced reinforcement congestion
rationale: At column-dowel interfaces, excessive reinforcement can cause congestion, hindering concrete placement and consolidation; design pressures aim to limit bar count and spacing while maintaining required strength.

name: adequate embedment depth
rationale: Adequate embedment depth into the supporting element (e.g., footing or beam) is critical for developing the full yield strength of the dowel bars, governed by code-prescribed development lengths.

name: minimised misalignment tolerances
rationale: Construction tolerances for dowel placement need tight control to avoid eccentricities that induce bending moments in the connection, potentially reducing column axial capacity.

name: increased structural integrity
rationale: The socket connection must provide adequate strength to transfer loads between column and foundation; increased structural integrity ensures safety and stability under gravity and lateral loads.

name: reduced installation tolerance
rationale: Tight tolerances in the socket pocket and column alignment are critical for proper load transfer and grouting; reduced tolerances improve fit and structural performance.

name: adequate grout bonding
rationale: The gap between column and socket is typically filled with grout or non-shrink mortar; adequate bonding is essential for composite action and load transfer between precast column and foundation.

name: reduced construction complexity
rationale: Socket connections should be simple to erect and align on site; reduced complexity minimises labour, equipment requirements, and potential for errors during assembly.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Fire protection wrap around column connections must meet or exceed the required fire-resistance rating (e.g., ASTM E119 or UL 263) for the structural assembly, driving a need for higher fire rating performance.

name: Reduced installation thickness
rationale: Thinner fire protection wraps are often preferred to minimize encroachment on adjacent structural elements or architectural finishes, though this must be balanced against the required fire rating.

name: Adequate durability against mechanical damage
rationale: Column connections are vulnerable to impact during construction and service life; fire protection wrap must have sufficient mechanical durability (e.g., resistance to abrasion, puncture) to maintain integrity.

name: Eliminated gaps at interface
rationale: Gaps or openings at the wrap-to-steel interface create weak points for fire and smoke penetration; design pressures work to eliminate such gaps through proper detailing and tight-fit application.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: The ceiling/soffit of a stair vault must be structurally stable to support its own weight and any imposed loads, ensuring safety and durability.

name: Higher fire resistance rating
rationale: Stair enclosures and their soffits typically require fire-resistance ratings per building codes to prevent fire spread between floors.

name: Reduced moisture infiltration
rationale: The soffit area may be vulnerable to moisture penetration from above or adjacent spaces, which can degrade materials and lead to maintenance issues.

name: adequate ventilation for smoke extraction
rationale: Stair vault ventilation must provide adequate airflow for smoke extraction during a fire, ensuring means of egress remains tenable.

name: restricted air leakage to adjacent spaces
rationale: Fire and smoke containment requirements limit uncontrolled air movement between stair vaults and adjacent areas.

name: optimised natural ventilation opening sizing
rationale: Building codes often require optimised sizing of natural ventilation openings in stair vaults to balance smoke exhaust with structural and spatial constraints.

name: reduced pressure drop
rationale: Ducts are designed to minimise pressure loss along the airflow path, which reduces fan energy consumption.

name: adequate airflow capacity
rationale: Duct cross-sectional area must be sufficient to carry the required volume of air without excessive velocity or noise.

name: reduced heat transfer
rationale: Thermal insulation aims to minimise heat gain or loss through duct walls to maintain supply air temperature.

name: reduced noise generation
rationale: Duct geometry and sizing should limit air velocity to avoid excessive aerodynamic noise transmission to occupied spaces.

name: minimised leakage
rationale: Duct joints and seams should be sealed to prevent air leakage, which wastes energy and compromises system balance.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Duct hangers/supports must withstand the weight of ductwork, including dead load of ducts and live loads such as ice accumulation or maintenance personnel. Greater load-bearing capacity ensures structural safety and prevents sagging or collapse.

name: Reduced vibration transmission
rationale: Duct hangers/supports should minimise vibration transfer from HVAC equipment to the building structure. Limiting vibration transmission reduces noise and structural fatigue.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Duct hangers and supports in HVAC systems are exposed to condensation, humidity, and potential chemical exposure. Enhanced corrosion resistance extends service life and maintains structural integrity.

name: Restricted thermal bridging
rationale: Metal duct hangers can act as thermal bridges through insulation, reducing energy efficiency. Constrained thermal bridging via thermal breaks or non-metallic materials helps maintain HVAC system performance.

name: improved fire safety compliance
rationale: Duct dampers are critical for fire and smoke containment within HVAC ducts. Building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 90A, 92A) mandate fire dampers and smoke dampers to close upon detection of heat or smoke, preventing fire and smoke spread. There is a design pressure to improve fire safety compliance through proper damper selection, placement, and integration with fire alarm systems.

name: reduced air leakage
rationale: Dampers must minimise air leakage when closed to maintain system performance, energy efficiency, and zone pressurisation control. Leakage classifications (Class I, II, III per AMCA/SMACNA standards) drive damper design selections. The design pressure is to reduce leakage rates through tighter seals and better construction.

name: optimised airflow control precision
rationale: Volume control dampers and balancing dampers are used to regulate airflow in ductwork. There is a design pressure to optimise control precision — achieving accurate flow modulation for zone temperature control, pressure-independent VAV operation, and system balancing — which influences damper actuator selection, blade geometry, and linkage design.

name: Higher cooling capacity
rationale: Radiant ceiling panels rely on sufficient cooling capacity to maintain comfort; design decisions often push for higher capacity to handle peak cooling loads.

name: Reduced condensation risk
rationale: Condensation on chilled ceiling panels is a critical concern; design pressures aim to minimise moisture accumulation by limiting surface temperature differentials or controlling humidity.

name: Improved thermal comfort distribution
rationale: Radiant panels must provide uniform temperature distribution across the occupied zone, pushing designs toward better layout and surface coverage.

name: Lower water supply temperature
rationale: To avoid condensation while maximising cooling output, the chilled water supply temperature must be carefully constrained above the dew point of the space.

name: Improved thermal comfort through radiant heat transfer
rationale: Radiant floor heating provides even heat distribution from the floor up, reducing cold spots and improving occupant comfort compared to forced air systems.

name: Reduced system thermal response time
rationale: The thermal mass of the floor slab introduces lag in heating response, creating a design pressure to minimise this lag through thinner slabs, higher conductivity materials, or embedded sensor control.

name: Higher energy efficiency via low-temperature operation
rationale: Radiant systems operate at lower supply water temperatures (30–50°C) than radiators or forced air, enabling compatibility with heat pumps and condensing boilers for better system efficiency.

name: Adequate floor covering thermal conductivity
rationale: Carpet and thick insulating floor coverings block heat transfer from the floor surface; designers are pressured to specify materials with low thermal resistance (R-value) to ensure adequate heat output.

name: Limited maximum floor surface temperature
rationale: Building codes and comfort standards (e.g., ASHRAE, ISO 11855) restrict floor surface temperature to around 29°C in occupied zones to prevent discomfort or burns, creating a design constraint on system sizing and layout.

name: Increased thermal efficiency
rationale: Radiant wall panels are designed for heat transfer; higher thermal efficiency directly improves their core function of heating or cooling a space.

name: Reduced surface temperature
rationale: For cooling applications, lower surface temperatures improve cooling capacity, but must be constrained to avoid condensation risk.

name: Optimised panel layout
rationale: Panel placement and spacing must be optimised to ensure uniform thermal distribution and avoid hot/cold spots.

name: Minimised installation cost
rationale: Cost pressures push toward simpler, less expensive installation methods while maintaining performance.

name: Increased heat distribution efficiency
rationale: As a component named 'Radiant Manifold', it likely distributes thermal energy (e.g., radiant heating or cooling fluid). Engineering design pressure favours optimising heat transfer and distribution uniformity.

name: Reduced pressure drop across manifold
rationale: Hydronic or air-based manifolds face pressure drop constraints; minimising this improves system efficiency and pump/fan energy use.

name: Reduced thermal losses to surroundings
rationale: Insulation and minimised heat loss from the manifold body are typical design pressures to maintain system efficiency.

name: Higher efficiency requirements
rationale: Building energy codes and sustainability targets (e.g., Part L, Net Zero goals) increasingly demand higher fuel-to-heat conversion efficiency from boilers and heat pumps. This drives selection of condensing boilers or high-COP heat pumps.

name: Reduced carbon emission limits
rationale: Regulatory pressure to lower operational carbon emissions pushes away fossil-fuel boilers toward heat pumps or hybrid systems, and limits the allowable emission rate from the chosen heat source.

name: Greater heating capacity demand
rationale: The building's heat loss calculation (driven by fabric, ventilation, climate) determines the required output capacity of the boiler or heat pump. Larger or poorly insulated buildings exert an upward pressure on capacity sizing.

name: Lower flow temperature requirements
rationale: Use of low-temperature heat emitters (underfloor heating, oversized radiators) or high-efficiency system design pushes toward lower flow temperatures, favouring heat pumps over traditional high-temperature boilers.

name: improved structural integration with roof
rationale: A dormer window unit must be structurally integrated into the roof assembly to transfer loads properly and prevent leakage or structural failure.

name: reduced thermal bridging at dormer-to-roof junction
rationale: The junction between a dormer and the roof is a common location for thermal bridging, requiring careful detailing to minimise heat loss and condensation risk.

name: adequate weather sealing against moisture infiltration
rationale: Dormer windows are exposed to wind-driven rain and snow accumulation; adequate flashing, weatherproofing, and sealing are critical to prevent water ingress.

name: Improved weather sealing pressure
rationale: Dormer window trim serves as a flashing and sealing interface between the window assembly and the roof. Design pressure exists to increase weathertightness (improved sealing) to prevent moisture intrusion at this vulnerable roof penetration.

name: Reduced material bulk pressure
rationale: Dormer window trim must often be kept slim/profiled to avoid excessive visual weight on the roofline and to fit within the available roof pitch and flashing constraints. There is a pressure to reduce trim bulkiness for aesthetic and fit reasons.

name: Increased durability pressure
rationale: The trim is directly exposed to rain, snow, wind, and UV at a roof intersection — a high-risk weathering zone. Strong design pressure exists to increase material durability (rot-resistant, UV-stable, corrosion-resistant) to achieve acceptable service life.

name: Increased water flow capacity
rationale: Dormer gutters and downspouts must handle rainwater runoff from the dormer roof. An increased capacity (larger cross-section, adequate slope, sufficient number of downspouts) ensures water is conveyed away without overflowing, protecting the dormer structure and adjacent roof areas.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Dormer gutters are often smaller and more prone to debris accumulation due to their position. Design pressures to minimise clogging (through leaf guards, proper sizing, adequate slope) ensure reliable drainage and prevent water backup that could damage the dormer.

name: Reduced ice dam formation
rationale: In cold climates, dormer gutters and downspouts are vulnerable to ice damming due to heat loss from the dormer. Design pressures to limit ice formation (proper insulation, heat tracing, adequate drainage slope) help maintain winter water flow and prevent structural damage.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: A shed dormer is typically added to bring more natural light into attic or upper-floor spaces. The design pressure is to increase or maximise daylight penetration through the dormer window.

name: Reduced roof complexity
rationale: Compared to a gabled dormer, a shed dormer has a simpler single-slope roof. There is a design pressure to minimise roof complexity, cost, and potential leak points by keeping the dormer form simple.

name: Adequate structural support for added volume
rationale: A shed dormer adds significant volume and roof load to the building structure. There is a design pressure to ensure sufficient/adequate structural support (rafters, headers, load paths) to carry the additional loads safely.

name: Improved headroom and usable floor area
rationale: A key purpose of a shed dormer is to increase usable headroom in a sloping roof space. The design pressure is to maximise or improve the interior floor area and ceiling height.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Flat-roof dormers introduce a break in the main roof's thermal envelope. Design decisions (e.g., insulation placement, roof deck detailing) aim to minimise thermal bridging at the junction between the dormer and the main roof.

name: adequate weatherproofing
rationale: Flat roofs are prone to water ponding and leakage. Flat-roof dormers require design decisions that ensure sufficient waterproofing, proper flashing, and membrane integrity at roof-to-wall intersections.

name: limited roof load
rationale: A flat-roof dormer must support its own dead load plus live loads (snow, maintenance). Design decisions constrain total roof load to remain within structural capacity of dormer framing and the supporting main roof structure.

name: enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Roof cap flashing is exposed to weather and moisture; corrosion resistance is a key design requirement to ensure durability and prevent leaks.

name: reduced thermal movement stress
rationale: Flashing experiences thermal expansion and contraction; design should minimise stresses from differential movement between flashing and adjacent roofing materials.

name: improved watertight sealing
rationale: The primary function of cap flashing is to prevent water infiltration at roof edges and penetrations; adequate sealing is critical.

name: limited wind uplift forces
rationale: As an edge component, roof cap flashing is vulnerable to wind uplift; design must constrain uplift vulnerability through secure fastening and aerodynamic profiling.

name: adequate structural support for roof loads
rationale: The roof cap substrate/deck must provide adequate structural support to withstand dead loads (self-weight, built-up roofing materials) and live loads (snow, maintenance personnel, equipment). Building codes require minimum load-bearing capacity for roof decks.

name: limited thermal bridging through deck
rationale: The substrate/deck material and thickness affect thermal bridging. Metal decks can conduct heat/cold, while structural wood or insulated panels reduce this effect. Energy codes and condensation risk drive the need to minimise thermal bridging at the roof deck level.

name: sufficient fire resistance rating
rationale: Roof decks must meet fire-resistance ratings per building code (e.g., IBC) based on occupancy and building type. The deck material (steel, concrete, wood) and any applied fireproofing directly affect fire performance of the roof assembly.

name: minimised deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection of the deck can damage roofing membranes, cause ponding water, and reduce service life. Stiffness requirements for the deck material and span are critical to roof performance.

name: Improved structural attachment
rationale: Roof cap coping must be securely attached to withstand wind uplift forces. An improved/stronger attachment prevents detachment during high winds, which is a primary design consideration.

name: Enhanced weather sealing
rationale: Roof cap coping serves as a weather barrier; better sealing prevents water infiltration at the parapet top, protecting the roof assembly and building interior.

name: Reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Metal coping can create thermal bridges at the parapet. Minimising thermal bridging through insulation breaks or non-thermal-conductive materials improves energy performance and prevents condensation.

name: Minimised material corrosion
rationale: Roof cap coping is exposed to weather and must resist corrosion. Using corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., aluminium, stainless steel, or coated metals) ensures long-term durability and reduces maintenance.

name: Increased durability against weathering
rationale: Roof cap gravel stops are exposed edge metal components at roof perimeters; they must resist corrosion, UV degradation, and thermal cycling. Higher material durability (e.g., thicker gauge metal, better coatings) extends service life and reduces maintenance.

name: Reduced water infiltration risk
rationale: Gravel stops serve as roof-edge flashing to prevent water from entering the roof assembly at the perimeter. Minimising leakage paths through secure fastening, proper overlap, and sealant is a primary design pressure.

name: Greater wind uplift resistance
rationale: As a perimeter edge metal, the gravel stop is subject to wind uplift forces. Stronger attachment methods (e.g., continuous cleats, proper fastener spacing) and stiffer profiles resist blow-off during high-wind events.

name: improved structural load-bearing capacity
rationale: As a roof cap component, the precast concrete element must bear dead loads (self-weight), live loads (maintenance access, snow), and wind uplift forces. Increasing load-bearing capacity ensures structural safety and compliance with building codes.

name: enhanced weather resistance and durability
rationale: As an exterior roof component exposed to rain, UV, freeze-thaw cycles, and thermal expansion, the precast concrete cap requires enhanced durability, proper curing, waterproofing, and adequate cover over reinforcement to prevent degradation and leakage.

name: reduced weight
rationale: Reducing the weight of the precast concrete roof cap lessens the dead load on supporting roof structure and foundations, which can lead to more economical structural design and easier installation/hoisting. This may be achieved through lightweight aggregates or optimized cross-sectional design.

name: restricted thermal bridging
rationale: Concrete has high thermal conductivity; a precast roof cap can create a thermal bridge at the roof edge or parapet. Limiting this thermal bridging through insulation integration or thermal breaks improves the building envelope's thermal performance and prevents condensation issues.

name: improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Metal roof caps are exposed to weather and require adequate corrosion resistance to maintain integrity and prevent rust over time.

name: higher wind uplift resistance
rationale: Roof caps are vulnerable to wind uplift forces; stronger attachment and aerodynamic design resist uplift pressures.

name: minimised thermal expansion stress
rationale: Metal components expand and contract with temperature changes; design must minimise stress from differential thermal movement to avoid buckling or seal failure.

name: adequate water shedding performance
rationale: The roof cap must effectively divert rainwater away from roof penetrations to prevent leakage and moisture damage.

name: Stronger wind uplift resistance
rationale: Roof cap fasteners and clips must resist wind uplift forces to prevent roof panel detachment during high wind events. Building codes (e.g., ASCE 7) require specific uplift resistance ratings for roof fastening components.

name: Higher corrosion resistance
rationale: Roof cap fasteners and clips are exposed to environmental moisture and temperature cycles; galvanized or stainless steel materials with higher corrosion resistance extend service life and maintain structural integrity.

name: Improved weathertightness
rationale: Sealant joints on roof caps must resist water ingress; this is a direct engineering requirement for roof cap sealant joints to maintain a weathertight building envelope.

name: Reduced thermal expansion effects
rationale: Thermal cycling causes expansion and contraction in roof cap materials; sealant joints need to accommodate movement without failure, so minimising the effects of expansion on joint integrity is a core design pressure.

name: Greater UV and weathering resistance
rationale: Roof cap sealants are directly exposed to solar radiation and environmental weathering, requiring enhanced material durability to avoid degradation and maintain performance over the service life.

name: Adequate adhesion to substrate
rationale: The sealant must bond reliably to the roof cap substrate materials (e.g., metal, concrete, or membrane); insufficient adhesion leads directly to joint failure.

name: Minimised joint movement constraints
rationale: Sealant joints must be designed to accommodate structural and thermal movements without being over-constrained, which would lead to tearing or debonding.

name: Improved moisture protection
rationale: A vapor barrier's primary function is to resist moisture diffusion. Designers aim to increase or improve this protective quality to prevent condensation and moisture damage within wall/roof assemblies.

name: Reduced permeability
rationale: To effectively block vapor migration, the membrane's permeability must be kept low (reduced). The lower the perm rating, the better the vapor barrier performs its function.

name: Adequate continuity and sealing
rationale: Gaps, tears, or poor sealing at laps and penetrations compromise the vapor barrier. Design and installation pressures push for sufficient/adequate continuity — fully sealed joints and transitions — to maintain an unbroken barrier.

name: Increased compressive strength
rationale: The screed/base layer must withstand compressive loads from floor finishes, furniture, and foot traffic. Higher compressive strength prevents cracking and deformation under load.

name: Reduced thickness
rationale: Thinner screed reduces self-weight on the structural slab and can help achieve floor-to-ceiling height requirements, but must be balanced against minimum thickness for durability and service integration.

name: Improved surface flatness
rationale: A flat, level screed surface is essential for proper installation of floor finishes (tiles, timber, vinyl) and to avoid unevenness that causes finishing failures or tripping hazards.

name: Reduced drying/shrinkage cracking
rationale: Excessive shrinkage during curing can lead to cracking, delamination, and loss of structural integrity in the screed layer. Fibre reinforcement or appropriate mix design mitigates this.

name: Adequate thermal conductivity
rationale: For underfloor heating systems, the screed should have sufficient thermal conductivity to efficiently transfer heat from pipes to the floor surface, influencing material selection (e.g., sand/cement vs. flowing screeds).

name: sufficient drainage capacity
rationale: Floor drains and trench drains must have adequate hydraulic capacity to handle anticipated water flow rates (stormwater, wash-down, or process water) without overflow, which is a fundamental sizing requirement.

name: reduced clogging risk
rationale: Debris, sediment, and solids accumulation can block drain inlets or piping; designs often incorporate traps, grates, or self-cleaning features to minimise blockages and maintenance needs.

name: adequate slope for drainage
rationale: Proper floor slope toward the drain/trench is essential for gravity flow; insufficient slope leads to ponding, stagnation, and ineffective drainage.

name: minimised odor emission
rationale: Floor drains without proper trap seals or with dried-out traps can emit sewer gases into occupied spaces; design pressures push for odor-control features such as deep-seal traps or trap primers.

name: Reduced thermal expansion stress
rationale: Expansion/control joints are specifically designed to accommodate thermal expansion and contraction, reducing stress and cracking in building materials.

name: Increased joint spacing for material stability
rationale: Proper spacing of control joints allows for adequate movement accommodation, preventing uncontrolled cracking in large concrete or masonry assemblies.

name: Improved movement accommodation capacity
rationale: Control joints must provide sufficient gap and filler material to allow differential movement between adjacent building elements without damage.

name: Reduced moisture intrusion risk at joints
rationale: Properly designed and sealed expansion joints prevent water and moisture ingress, which is a common failure point in building envelopes.

name: increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Access floor panels must support equipment loads (servers, heavy machinery) and foot traffic without deflection or failure. Higher load ratings are a primary design pressure.

name: improved accessibility to underfloor services
rationale: Access floor panels are designed to be easily removable to provide access to cabling, wiring, and air distribution below; easy lift-out is a core functional requirement.

name: minimised panel deflection under point load
rationale: Excessive deflection under concentrated loads (e.g., a server cabinet corner) can damage equipment and cause instability, so deflection must be tightly controlled.

name: reduced fire propagation risk
rationale: Access floor panels in plenum spaces must meet fire-rated material requirements to limit flame spread and smoke generation in the underfloor cavity.

name: sufficient electrostatic discharge (ESD) control
rationale: In data centers and server rooms, access floor panels must provide ESD protection to prevent damage to sensitive electronic equipment, often via conductive or dissipative surfaces.

name: increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Raised access floors must support concentrated loads from equipment (servers, cabinets) and pedestrian traffic. Engineering design standards specify minimum load-bearing ratings to prevent floor collapse or excessive deflection.

name: sufficient underfloor clearance height
rationale: The raised floor must provide adequate vertical space beneath the panels for routing cables, cooling ducts, and other services. Insufficient clearance restricts MEP distribution and maintenance access, a core functional requirement.

name: reduced floor vibration
rationale: Excessive vibration in raised access floors can disrupt sensitive electronic equipment (e.g., servers, data storage) and reduce occupant comfort. Stiffening the floor structure and limiting panel deflection reduces vibration transmission.

name: minimised panel deflection under point loads
rationale: Large point loads from heavy equipment cause local panel deflection, which can lead to instability, panel cracking, or misalignment. Engineering standards (e.g., ANSI/CEA) limit deflection to maintain structural integrity and walkability.

name: improved fire resistance rating
rationale: Raised access floors create concealed plenum spaces that can spread fire and smoke. Building codes require fire-resistant materials and rated construction to limit fire propagation, which influences panel material selection and underfloor firestopping.

name: Improved thermal comfort
rationale: Radiant floor systems provide even temperature distribution and reduce stratification, improving occupant comfort compared to forced air systems.

name: Reduced energy consumption
rationale: Radiant systems operate at lower water temperatures for heating and higher temperatures for cooling, improving heat pump and boiler efficiency.

name: Reduced system thermal response time
rationale: The high thermal mass of the floor slab results in slower response to temperature changes, which can be a design pressure to minimise lag through thinner screeds or embedded sensors.

name: increased load-bearing capacity
