rationale: Structural floor slabs must support vertical loads (dead, live, and dynamic loads). An increased load-bearing capacity ensures safety and serviceability, influencing decisions on slab thickness, reinforcement, and material strength.

name: reduced slab thickness
rationale: Minimising slab thickness reduces self-weight, material cost, and storey height. This design pressure competes with load-bearing and span requirements, affecting decisions on concrete grade, reinforcement layout, and structural system.

name: reduced deflection
rationale: Excessive deflection under load can cause cracking and serviceability failures. Limiting deflection drives decisions on slab depth, reinforcement ratio, span-to-depth ratios, and concrete modulus of elasticity.

name: adequate fire resistance
rationale: Floor slabs must achieve sufficient fire-resistance ratings per building codes. This affects decisions on concrete cover to reinforcement, slab thickness, and material selection (e.g., fire-resistant aggregates or supplementary reinforcement).

name: reduced material cost
rationale: Cost efficiency drives optimisation of slab design — balancing concrete volume, reinforcement quantity, and formwork complexity against structural requirements.

name: Improved slip resistance
rationale: Stair treads and landing surfaces must have sufficient friction to prevent slipping, which is a primary safety concern. Surface texture, material selection, and finish all contribute to slip resistance.

name: Adequate structural load capacity
rationale: Treads and landings must be designed to support anticipated live loads (people, goods) and dead loads (self-weight) without excessive deflection or failure.

name: Reduced tripping hazard at nosing
rationale: The leading edge or nosing of stair treads must be designed to minimise abrupt changes in level that could cause tripping, balanced with visual clarity of step edges.

name: Higher durability against wear
rationale: Stair treads experience concentrated foot traffic wear, especially at nosings. Material durability directly affects longevity and maintenance frequency.

name: Minimised积水 (water pooling)
rationale: For exterior stairs or landings, water ponding creates slip and ice hazards. Surface drainage and slope are critical design factors.

name: increased accessibility and convenience
rationale: Floor sockets/boxes provide power and data connectivity at floor level, reducing cable trip hazards and improving access compared to wall sockets, especially in open-plan or flexible workspaces.

name: reduced tripping hazard
rationale: Floor sockets/boxes are designed to be flush with the finished floor level, eliminating protruding cables and reducing the risk of tripping, which is a primary safety advantage over surface-mounted alternatives.

name: limited depth constraints for subfloor installation
rationale: Floor sockets require adequate subfloor depth for the enclosure body; shallow slab depths or existing underfloor services may restrict installation options or require custom shallow boxes.

name: improved aesthetic integration
rationale: Flush floor sockets are less visually intrusive than wall-mounted alternatives in spaces with glass walls, open layouts, or minimalist design intent, supporting a clean floor plane.

name: reduced weight
rationale: Floor gratings are designed to be lightweight for ease of handling, installation, and to minimise structural load on supports, while still providing adequate strength.

name: adequate load-bearing capacity
rationale: Floor gratings must support specified live loads (e.g., personnel, equipment, foot traffic) without excessive deflection or failure, driving decisions on bar size, spacing, and material thickness.

name: improved slip resistance
rationale: Grating surfaces need adequate friction (e.g., serrated bars, gritted surfaces) to prevent slipping, especially in wet or industrial environments.

name: maximised open area
rationale: Larger open area improves light transmission, airflow, and drainage, influencing decisions on bar pitch and pattern selection.

name: reduced corrosion susceptibility
rationale: Material selection (e.g., galvanized steel, stainless steel, fibreglass) and coatings are driven by the need to minimise corrosion in the service environment.

name: Improved slip resistance
rationale: Entrance mats must increase slip resistance to prevent falls in wet or dirty entry conditions, a primary function of floor mat products.

name: Higher dirt-and-moisture trapping capacity
rationale: The core functional purpose of an entrance mat is to trap dirt and moisture from footwear, requiring adequate material depth and texture to achieve this.

name: Reduced tripping hazard at edges
rationale: Entrance mats must have low-profile or beveled edges to minimize the tripping risk where the mat meets the surrounding floor surface.

name: Eliminated slipping of mat on floor
rationale: The underside of an entrance mat must prevent the mat itself from sliding across the floor, typically through anti-slip backing, to maintain safety.

name: Increased structural support for cladding
rationale: Lapped wall battens/counter-battens provide a structural substrate that supports cladding materials; increasing their structural capacity improves overall wall assembly performance.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through wall assembly
rationale: Counter-battens create a drainage and ventilation cavity while also reducing thermal bridging by separating cladding from the insulated structure; this is a well-documented design function.

name: Enhanced moisture drainage and ventilation behind cladding
rationale: Counter-battens create a vertical cavity that allows moisture to drain and air to circulate behind cladding, preventing trapped moisture and rot.

name: improved weather sealing
rationale: Lapped wall trim and corner boards serve as critical weather barriers at building envelope transitions. Increased sealing effectiveness prevents moisture intrusion at joints and corners.

name: reduced material warping
rationale: Warping of trim and corner board materials compromises both aesthetics and weatherproofing performance. Minimising warping through proper material selection and installation is a key design pressure.

name: enhanced dimensional stability
rationale: Dimensional stability under temperature and moisture cycles is essential for lapped trim components to maintain tight joints and prevent gaps over time.

name: minimised thermal bridging at corners
rationale: Corner boards can act as thermal bridges if made of highly conductive materials. Reducing thermal bridging improves overall envelope thermal performance.

name: greater pull-out resistance
rationale: Lapped wall fasteners must resist pull-out forces from wind suction and lateral loads on wall cladding. A greater pull-out resistance ensures the fasteners remain secure under tensile loading.

name: reduced corrosion susceptibility
rationale: Fasteners in external wall assemblies are exposed to moisture and environmental conditions. Reduced corrosion susceptibility prolongs service life and maintains clamping force over time.

name: reduced thickness
rationale: Thinner partition walls save floor area and reduce dead load on the structure, which is a common design pressure in multi-storey buildings.

name: adequate acoustic insulation
rationale: Partition walls between rooms (e.g., offices, bedrooms) require sufficient sound transmission class (STC) performance to meet building codes and occupant comfort expectations.

name: sufficient fire resistance
rationale: Partition walls often need fire-rated construction to comply with building codes for compartmentation, especially in egress paths and between different occupancies.

name: Higher impact resistance
rationale: Wall corner beads are exposed to frequent physical impacts (furniture, foot traffic, equipment). Higher impact resistance prolongs service life and reduces maintenance.

name: Reduced material cost
rationale: Cost pressure on construction materials pushes toward cheaper alternatives (e.g., vinyl vs. metal corner beads), especially in large-scale projects.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Metal corner beads in damp environments (bathrooms, kitchens, exterior walls) require corrosion resistance to prevent rust bleeding through paint.

name: adequate structural support for wall finishes
rationale: Interior wall framing must provide sufficient rigidity and straightness to support drywall attachment without cracking or bowing over time.

name: minimised thermal bridging through framing
rationale: Metal or timber studs can conduct heat across the building envelope; interior wall framing design decisions (e.g., spacing, material) affect thermal performance, particularly on exterior-facing interior walls.

name: reduced material cost of framing members
rationale: Cost pressure drives decisions on stud spacing (e.g., 24" o.c. vs 16" o.c.), gauge/thickness of metal studs, and grade of lumber to minimise overall construction budget.

name: improved acoustic separation between rooms
rationale: Framing configuration — stud spacing, staggered studs, resilient channels, and double-layer construction — directly influences sound transmission class (STC) ratings for interior partitions.

name: maximised usable floor area
rationale: Thinner wall framing assemblies (e.g., 2x4 vs 2x6, or slim metal stud profiles) compete with the need for deeper cavities, creating a pressure to minimise wall thickness to preserve interior space.

name: improved structural continuity
rationale: Expansion joints must effectively transfer lateral loads while accommodating movement; improved continuity ensures structural stability across the joint.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Expansion joints can act as thermal bridges if not properly insulated; minimising this improves energy performance and prevents condensation.

name: adequate movement capacity
rationale: The joint must accommodate thermal expansion/contraction and building sway to prevent cracking or damage; sufficient movement capacity is the primary design function.

name: limited acoustic leakage
rationale: Expansion joints can transmit sound between spaces; restricting acoustic leakage is important for interior wall assemblies in occupied buildings.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Horizontal sliding windows often have less effective seals than casement windows. There is a design pressure to increase thermal insulation performance, e.g., through double/triple glazing, thermal breaks in the frame, or improved weatherstripping.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: The sliding mechanism typically has a less airtight seal than hinged windows. A key design pressure is to minimise uncontrolled air leakage around the sash interfaces and tracks.

name: Enhanced ease of operation
rationale: Sliding windows are chosen for user-friendly horizontal operation. Design pressure exists to ensure smooth gliding with low friction (e.g., roller systems, low-maintenance tracks) so the window remains easy to open and close.

name: Restricted water penetration
rationale: Horizontal sliding windows are vulnerable to rainwater ingress at the meeting stile and bottom track. Design pressure to limit water penetration via weeps, sloped sills, and overlapping profiles.

name: improved ventilation efficiency
rationale: Pivot windows can be opened at various angles, allowing controlled airflow direction and improved natural ventilation compared to standard sliding windows.

name: reduced effective opening area
rationale: When a pivot window opens, the sash protrudes into the opening, partially obstructing the clear opening area and reducing the effective free ventilation area compared to the full frame size.

name: higher ease of cleaning access
rationale: Horizontal or vertical pivot windows can rotate fully, allowing both sides of the glass to be cleaned from inside the building, which increases maintenance convenience.

name: limited weather sealing performance
rationale: The pivot mechanism and central hinge design can make it more difficult to achieve consistent compression seals around the entire perimeter compared to casement or tilt-turn windows, potentially reducing weather tightness.

name: restricted insect screen integration
rationale: The inward or outward swing path of a pivot window makes it challenging to install standard insect screens without obstructing the window operation.

name: Improved ventilation performance
rationale: Jalousie/louvre windows are designed with adjustable slats that allow fine control of airflow. The design pressure is to optimise the ventilation performance by increasing the angle and size of openings when natural ventilation is desired.

name: Reduced water infiltration
rationale: A primary design concern for louvre windows is preventing rain and moisture entry through the slats. Design pressures push toward minimising water ingress via tighter seals, overhangs, or slat geometry.

name: Enhanced privacy control
rationale: The adjustable slats of jalousie windows allow occupants to control sightlines and privacy by angling the louvres, creating a design pressure to improve this adjustable screening capability.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Louvre slats can be angled to block direct solar radiation while still permitting airflow. There is a design pressure to minimise unwanted solar heat gain through the window assembly.

name: Improved thermal insulation
rationale: Folding/bi-fold windows have extensive glazing and multiple panel junctions, creating thermal bridging and heat loss risks. Design decisions often push for improved (e.g., double/triple glazing, thermally broken frames) to meet energy codes.

name: Higher structural rigidity
rationale: The folding mechanism and wide spans of bi-fold windows create structural challenges. Design decisions must push for higher rigidity to resist wind loads and prevent sagging or mechanism failure.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: The multiple interlocking panels of folding windows are prone to air leakage at seals and joints. Design decisions aim to minimise infiltration to maintain indoor comfort and energy performance.

name: Optimised sightline profile
rationale: For aesthetic and visibility reasons, there is pressure to achieve optimised (slim) frame sightlines so that the folded-open view is maximised, but this competes with structural/thermal requirements.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Window hinges and hardware are exposed to moisture and environmental conditions; higher corrosion resistance ensures long-term functionality and prevents failure.

name: Higher load-bearing capacity
rationale: Hinges must support the weight of window sashes; greater load capacity is needed for larger or heavier window types to prevent sagging or binding.

name: Reduced friction/wear
rationale: Lower friction between moving parts of hinges and hardware extends service life and ensures smooth operation over repeated opening and closing cycles.

name: Adequate adjustability
rationale: Sufficient adjustability in hinges allows for proper alignment during installation and compensates for building settling or minor manufacturing tolerances.

name: higher thermal insulation
rationale: Operable glazing panels (sashes) are a primary envelope element where heat loss occurs; increasing thermal insulation (e.g., via double/triple glazing, low-E coatings, insulated frames) reduces heat transfer and improves energy performance.

name: reduced air leakage
rationale: Operable sashes are a common source of air infiltration at the junction between the sash and frame; reducing air leakage through better weatherstripping, tighter tolerances, and improved seals is critical for thermal comfort, energy efficiency, and preventing condensation.

name: improved structural rigidity
rationale: The sash must resist wind loads and operational forces without excessive deflection; improved structural rigidity ensures the panel remains functional, airtight, and safe under design wind pressures.

name: reduced weight
rationale: A lighter sash reduces strain on hinges, friction stays, and operating hardware, making the window easier to open/close and reducing long-term wear; this is particularly important for larger operable panels.

name: Reduced operational force
rationale: The crank mechanism should require low manual effort to operate, especially for accessibility and ease of use. High crank resistance is undesirable.

name: Increased mechanical durability
rationale: The mechanism undergoes repeated use and must resist wear, corrosion, and fatigue over the building's lifespan.

name: Reduced mechanism size / footprint
rationale: A compact operator is preferred to minimise visual intrusion and fit within slim window frame profiles, though this may conflict with mechanical leverage requirements.

name: Improved window sash operability
rationale: The window balance system directly controls the ease of opening and closing the window sash. A well-tensioned, properly matched balance mechanism increases operability by counterbalancing the sash weight, reducing effort required.

name: Reduced risk of sash drift or slam
rationale: Window balance systems (spiral balances, block-and-tackle, or constant-force coils) are specifically designed to prevent uncontrolled sash movement. A properly functioning system decreases the chance of the sash drifting closed or slamming shut under gravity.

name: Enhanced long-term cycle durability
rationale: The balance system undergoes repeated tension/compression cycles over the life of the window. Material selection, spring fatigue resistance, and nylon/steel component quality directly affect how many open-close cycles the system can withstand before failure.

name: Increased natural ventilation effectiveness
rationale: Larger window openings improve cross-ventilation and passive cooling, reducing reliance on mechanical systems.

name: Reduced heat gain and solar penetration
rationale: Smaller or fewer openings limit direct solar gain and heat ingress, improving thermal comfort and energy efficiency in hot climates.

name: Greater structural rigidity for glass panel support
rationale: The solid core provides structural support for the glass panel; greater rigidity is needed to prevent glass deflection or breakage under wind load or impact.

name: Reduced overall weight for easier operation
rationale: Solid core with glass panel can be heavy; weight reduction pressure exists for hinge durability and ease of manual operation, though solid core inherently adds weight.

name: Improved thermal insulation performance
rationale: The glass panel in the door creates a thermal weak point; there is design pressure to improve insulation via double/triple glazing or low-E coatings to meet building energy code requirements.

name: Enhanced impact resistance
rationale: The glass panel introduces fragility; design pressure exists to use tempered or laminated glass and robust edge fixings to resist impact in high-traffic applications.

name: Increased structural rigidity for rebate integrity
rationale: The glazing rebates in a door frame require sufficient structural rigidity to hold glass panels securely without deformation, preventing glass breakage and ensuring weather sealing.

name: Reduced moisture ingress at rebate joints
rationale: Rebates where glazing sits are critical moisture penetration points; design pressure exists to minimise water entry through sealant or gasket failures around the glass.

name: Greater dimensional stability for rebate depth
rationale: Consistent rebate depth and squareness are essential for proper glass setting and glazing bead retention; thermal and moisture movements create pressure to maintain dimensional precision.

name: Reduced closing force
rationale: The door closer must not apply excessive force that would make the door difficult to open or create safety hazards, especially for accessibility compliance (ADA).

name: Increased closing power
rationale: Sufficient closing power is needed to overcome door weight, wind pressure, and HVAC stack effects to reliably close and latch the door.

name: Enhanced durability
rationale: Door closers experience repetitive cycling and must resist wear, corrosion, and fluid leakage over the service life.

name: Reduced size/compactness
rationale: Concealed closers especially need to fit within door/frame profiles; smaller mechanism size aids concealment and aesthetic integration.

name: Higher load-bearing capacity
rationale: Hinges, especially continuous/piano hinges on doors or panels, must bear the weight of the door/panel repeatedly. Increased load capacity ensures structural integrity and prevents sagging or failure over time.

name: Reduced friction and wear
rationale: Lower friction at the hinge pin interface reduces wear over repeated cycles, prolonging hinge life and maintaining smooth operation. This is especially important for high-use doors.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Hinges exposed to exterior or humid environments require better corrosion resistance (e.g., stainless steel or coated finishes) to avoid rusting and binding.

name: Minimised installation misalignment
rationale: Poor alignment during installation causes binding, uneven gaps, and premature wear. Design pressure to reduce misalignment leads to better tolerance specifications and quality control.

name: Improved security resistance
rationale: The lock/latch set with key cylinder is a primary security component; design pressure exists to increase its resistance to forced entry, picking, and bumping.

name: Reduced mechanical wear and failure
rationale: Frequent use creates wear on latch and cylinder mechanisms; design aims to minimise friction, sticking, and internal component degradation over time.

name: Enhanced ease of operation
rationale: Users require smooth key insertion, rotation, and latch retraction without excessive force; low-friction mechanisms and precise tolerances support usability.

name: Limited key duplication risk
rationale: Design pressure to restrict unauthorised key copying through patented keyways or restricted blank distribution, particularly in high-security contexts.

name: Increased grip accessibility
rationale: Back-to-back door pulls on double-acting or paired doors must provide sufficient grip diameter and clearance for all users, including those with limited hand dexterity. Building codes (e.g., ADA, EN 17210) specify minimum clearances and lever/pull dimensions.

name: Reduced pull protrusion (projection from door face)
rationale: The back-to-back configuration must minimise excessive projection that could catch on clothing, cause injury in corridors, or interfere with adjacent hardware. This is a safety and clearance constraint.

name: Optimised load-transfer symmetry between paired pulls
rationale: Back-to-back pulls share a common mounting through the door. The design must ensure symmetric load transfer so that neither side bears disproportionate stress during repeated pulling, preventing loosening or failure.

name: Improved durability for high-traffic areas
rationale: Kick plates protect the bottom of doors from scuffs, impacts, and abrasion in high-traffic corridors and rooms. A design pressure is to increase (improve) the durability and impact resistance of the kick plate material to withstand repeated foot traffic, cart impacts, and cleaning equipment.

name: Reduced protrusion for safety and aesthetics
rationale: Kick plates must be mounted flush or with minimal protrusion to avoid being a tripping hazard and to maintain a clean visual appearance. There is a design pressure to reduce (minimise) the thickness or edge profile of the kick plate.

name: Greater corrosion and moisture resistance
rationale: In environments with frequent mopping, cleaning, or exposure to moisture (e.g., restrooms, kitchens, entryways), metal kick plates may corrode. A design pressure is to increase corrosion resistance through material selection (e.g., stainless steel, anodised aluminium, or durable plastic) or protective coatings.

name: Increased daylight penetration depth
rationale: Light shelves are designed to bounce daylight deeper into a room, so there is a design pressure to increase the depth of daylight penetration to improve natural lighting and reduce artificial lighting needs.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: Light shelves block direct sun near the window and reflect light onto the ceiling, reducing glare for occupants near the facade.

name: Optimised light shelf geometry for solar angle
rationale: The angle, width, and position of a light shelf must be optimised relative to the local solar altitude and facade orientation to maximise useful daylight reflection.

name: Reduced cooling load
rationale: By shading the window zone and reducing solar heat gain while still admitting daylight, light shelves contribute to lower cooling energy demand.

name: Increased daylight penetration
rationale: Light-directing louvers are designed to redirect sunlight deeper into interior spaces, increasing daylight penetration and reducing reliance on artificial lighting.

name: Reduced glare
rationale: By redirecting and diffusing incoming sunlight, light-directing louvers help reduce direct glare for building occupants, improving visual comfort.

name: Reduced solar heat gain
rationale: Light-directing louvers can be angled to block direct solar radiation while admitting daylight, thereby reducing cooling loads on the HVAC system.

name: Increased natural light penetration
rationale: A light well/atrium is designed to channel daylight into surrounding spaces; deeper or wider wells increase daylight penetration into adjacent areas.

name: Reduced heat loss through glazing
rationale: Atriums often have extensive glazing which can be a source of thermal loss; designing for lower U-values or smaller glazed areas reduces heat loss.

name: Improved stack ventilation effect
rationale: A tall atrium can act as a solar chimney, drawing air through adjacent spaces via stack effect; increased height and proper opening design enhance natural ventilation.

name: Greater structural load capacity
rationale: Larger or taller atriums require stronger structural frames to support glazing, walkways, and lateral loads.

name: sufficient structural strength
rationale: The bracket and support assembly must have adequate strength to carry the dead load of the lightshelf plus any additional live loads (e.g., maintenance access, snow accumulation if exterior). Insufficient strength would lead to failure or excessive deflection.

name: optimised corrosion resistance
rationale: If made of ferrous metals (steel brackets, fasteners) and exposed to humidity or exterior conditions, corrosion resistance is critical to maintain long-term structural integrity and avoid staining adjacent building surfaces.

name: restricted thermal bridging
rationale: Penetrations through the building envelope for bracket attachments can create thermal bridges. The assembly design should minimise conductive heat transfer through brackets to preserve envelope thermal performance.

name: Increased thermal insulation from small divided lights
rationale: Small divided lights (munitins/mullions) create more framing members, which reduce the overall glass area and increase the thermal bridging, so there is a pressure to improve/optimize insulating performance (e.g., double/triple glazing, low-e coatings) to compensate for the divided-light aesthetic.

name: Reduced light transmission due to divided-light frame members
rationale: The grid of small divided lights includes mullions/muntins that block a portion of the glazing area, reducing daylight transmission. This creates a design pressure to maximize the effective glass-to-frame ratio to maintain adequate daylighting.

name: Higher structural wind load resistance required for divided-light configuration
rationale: Small divided lights typically use a grid frame system that must resist wind loads across multiple smaller panes. There is a pressure to ensure adequate structural capacity in the frame members and glazing seals to withstand wind pressures without failure.

name: Improved thermal performance
rationale: Small-pane double-hung windows typically use many individual panes and have higher frame-to-glass ratio, making them less thermally efficient than larger-pane or modern assemblies. There is a design pressure to increase (improve) thermal performance through options like low-E coatings, insulated glass, or weatherstripping upgrades.

name: Reduced air infiltration
rationale: Double-hung windows are prone to air leakage at the meeting rail and sash interfaces. Small-pane configurations with many muntins create additional joints. There is a design pressure to decrease (reduce) air infiltration via improved gaskets, compression seals, or sash locks.

name: Greater structural adequacy for wind load
rationale: Individual small panes of glass must resist wind pressures without breakage, and the overall frame must withstand design wind loads. This creates pressure for greater (increased) structural adequacy in glazing thickness and frame reinforcement.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through frame
rationale: Fixed window assemblies with small panes and muntins/mullions have more framing per unit area, increasing thermal bridging. Design pressure is to reduce this heat loss through frame improvements.

name: Improved structural rigidity for wind load resistance
rationale: Small-pane fixed windows often have more dividing members, which can increase overall stiffness. However, design pressure exists to ensure adequate structural rigidity against wind loads, especially for larger overall assemblies.

name: Reduced air infiltration at frame joints
rationale: More frame-to-glass and muntin/mullion joints are present with small panes, creating more potential leak paths. Design pressure is to minimise air leakage through these many joints.

name: Optimised daylight transmission despite smaller panes
rationale: Smaller panes and more framing reduce the overall glass area and can limit daylight entry. Design pressure exists to optimise the glazing and frame proportions for adequate natural light.

name: Increased structural rigidity for small-pane retention
rationale: Small-pane window sashes require sufficient rigidity to securely hold individual panes of glass without flexing or loosening over time, especially under wind loads.

name: Reduced thermal bridging through sash frames
rationale: The multiple muntins and frame elements in a small-pane sash create many thermal bridges; minimizing these improves energy performance.

name: Reduced sash weight for operability
rationale: Small-pane sashes are inherently heavier due to additional muntin bars and more glass edge seals, so minimizing weight is important for ease of opening and to reduce wear on hardware.

name: Improved load transfer capacity
rationale: A coped joint (beam cope) has reduced cross-section at the flange/web, creating stress concentrations. Engineering principles dictate designing for increased load capacity through reinforcement or better detailing to prevent web buckling or fracture at the cope.

name: Reduced stress concentration at cope notch
rationale: The cope cut introduces sharp re-entrant corners that act as stress raisers, which can initiate fatigue cracks. Design pressure is to minimise these stress concentrations via smooth transitions, adequate radii, or weld improvements.

name: Sufficient cope hole size for erection clearance
rationale: The cope geometry must provide adequate clearance for bolting or welding during steel erection while not excessively weakening the section — a balance driven by constructability and structural performance.

name: Reduced risk of edge damage
rationale: The corner guard's primary function is to protect inside/outside corners from impact damage. A half-inch profile provides a physical barrier that reduces damage to the underlying wall corner.

name: Improved impact resistance
rationale: The half-inch thickness of the corner guard increases its ability to absorb and resist impacts, making the wall assembly more durable in high-traffic areas.

name: Minimised visual protrusion
rationale: A half-inch corner guard is relatively slim, which reduces its visual prominence on the wall compared to larger guards, supporting a cleaner architectural aesthetic.

name: increased shear strength
rationale: Scarf joints are used to join timber end-to-end; their primary structural requirement is to develop sufficient shear strength along the sloped glue line or mechanical fastener plane to resist axial forces without splitting.

name: reduced joint slip
rationale: Minimising relative displacement (slip) between the two spliced members is critical for the joint to behave as a continuous member under load.

name: minimised stress concentration at scarf tips
rationale: Sharp transitions at the termination of the scarf create stress risers that can initiate cracks; a longer scarf ratio or rounded geometry reduces this effect.

name: improved spectator comfort
rationale: Bench seating in stadiums creates pressure to increase comfort for spectators during extended events, driving ergonomic design considerations such as cushioning, back support, and spacing.

name: maximised seating capacity
rationale: Stadium operators typically face pressure to maximize the number of seats within a given footprint, which directly influences bench dimensions, row spacing, and layout density.

name: reduced cost per seat
rationale: Bench seating is often chosen over individual seats for its lower per-seat cost; there is continuous pressure to minimize material and installation expenses.

name: limited maintenance requirements
rationale: Stadium seating is exposed to weather and heavy use, creating pressure to use durable, low-maintenance materials (e.g., coated metal, weather-resistant plastics) to reduce long-term upkeep.

name: increased seating capacity
rationale: Bleacher systems are fundamentally designed to provide spectator seating; a key design pressure is to maximise seating capacity within the available footprint and structural constraints.

name: reduced structural load
rationale: Bleacher structures must minimise dead and live loads for safety and cost-efficiency, driving lighter materials and optimised structural design.

name: improved spectator sightlines
rationale: A core architectural requirement for bleachers is ensuring unobstructed views for all spectators, which influences tiering, riser height, and layout.

name: enhanced accessibility compliance
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA) require accessible seating, paths, and egress from bleacher systems, creating a strong design pressure.

name: restricted footprint area
rationale: The available site area or venue geometry often constrains how far the bleacher system can extend horizontally, limiting its overall footprint.

name: optimised sightlines from Theater Box Seat to stage
rationale: Theater box seats are designed to provide superior viewing angles; sightline optimization is a primary design pressure.

name: adequate seating capacity within Theater Box Seat
rationale: Box seats need to accommodate a small group comfortably; there is a pressure to have sufficient seating without overcrowding the limited space.

name: reduced obstruction between Theater Box Seat and stage
rationale: Box seats are positioned to avoid columns, railings, or other structural elements blocking the view; minimizing visual obstruction is a key design driver.

name: enhanced acoustic isolation for Theater Box Seat
rationale: Theater box seats may require tailored acoustics — good sound projection from stage while minimizing reverberation or noise within the enclosed box.

name: Sufficient row spacing for egress and accessibility
rationale: Building codes (e.g., IBC) mandate minimum row spacing to ensure safe egress and wheelchair accessibility.

name: Greater legroom for spectator comfort
rationale: Larger tread depth improves occupant comfort and experience in assembly seating.

name: Reduced overall row spacing to maximise seating count
rationale: Tighter spacing allows more rows within a fixed floor plate, increasing venue capacity and revenue.

name: Improved legibility for wayfinding
rationale: The plate's primary function is to support wayfinding; higher legibility (font size, contrast, tactile features) directly improves user orientation.

name: Reduced visual clutter on the plate
rationale: Minimising extraneous graphics or text on the plate helps users quickly locate seat numbers and directions, reducing cognitive load.

name: Sufficient durability for repeated tactile contact
rationale: Plates at seat locations may be touched, leaned on, or cleaned repeatedly; adequate material strength and wear resistance extend service life.

name: Restricted size to fit seat geometry
rationale: The plate must be compact enough to integrate into seat-rail or armrest profiles without interfering with seating function or occupant comfort.

name: Reduced weight
rationale: A fold-down seat mechanism must be lightweight to allow easy manual folding and unfolding by users, and to minimise structural load on the mounting surface (e.g., wall or floor).

name: Improved durability
rationale: The mechanism undergoes repeated folding cycles and bears occupant weight, so increased durability in hinges, latches, and moving parts is required to ensure long-term reliability and safety.

name: Reduced complexity
rationale: A simpler mechanism with fewer moving parts is less prone to jamming or failure, easier to manufacture, and more cost-effective for a component that must operate reliably over many cycles.

name: Adequate load capacity
rationale: The mechanism must support the static and dynamic loads of a seated occupant without deformation or failure, requiring sufficient strength in latch, pivot, and frame elements.

name: enhanced comfort and space
rationale: VIP/premium seating sections typically demand greater legroom, wider seats, and higher comfort standards compared to standard sections, driving a design pressure to increase spatial allocation and premium finishes.

name: improved sightlines and proximity
rationale: Premium seat sections are strategically positioned for optimal viewing angles (e.g., centerline, mid-tier), creating a pressure to maximize visual and acoustic quality of the space.

name: restricted public access
rationale: VIP areas often require controlled access, separation from general admission zones, and dedicated circulation, exerting pressure to limit or restrict general public permeability into the space.

name: higher structural load capacity
rationale: Premium seating may involve heavier, more luxurious seating fixtures, larger spacing, and potential for additional amenities (tables, bars), increasing structural loading requirements.

name: adequate companion seating proximity
rationale: Building codes and accessibility standards (e.g., ADA, ANSI A117.1) require that companion seats be immediately adjacent to wheelchair spaces so the wheelchair user and companion can sit together. This drives the need for adequate proximity and arrangement of the companion seat relative to the wheelchair space.

name: minimised obstruction of companion seat path
rationale: Companion seats must have clear, unobstructed access paths and cannot be placed where they block aisles, egress, or circulation routes. This constrains seat placement and orientation.

name: sufficient companion seating dimensions
rationale: Companion seats must have minimum width, depth, and armrest configuration to be usable by a companion. Standards specify dimensional requirements that drive design decisions about the seat's size.

name: increased structural stability
rationale: A bench backrest must resist loads from users leaning back; greater structural stability ensures safety and durability under lateral and vertical forces.

name: reduced material weight
rationale: Lighter backrest components reduce load on supporting bench frame and ease installation, but must be balanced against strength requirements.

name: improved ergonomic comfort
rationale: A backrest should provide comfortable lumbar support and appropriate recline angle for prolonged sitting; this directly shapes its curvature, height, and inclination design decisions.

name: adequate seating width
rationale: Bench seats need sufficient width to comfortably accommodate users, driven by human factors and comfort requirements.

name: adequate seating height
rationale: Bench seat height must be appropriate for sitting (typically ~450mm) to ensure comfort and proper leg positioning.

name: sufficient structural load capacity
rationale: The bench must be designed to support expected loads (users, occasional extreme loads) without failure.

name: reduced material cost
rationale: Budget constraints push toward minimizing material usage and cost in bench construction without compromising safety.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: Bench leg/base anchors must withstand vertical loads (weight of bench and occupants) and lateral loads (e.g., leaning, seismic, wind). Higher load capacity ensures safety and durability.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Anchors are often exposed to outdoor or moist environments; corrosion resistance (via galvanisation, stainless steel, or coatings) is needed to prevent degradation and maintain holding strength over time.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler installation procedures (e.g., fewer steps, standard tools) lower labour cost and error risk. This affects anchor type selection (e.g., wedge anchors vs. adhesive anchors).

name: Adequate pull-out resistance
rationale: Anchors must resist upward/uplift forces that could pull them out of the substrate (concrete, wood, or ground). This is a fundamental requirement for base anchor performance.

name: adequate armrest width for user comfort
rationale: Armrests must be wide enough to provide comfortable forearm support for users, preventing pressure points and accommodating various arm sizes.

name: restricted armrest height to avoid elbow interference
rationale: Excessively high armrests can cause shoulder elevation and discomfort, while excessively low ones provide no support. Height is constrained to ergonomic norms.

name: reduced protrusion to avoid obstruction
rationale: Armrests that extend too far beyond the bench profile can obstruct circulation paths or interfere with adjacent benches/furniture, so protrusion must be minimised.

name: sufficient structural strength for loading
rationale: Armrests must withstand static and dynamic loads (e.g. pushing down to stand up, leaning sideways) without failure, requiring adequate material thickness and connection strength.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: As a freestanding system, the bench must resist tipping, sliding, and lateral loads without connection to a wall or floor anchors. Increased structural stability ensures safety under live loads (people sitting/leaning) and environmental loads (wind, seismic).

name: Reduced footprint intrusion
rationale: An entry bench must not obstruct circulation paths, door swing zones, or egress routes. A smaller footprint or minimised projection into walkways is a key design pressure for entryway furniture.

name: Adequate seating surface depth
rationale: The bench seat must be deep enough for comfortable sitting (typically 400-500mm). Insufficient depth makes seating unusable, while excessive depth wastes space — a specific ergonomic pressure acting on this bench type.

name: Enhanced durability for high-traffic entry
rationale: Entry benches face heavy use with wet shoes, bags, and frequent sitting/standing cycles. Greater resistance to wear, moisture damage, and impact from dropped items is a specific design pressure.

name: Increased storage capacity
rationale: The primary purpose of a mudroom storage bench is to provide storage (for shoes, coats, bags, etc.). There is a design pressure to increase the storage capacity of the bench to accommodate household needs, especially in family-oriented homes.

name: Optimised space utilisation
rationale: Mudrooms are often compact transitional spaces, so the bench must efficiently use available footprint and vertical space, driving design toward built-in or modular configurations that maximise usable area without overcrowding.

name: Improved durability
rationale: The bench will face heavy daily use, wet/muddy gear, and frequent sitting/standing. This creates a design pressure for robust materials (e.g., hardwood, marine-grade plywood, sealed finishes) and sturdy construction to withstand wear, moisture, and weight loads.

name: Eliminated clutter visibility
rationale: There is a pressure to design the bench with concealed or organised storage (e.g., cubbies with doors, closed baskets, drawers) to keep the mudroom looking tidy and reduce visual clutter, a key functional-aesthetic requirement for entryway furniture.

name: adequate seating capacity
rationale: Entry vestibule benches serve waiting, sitting, or temporary resting near an entrance. A design pressure exists to provide enough seating (benches) for users entering/exiting, without overcrowding the transition space.

name: reduced circulation obstruction
rationale: Benches in a vestibule must not block the primary circulation path between inner and outer doors. There is a pressure to minimise the footprint or intrusion of the bench zone into pedestrian flow.

name: limited bench depth
rationale: Vestibules are typically shallow transitional spaces; deep seating protrusions compete with clearance zones. Depth of bench zone should be constrained to preserve minimum passage width.

name: enhanced durability for high-traffic
rationale: Entry vestibule benches endure heavy use, weather exposure (from door openings), and dirt/moisture. The design pressure calls for stronger, more durable materials and construction.

name: Improved fire resistance rating
rationale: As a fire-rated assembly, the primary design pressure is to increase its fire resistance rating (e.g., minutes of fire exposure withstand) to meet code-required fire separation or compartmentation requirements.

name: Reduced combustibility of materials
rationale: Fire-rated assemblies require materials with limited or no combustibility to prevent flame spread and maintain structural integrity during fire conditions, driving selection of non-combustible or fire-retardant materials.

name: Adequate structural stability under fire exposure
rationale: The bench assembly must maintain its load-bearing capacity and dimensional stability when exposed to high temperatures during a fire, ensuring it does not collapse or deform in a way that compromises the fire barrier.

name: Restricted thermal conductivity
rationale: Low thermal conductivity of the bench assembly materials prevents heat transfer through the fire-rated element, which is critical for maintaining temperature limits on the unexposed side during a fire test.

name: adequate clearance space
rationale: Accessible bench clearance zones require sufficient space (typically 30x48 inches of clear floor space) to allow wheelchair users to approach and use the bench. Building codes and ADA standards mandate adequate clearance for accessibility.

name: Enhanced structural stability
rationale: The sitting wall bench must have adequate structural stability to safely support the weight of people sitting on it, resisting overturning and settlement.

name: Reduced tripping hazard
rationale: The bench should be designed with minimal protrusions or edge hazards at ground level to prevent pedestrians from tripping over the base.

name: Optimised seating height and depth
rationale: Ergonomic design pressure to ensure the bench's seat height and depth are comfortable for typical human use (e.g., seat height around 430-460 mm).

name: improved structural stability
rationale: The backrest must resist forces from users leaning back, requiring increased structural stability to prevent tipping or failure.

name: increased ergonomic comfort
rationale: As a seating component, the backrest angle, height, and contour exert pressure toward greater ergonomic comfort for users.

name: limited material weight
rationale: The cantilevered or attached nature of a wall backrest calls for reduced weight to minimise load on the supporting wall structure.

name: improved ergonomic support
rationale: Armrests on sitting walls need to provide comfortable support for users' arms while seated. Higher-quality ergonomic design (appropriate height, width, padding) increases usability and user satisfaction.

name: reduced protrusion hazard
rationale: Armrests that protrude excessively into walking paths or have sharp edges create safety hazards. Design should minimise these risks through careful geometry and placement.

name: increased structural stability
rationale: The armrest must be securely anchored to the wall structure to withstand lateral loads from users pushing down or leaning on it without detaching or failing.

name: adequate structural support for seating load
rationale: As a sitting wall, the planter must bear live loads from people sitting on it, so adequate structural capacity is required to prevent collapse or damage.

name: sufficient soil volume for plant health
rationale: The planter portion must hold enough soil volume to sustain the intended plants, influencing the wall's depth and dimensions.

name: restricted wall height for comfortable seating
rationale: Sitting walls require a constrained height range (typically 16-20 inches) for ergonomic seating comfort, limiting how tall the planter wall can be.

name: minimised water leakage risk
rationale: The combined seating and planting function creates risk of water seeping through the wall structure, so leakage must be prevented through proper waterproofing and drainage.

name: adequate illumination for safety and wayfinding
rationale: Wall-mounted sitting area lighting must provide sufficient illumination for people to safely navigate and use the seating area, especially during evening hours.

name: reduced glare discomfort for seated users
rationale: Since people sit facing or adjacent to wall lighting, excessive brightness or poorly shielded fixtures cause visual discomfort; glare must be minimized.

name: lower energy consumption
rationale: Building energy codes and sustainability goals typically impose limits on lighting power density, pushing toward efficient fixtures and lower wattage.

name: Reduced protrusion from wall
rationale: Sitting wall outlets must be flush or minimally protruding to avoid discomfort or damage when someone sits against or leans on the wall.

name: Adequate clearance around outlet
rationale: Building codes require minimum clearances around electrical outlets for safe plug insertion and heat dissipation; applies to any outlet including those on sitting walls.

name: Higher durability and weather resistance
rationale: Sitting walls are often exterior or semi-exposed elements; outlets on them need enhanced durability against moisture, UV, and physical abrasion from people sitting.

name: increased lateral earth pressure resistance
rationale: As a retaining wall, it must resist lateral earth pressures from retained soil; increased resistance ensures structural stability against sliding and overturning.

name: reduced hydrostatic pressure buildup
rationale: Water accumulation behind the wall creates hydrostatic pressure that can cause failure; adequate drainage to reduce this pressure is critical for wall integrity.

name: adequate structural stability for seating loads
rationale: As a sitting wall, it must support vertical live loads from people sitting; sufficient structural capacity and stability under these loads is required.

name: reduced frost heave effects
rationale: Freeze-thaw cycles in the retained soil can exert additional pressures on the wall; limiting frost heave through proper foundation depth or insulation is important for long-term durability.

name: improved structural stability
rationale: As a freestanding wall not tied to a primary structure, it must resist overturning, sliding, and settlement under its own weight and lateral loads (wind, accidental leaning). Increased stability ensures safety and durability.

name: adequate seating comfort
rationale: As a sitting wall, its height, width, cap profile, and material finish directly affect user comfort. Adequate dimensions and smooth finish improve ergonomic suitability for seating.

name: reduced material cost
rationale: Material quantity directly impacts project budget. Optimizing wall cross-section and using locally available materials while maintaining structural and functional requirements reduces overall cost.

name: minimised thermal cracking risk
rationale: Masonry or concrete freestanding walls exposed to outdoor temperature fluctuations are prone to thermal cracking. Proper joint spacing, reinforcement, and material selection mitigate this risk to maintain appearance and structural integrity.

name: Increased structural stability
rationale: As a curved wall, its geometric curvature provides inherent structural rigidity compared to a flat wall, resisting lateral loads and potential overturning. The curvature creates arch-like action, distributing compressive forces more effectively.

name: Reduced material stress concentrations
rationale: The smooth continuous curve of the sitting wall eliminates sharp corners where stress concentrations typically develop, resulting in more uniform load distribution across the structure.

name: Improved seating ergonomics
rationale: The curved form of the sitting wall can accommodate more natural human seating postures and encourage social interaction by creating concave gathering spaces, influencing the wall's height, depth, and surface finish decisions.

name: Improved structural stability
rationale: Terraced sitting walls function as retaining structures on slopes; increased structural stability ensures safety against sliding and overturning under soil and live loads.

name: Adequate drainage provision
rationale: Proper drainage behind and beneath the wall prevents hydrostatic pressure buildup, which is critical for the wall's longevity and structural performance.

name: Reduced lateral earth pressure
rationale: Minimising lateral earth pressure (through drainage, soil reinforcement, or geometry) reduces the structural demand on the wall section.

name: Enhanced user comfort
rationale: As a sitting surface, the wall's finish, thermal properties, and ergonomic dimensions directly affect comfort of users.

name: Limited wall height
rationale: Wall height is constrained by structural limits, safety railing requirements, and code restrictions for unguarded seating surfaces.

name: adequate thermal insulation
rationale: As a heated sitting wall, adequate thermal insulation is needed to retain heat and ensure efficient operation, preventing heat loss to the surrounding structure or ground.

name: reduced heat loss
rationale: Minimising thermal bridging and heat loss is critical for an outdoor or semi-outdoor heated element to maintain comfortable surface temperature and avoid excessive energy consumption.

name: sufficient structural capacity
rationale: The wall must structurally support both its own weight and the live loads from people sitting on it, especially with embedded heating elements or pipes.

name: increased cable tension
rationale: Increased tension in the steel cables is required to maintain structural stability and prevent sagging under load conditions.

name: reduced cable corrosion risk
rationale: Corrosion degrades steel cables over time; protective measures (coatings, galvanisation, maintenance) aim to minimise corrosion risk and extend service life.

name: reduced cable fatigue failure
rationale: Cyclic loading (wind, thermal, vibration) can cause fatigue in steel cables; design details and damping strategies aim to reduce fatigue stress concentrations.

name: Higher compressive strength
rationale: Compression struts and masts must withstand axial compressive loads without buckling, so higher material compressive strength is a key design pressure.

name: Reduced slenderness ratio
rationale: A lower slenderness ratio (effective length / radius of gyration) reduces the risk of Euler buckling, which is the primary failure mode for slender compression members.

name: Adequate buckling resistance
rationale: Buckling is the critical limit state for compression struts; design must ensure sufficient buckling resistance through section geometry, bracing, and material properties.

name: Minimised eccentricity of load
rationale: Load eccentricity induces secondary bending moments in compression members, which reduces axial load capacity; minimising eccentricity is a fundamental design pressure.

name: Increased tension capacity
rationale: Edge catenary cables must be designed with sufficient tension capacity to support the roof membrane and resist wind uplift, snow loads, and self-weight. The cable's tension capacity directly determines its structural adequacy.

name: Reduced sag under load
rationale: Sag in the catenary cable must be limited to maintain proper roof drainage, avoid ponding, and ensure the architectural profile is maintained. Excessive sag can compromise structural performance and water runoff.

name: Optimized corrosion resistance
rationale: The edge catenary cable is exposed to environmental conditions requiring adequate corrosion protection (e.g., galvanization or stainless steel) to ensure long-term durability and avoid premature failure.

name: Increased load-bearing capacity
rationale: Foundation anchors must resist uplift, overturning, and lateral forces from mast structures under wind and self-weight; higher load-bearing capacity directly governs their design adequacy.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: Anchors embedded in concrete or soil are exposed to moisture and chemical attack; corrosion resistance is essential for long-term durability and structural integrity.

name: Reduced anchor displacement
rationale: Minimising movement/slip of anchors under cyclic or sustained loads is critical to maintain mast alignment and structural stability; excessive displacement leads to serviceability failure.

name: Sufficient embedment depth
rationale: Adequate depth into the ground or foundation block is required to develop full pullout resistance and prevent uplift failure in masts.

name: Increased structural capacity for roof loads
rationale: The perimeter ridge or compression ring must transfer roof loads (dead, live, wind, snow) to vertical supports. Adequate compressive strength is required to prevent buckling or failure.

name: Reduced deflection under asymmetric loading
rationale: A compression ring or ridge under uneven loads (e.g., unbalanced snow, wind suction) must limit out-of-plane deflection to maintain structural integrity and prevent progressive collapse.

name: Optimised connection detailing for continuity
rationale: The compression ring/ridge relies on continuous load paths through joints. Optimised connections ensure moment and axial force transfer without localised failure or excessive stress concentrations.

name: Reduced thermal bridging at perimeter
rationale: As a perimeter structural element, the compression ring can create a thermal bridge. Design pressures aim to minimise heat loss through this element to meet energy performance targets.

name: Sufficient stiffness for diaphragm action
rationale: The perimeter ring/ridge often acts as the edge member of a roof diaphragm. Adequate in-plane stiffness is needed to distribute lateral loads (wind, seismic) to vertical lateral-force-resisting elements.

name: Adequate capacity for rainwater handling
rationale: Gutters and downpipes must have sufficient cross-sectional area and slope to handle expected rainfall intensities without overflowing, a core hydraulic engineering requirement.

name: Reduced risk of blockage and clogging
rationale: Blockages from leaves and debris are a primary failure mode; design pressures include preventing obstructions through guards, larger diameters, or self-cleaning geometries.

name: Sufficient structural support and attachment strength
rationale: Gutters and downpipes must be securely fastened to withstand wind loads, snow loads, and the weight of accumulated water and debris without detachment.

name: Reduced corrosion and material degradation
rationale: Constant exposure to water and weathering necessitates corrosion-resistant materials (e.g., galvanised steel, aluminium, PVC) or protective coatings to ensure longevity.

name: adequate structural support for soil and water weight
rationale: A planter box must support the dead load of soil, water, and plants, plus live loads from maintenance. This structural adequacy is a core engineering requirement.

name: sufficient drainage and waterproofing
rationale: Planter boxes require proper drainage to prevent waterlogging of plants and waterproofing to protect the underlying building structure from moisture damage.

name: adequate soil depth for plant root growth
rationale: The depth of the planter box must accommodate root systems of selected plants, which influences the physical dimensions of the planter box design.

name: restricted water leakage risk
rationale: Water leakage from planter boxes can damage building finishes and structure, so design must minimize leakage paths through proper sealing and detailing.

name: limited overall weight on structure
rationale: Saturated soil is very heavy; the planter box design should constrain weight to what the supporting structure can safely bear, possibly by using lightweight soil media.

name: increased structural stability
rationale: Planter walls must withstand soil lateral pressure and retained moisture weight. Increased structural stability ensures the wall does not bulge, crack, or overturn under these loads.

name: increased drainage capacity
rationale: Proper drainage reduces hydrostatic pressure behind the planter wall. Increased drainage capacity prevents water accumulation that could compromise wall integrity.

name: reduced soil leakage
rationale: Planter walls need to contain growing medium without losing soil through joints or weep holes. Reduced soil leakage maintains the planter's function and prevents staining or damage to adjacent surfaces.

name: increased moisture resistance
rationale: Constant contact with damp soil and irrigation water requires planter walls to have increased moisture resistance to prevent material degradation, efflorescence, or freeze-thaw damage.

name: adequate thermal expansion accommodation
rationale: Temperature fluctuations cause expansion and contraction. Adequate accommodation of thermal movement prevents cracking in planter walls, especially when constructed of concrete or masonry.

name: Improved water distribution coverage
rationale: Raised planters require even water distribution across the planting area; irrigation systems are designed to ensure adequate coverage to all plants, preventing dry spots.

name: Reduced water waste
rationale: Efficient irrigation design minimises runoff and overspray, especially in raised planters where drainage and water retention are critical considerations.

name: Greater system integration with planter structure
rationale: The irrigation layout must be coordinated with the planter's geometry, material, and drainage provisions to function effectively within the architectural design.

name: Increased structural load capacity
rationale: The mounting system must bear the weight of vegetation, growing media, irrigation, and live loads from maintenance. Structural safety demands adequate load capacity.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: Continuous exposure to irrigation water, humidity, soil/root contact, and fertilisers accelerates corrosion, requiring materials with high corrosion resistance.

name: Reduced maintenance access constraints
rationale: The system must allow practical access for plant replacement, pruning, and irrigation servicing; overly constrained access increases long-term costs and safety risks.

name: Adequate drainage provision
rationale: Stagnant water behind the facade causes structural damage, mould, and impaired plant health. Proper drainage paths must be integrated into the mounting design.

name: Optimized thermal expansion accommodation
rationale: The system must accommodate differential thermal movements between the building structure, the mounting frame, and the growing medium without causing stress or detachment.

name: Increased water efficiency
rationale: Water efficiency is a core design pressure for irrigation systems, especially in green wall contexts where water conservation is critical. The system should be designed to maximise water use efficiency through drip irrigation, recirculation, and smart controls.

name: Reduced water consumption
rationale: Minimising total water usage is a key design pressure driven by sustainability goals and operational cost reduction. This pressure influences system sizing, component selection (e.g., low-flow emitters), and control strategies.

name: Adequate pressure delivery
rationale: The system must deliver water at sufficient pressure to reach all plants distributed vertically across the green wall, especially at upper elevations. This pressure must be adequate to overcome elevation head and friction losses.

name: Reduced maintenance requirements
rationale: Green wall irrigation systems are often difficult to access for maintenance. Design pressures push toward minimising clogging risk, using self-cleaning components, and reducing the frequency and complexity of maintenance interventions.

name: Enhanced plant health support
rationale: The irrigation system must support optimal plant health by delivering appropriate water volumes and schedules tailored to plant species, wall orientation, and microclimate conditions. This drives design toward precision irrigation and zoning capabilities.

name: adequate soil volume for root growth
rationale: A planter must hold sufficient soil volume to support healthy root development of the plants it contains; this is a fundamental physical requirement.

name: reduced waterlogging risk
rationale: Planters require drainage provisions to prevent water accumulation that would harm plant roots; this is an engineering design pressure.

name: reduced weight for structural support
rationale: The planter's weight (including soil and water) must be limited to stay within the structural capacity of the supporting surface or building structure.

name: sufficient drainage capacity
rationale: Adequate drainage outlets and weep holes are needed to allow excess water to escape, preventing root rot and structural water damage.

name: Increased inflow capacity
rationale: The inlet must handle peak stormwater runoff volumes. Greater hydraulic capacity (via larger grate area, deeper sump, or more inlets) is needed to prevent ponding and surface flooding during design storm events.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Debris accumulation (leaves, litter, sediment) blocks inlet grates and reduces effective flow area. Design features such as wider bar spacing, curved vanes, or trash racks aim to minimise blockages and maintain performance.

name: Reduced maintenance frequency
rationale: Accessibility for cleaning and the self-cleaning geometry of the inlet (e.g., scouring velocity, debris bypass) reduces the required intervention frequency by maintenance crews.

name: Adequate structural load capacity
rationale: The inlet cover and frame must withstand traffic loads (pedestrian, vehicular) without collapse or excessive deflection. Using stronger materials or thicker sections ensures structural integrity.

name: Improved stormwater infiltration
rationale: A core function of permeable interlocking concrete pavement is to allow stormwater to infiltrate through the surface. Design decisions often aim to increase infiltration capacity through proper joint material selection (e.g., open-graded aggregate) and base layer design.

name: Reduced surface runoff volume
rationale: Permeable pavement systems are specifically designed to reduce stormwater runoff by capturing rainfall and allowing it to percolate into the subbase. This is a primary design pressure driving the selection of appropriate aggregate layers and storage capacity.

name: Higher structural load-bearing capacity
rationale: Despite being permeable, the pavement must still support traffic loads. There is a design pressure to increase structural capacity through adequate paver thickness, base course depth, and subgrade preparation, especially for vehicular applications.

name: Reduced clogging and maintenance frequency
rationale: Clogging of joints by sediment reduces permeability over time. Design decisions such as joint width, aggregate gradation, and use of offset joints are influenced by the pressure to minimize clogging frequency and ease maintenance.

name: Adequate freeze-thaw durability
rationale: In cold climates, the pavement system must resist freeze-thaw damage. This creates a design pressure to ensure adequate durability through appropriate concrete mix design, air entrainment, and proper base drainage to prevent ice lens formation.

name: improved compressive strength
rationale: Higher compressive strength in the mortar joint improves load-bearing capacity and structural integrity of the masonry assembly.

name: enhanced bond adhesion
rationale: Stronger adhesion between brick and mortar prevents delamination and improves shear resistance and durability.

name: reduced water permeability
rationale: Lower water ingress through the joint prevents freeze-thaw damage, efflorescence, and moisture-related deterioration.

name: minimised mortar shrinkage
rationale: Reduced shrinkage cracking in the mortar joint maintains watertightness and prevents loss of bond with bricks.

name: adequate joint width consistency
rationale: Uniform joint width is essential for aesthetic regularity and even load distribution across the masonry wall.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: Ornamental cladding is typically a non-structural skin where lighter materials (e.g., aluminium composite panels, thin stone veneers) reduce structural load on the building frame and simplify attachment.

name: Improved weather resistance
rationale: Ornamental cladding serves as the building envelope's outer layer, so it must resist moisture ingress, UV degradation, and thermal cycling to protect the building interior and maintain appearance.

name: Reduced installation complexity
rationale: Simpler attachment systems and modular panel sizes lower labour costs, erection time, and risk of installation defects for ornamental cladding systems.

name: Increased aesthetic expressiveness
rationale: As an ornamental (decorative) element, the cladding's visual qualities — colour, texture, pattern, and articulation — are primary design drivers that influence material selection, joint detailing, and panel geometry.

name: improved acoustic performance
rationale: Ornamental ceilings often incorporate acoustic panels or tiles to improve sound absorption in spaces like auditoriums, lobbies, or meeting rooms.

name: reduced weight load
rationale: Ceiling components must be lightweight to minimize structural load on supporting beams and hangers, especially for ornamental designs that may use heavy materials like plaster or metal.

name: enhanced fire resistance
rationale: Building codes require ceiling assemblies to meet fire-resistance ratings to prevent fire spread through ceiling plenums.

name: Improved structural load-bearing capacity
rationale: Ornamental columns and pilasters, while decorative, still serve a structural role in many classical and neoclassical buildings. There is an engineering pressure to increase their load-bearing capacity to ensure they adequately support entablatures, arches, or other superstructure elements.

name: Enhanced aesthetic detail and proportion
rationale: As an ornamental element, there is a strong architectural pressure to enhance the visual detail, fluting, capital ornamentation, and proportional correctness (e.g., following classical orders) of the column or pilaster to achieve the desired stylistic effect.

name: Reduced material usage and weight
rationale: There is an engineering/economic pressure to minimise the material quantity (stone, concrete, or wood) used in ornamental columns and pilasters to reduce cost, weight, and foundation loading, while still maintaining the desired appearance.

name: Limited corrosion or weathering deterioration
rationale: For exterior ornamental columns and pilasters, there is a design pressure to minimise deterioration from moisture, freeze-thaw, pollution, and salt exposure to preserve the decorative surface and structural integrity over time.

name: Reduced structural load on frieze & entablature
rationale: Structural engineering requires that the weight of the ornamental frieze and entablature be minimised to reduce load on supporting columns and walls, especially in classical and neoclassical architecture where these elements are non-structural decorations.

name: Enhanced ornamental detailing
rationale: Architectural design intent often calls for richer, more elaborate carving, sculptural relief, and decorative mouldings on the frieze and entablature to achieve aesthetic prominence, proportion, and visual hierarchy.

name: Improved material durability for weather exposure
rationale: As exterior components, friezes and entablatures require greater resistance to weathering, freeze-thaw cycles, and moisture penetration, driving selection of durable stone or treated materials and adequate thickness.

name: Reduced cost of craftsmanship
rationale: Budget constraints and the declining availability of skilled stone-carvers create pressure to limit the complexity, depth, or extent of ornamental carving on the frieze and entablature, sometimes favouring prefabricated or simplified profiles.

name: Improved structural integrity
rationale: Balustrades and handrails must resist lateral loads (e.g., crowd pushing, leaning) per building codes; increased structural integrity ensures safety and code compliance.

name: Enhanced corrosion resistance
rationale: As an ornamental component often exposed to weather or condensation, improved corrosion resistance (via material selection or coating) extends service life.

name: Limited deflection under load
rationale: Excessive deflection feels unsafe and violates serviceability limits in guardrail design standards; restricted deflection is a governing design pressure.

name: Adequate graspability for handrail
rationale: Handrail profiles must be designed for ergonomic grip and accessibility code compliance (e.g., ADA requirements); sufficient graspability is a key design driver.

name: Eliminated sharp edges
rationale: Safety codes require that balustrade components have smooth, rounded edges to prevent injury; sharp edges must be prevented in fabrication.

name: improved structural stiffness
rationale: As a component that spans between structural supports, increased stiffness reduces deflection under wind load and improves the mullion/transom's ability to support glazing without excessive flexure.

name: reduced thermal bridging
rationale: Ornamental mullions and transoms often penetrate or bridge the thermal envelope; minimising conductive heat transfer through the metal frame improves overall facade thermal performance.

name: adequate load transfer capacity
rationale: The mullion and transom assembly must transfer wind and gravity loads (from glazing and self-weight) to the primary structure; sufficient capacity prevents serviceability or strength failures.

name: Improved water drainage capacity
rationale: Gutters and downspouts must have adequate capacity to handle rainwater runoff from the roof. Increasing drainage capacity prevents overflow, water damage to the building facade, and foundation issues.

name: Reduced clogging risk
rationale: Ornamental gutters and downspouts are susceptible to debris accumulation (leaves, dirt) which can block water flow. Minimising clogging risk is essential for functional performance and to avoid maintenance issues or water overflow.

name: Improved corrosion resistance
rationale: As an exterior metal component exposed to rain and moisture, the gutter and downspout material must resist corrosion to maintain both its ornamental appearance and structural integrity over time.

name: Reduced material weight
rationale: The weight of the gutter and downspout system affects the structural load on its mounting brackets and the building facade. Lighter materials reduce fastening demands, though this must be balanced against durability and ornamental quality.

name: Reduced structural load on voussoir
rationale: As an ornamental (non-structural) element, the keystone and voussoir are designed to carry minimal or no structural load, unlike their functional counterparts in true arches.

name: Increased aesthetic prominence of keystone
rationale: The keystone in an ornamental context is often emphasized visually through size, color, or carving to serve as a focal point in the facade composition.

name: Improved weathering resistance of stonework
rationale: Ornamental stone elements at exposed positions (e.g., above openings) require enhanced resistance to rain, freeze-thaw cycles, and pollutant deposition to maintain appearance and integrity.

name: Reduced material usage in voussoir
rationale: Since the voussoirs are decorative rather than load-bearing, they can be thinner or made from lighter materials than structural arch stones, reducing material consumption.

name: Reduced structural load on pediment & gable
rationale: Pediments and gables are often ornamental components mounted on building façades. There is an engineering pressure to minimise dead load (weight) and wind load on these elements to reduce the risk of detachment or structural failure, especially when they project above the roof or wall line.

name: Enhanced decorative detailing
rationale: As an ornamental feature, there is a design pressure to increase the visual prominence, complexity, and aesthetic quality of the pediment/gable to contribute to the building's architectural expression, style (e.g., Classical, Gothic, Renaissance), and curb appeal.

name: Increased weathering resistance
rationale: Being exposed to rain, sun, and wind as a projecting top element, there is a pressure to improve material durability and water shedding (e.g., through proper flashing, drip edges, and materials like stone or treated wood) to prevent deterioration.

name: Limited construction cost for ornament
rationale: Ornamental elements can be budget-sensitive; there is often a pressure to restrict expenditure on non-structural decorative features in favour of core building functions, leading to simplified profiles or less expensive materials.

name: Increased structural stability for wind resistance
rationale: Parapets and balustrades are exposed to wind loads, especially on rooftops and balconies. Structural stability must be adequate to resist lateral wind pressures without failure or excessive deflection.

name: Reduced weight for structural loading
